2.title: Proverbs 2 — The Search for Wisdom and Its Rewards

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Seeking Wisdom Like Silver: The Conditions and Consequences
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 2 is a single extended poem structured as a conditional argument: if you receive, treasure, incline your ear, apply your heart, call out, and seek wisdom as silver—then you will understand the fear of the LORD, then the LORD will give wisdom, then discretion will guard you, then wisdom will deliver you from the evil man and the forbidden woman, then you will walk in the way of the good and remain in the land. The entire chapter is one massive if-then, structured to show that wisdom's benefits are real but require serious pursuit.
verseByVerse.theology: The 'seek wisdom like silver' image (vv. 3–4) is one of the most important in Proverbs. Silver is not found by accident or by passive waiting; it requires systematic, sustained, directed effort—excavation, sifting, refining. Wisdom requires the same. This immediately qualifies any notion that wisdom is simply inherited through osmosis or religious attendance. It must be actively sought. Yet the paradox is that the seeking is itself a gift: verse 6 declares that the LORD gives wisdom. Human seeking and divine giving are not in competition; they are the two sides of the same coin.
verseByVerse.examples: The two dangers Wisdom protects against (the evil man, vv. 12–15, and the forbidden woman, vv. 16–19) will recur throughout Proverbs 1–9. Both represent fundamental threats to the young person: external violence and internal enticement. Wisdom guards against both—not by isolation from them but by forming the person so thoroughly in the way of the good that neither temptation has a foothold. Kidner: 'Wisdom does not merely forbid; it forms—and the formed person finds that what once tempted no longer attracts.'

verseByVerse.quote: My son, if you receive my words and treasure up my commandments with you, making your ear attentive to wisdom and inclining your heart to understanding; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything in this chapter hangs on the word if, and the reader should know at the outset that it will not be resolved until v. 5. In Hebrew the whole of Proverbs 2 is a single sentence: four verses of conditions, then then, and the sentence keeps going to the end of the chapter. It is built that way on purpose. Wisdom is being described as something with a shape — this, and then this follows.

The first two conditions are ordinary and easily missed. Receive my words — the verb is laqah, to take, the word you would use of a hand closing round something. Then treasure up my commandments with you, and that is tsaphan, to hide away, to store somewhere safe. Not a merchant handling silver across a counter all day. A merchant who puts it somewhere at night.

Hold on to tsaphan, because it will come back in v. 7 with God as the subject, and the echo is the point of the chapter.

Then the two organs: making your ear attentive and inclining your heart. The heart in Hebrew is not the seat of feeling as against thought; it is the whole inner man — mind, will and affections in one word. And the verb incline means to stretch or lean, the way you tilt a jug toward a cup. It is a deliberate, slightly uncomfortable posture. Nothing pours into a vessel sitting flat and upright.

So four verbs and no shortcut in any of them. This is the answer to a question most Christians have quietly asked: why, after years of sermons, does so little of it seem to have gone in? Verse 1 suggests it did go in. It was received and never stored, and what is not stored is not there on the day it is needed.

verseByVerse.quote: yes, if you call out for insight and raise your voice for understanding, if you seek it like silver and search for it as for hidden treasures, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The conditions intensify, and the first pair are startling. If you call out for insight and raise your voice for understanding. That is not the language of study. It is shouting. In ch. 1 Wisdom was crying aloud in the street; now the seeker is doing the same thing back, and the picture is of a man who wants something badly enough to be heard wanting it.

Which is to say: wisdom is asked for, not merely worked for. James says it in plain terms — if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach (James 1:5). Without reproach. He does not sigh at the request.

And then the other half, and it is all labour. If you seek it like silver and search for it as for hidden treasures. Silver in the ancient world was not picked up. It was found by identifying the right rock, cutting it out, hauling it up, crushing it, and burning it until what you wanted separated from what you did not. Every stage was hot, dark and slow, and the yield of a day’s work would sit in a cupped hand.

Nobody does that by accident, and nobody does it out of general good intentions. A man mines because he has decided there is silver in that hill.

Which gives a very ordinary test. If a friend asked what you are currently doing to get wisdom — not what you believe, what you are doing — could you name it? A time, a book, a person you have asked to tell you the truth about yourself, a habit that costs you something? Verses 3 and 4 describe a man shouting and digging. It is difficult to mistake that man for one who has merely been meaning to get round to it.

verseByVerse.quote: then you will understand the fear of the LORD and find the knowledge of God. For the LORD gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and understanding; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here at last is the then, and it is not what a reader expects after four verses of mining. Then you will understand the fear of the LORD and find the knowledge of God.

Not: then you will make better decisions. Not: then your life will go more smoothly. The prize at the end of the shaft is God himself. All that digging, and what comes up in the cupped hand is a Person — which reframes the whole enterprise, because it means Proverbs is not a manual for managing life successfully. It is a book about getting to know somebody.

And then v. 6, which turns the chapter completely over. For the LORD gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and understanding.

Read that against the four verses that preceded it. The seeker has been told to receive, store, listen, lean, shout and dig — and the moment he arrives, he is told that the thing he has been mining for is a gift, and always was. The silver was not in the hill because geology put it there.

These two truths are held together here without embarrassment, and any account of the Christian life that drops one of them goes wrong quickly. Drop the giving and you get a religion of effort, in which a man is finally responsible for producing his own transformation and can never be sure he has done enough. Drop the seeking and you get a passivity that waits for God to do something to it, and mistakes drift for trust. Waltke puts the relation exactly: the seeking is itself the evidence that God has already begun to give.

In the fullness of time the mouth of God said everything at once. The Word that was with God and was God took flesh and lived among us, and in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (John 1:1, 14; Colossians 2:3). The man who has been digging for hidden treasure is told at last where the seam runs — and it runs to a manger, and a carpenter’s bench, and a cross, and the whole vein is Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: he stores up sound wisdom for the upright; he is a shield to those who walk in integrity, guarding the paths of justice and watching over the way of his saints. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
He stores up sound wisdom for the upright. That is tsaphan again, the word from v. 1. The son was told to store God’s words away somewhere safe; now it turns out God has been doing the same thing with wisdom, and doing it first.

The picture is of a store already laid in. Not wisdom that will be manufactured when somebody asks, but a supply put by in advance for people who are not yet there to collect it — which is the way this book keeps describing God, always a step ahead of the man who thinks he initiated the search.

Then three protective images stacked one on another: a shield, a guarding of the paths, a watching over the way. And the shield is worth a moment. In the ancient world, a shield was not worn. It was carried, and a man behind a shield is a man who has stopped trying to be armoured himself and has got behind something else.

Notice, too, what is guarded. Not the man — the paths of justice, and the way of his saints. God is described as protecting a route rather than an individual, and the difference matters enormously in practice. A man is safe on that road and not elsewhere, and this book is under no obligation to protect him while he walks somewhere else.

The last phrase names who these people are: his saints, in Hebrew his hasidim — those bound to God by covenant loyalty, and named after the word for his own steadfast love, hesed. They are not called the clever or the successful. They are called by his love for them, and the loyalty in the name is his before it is ever theirs.

verseByVerse.quote: Then you will understand righteousness and justice and equity, every good path; for wisdom will come into your heart, and knowledge will be pleasant to your soul; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A second then, and the chapter widens. Then you will understand righteousness and justice and equity, every good path. Those are the three words from 1:3, and their return here is deliberate: what was announced as the book’s aim is now promised as the reader’s possession.

But the interesting word is understand. He does not merely know that fairness is required — anybody knows that. He can see, in a situation that has not been labelled, which course is the fair one. That is a different faculty, and it is the one most people lack when it matters. The moral difficulty in real life is almost never identifying that honesty is good. It is recognising, at four o’clock on a Thursday, that what is being proposed is dishonest.

Then v. 10 explains how the change happens, and it is not by rules. Wisdom will come into your heart, and knowledge will be pleasant to your soul.

Pleasant. That is the word the whole chapter has been walking toward. There is a way of living rightly that is entirely joyless — a man doing what he ought while wanting something else, holding the line by grip strength alone. It is real obedience and it is exhausting, and it usually fails eventually, because nobody grips for forty years.

What is promised here is a change of taste. Not a stronger will, but a different appetite — the point at which honesty stops being the expensive option and starts being the one the man actually prefers. That is what formation is, and it is why Proverbs spends so much time on the young: appetites are far easier to plant than to replace.

verseByVerse.quote: discretion will watch over you, understanding will guard you, delivering you from the way of evil, from men of perverted speech, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the protection begins to work, and notice who is doing it. Discretion will watch over you, understanding will guard you. The virtues themselves are the sentries. God’s way of keeping this young man safe is not to fence the road but to change the traveller.

Both words are precise. Discretion is mezimmah, the capacity to think a thing through to its end before it happens — foresight, the ability to see Thursday from Monday. Understanding is binah, from a root meaning to separate: the ability to tell two things apart that look alike.

Those are exactly the two faculties a person needs against the danger named next: men of perverted speech. Foresight, because their offer is always about the next five minutes and never about the year. Discernment, because what they say sounds very like the truth. If it did not, nobody would be taken in.

Say this to anyone raising children, or teaching young Christians, or trying to keep himself out of trouble. The instinct is to build a list — do not go there, do not read that, do not talk to him. Lists are not useless; the father in ch. 1 gave one. But a list can only cover the situations somebody thought of in advance, and life presents the other kind.

What Proverbs is after is the man who can smell it. Not the man who has memorised which offers are bad, but the man in whom something goes quiet and watchful when the conversation turns, before he could tell you why. That is not suspicion and it is not worldly-wisdom. It is what a formed conscience does, and God gives it in the ordinary way — by long exposure to what is true, until the false has a taste.

verseByVerse.quote: who forsake the paths of uprightness to walk in the ways of darkness, who rejoice in doing evil and delight in the perverseness of evil, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The men of perverted speech are now described, and their history is given in a single verb. They forsake the paths of uprightness. They did not begin in the dark. They knew the right road, walked on it, and left.

That is a more uncomfortable account than the one we prefer. It is comfortable to imagine that corrupt men were always corrupt — a separate species, raised elsewhere, nothing to do with us. Proverbs says they were on the path. Whatever else they are, they are people who once knew better, and every one of them passed through a stage that felt entirely reasonable at the time.

Then the descent is traced in three steps, and the third is the terrible one. First they walk in the ways of darkness. Then they rejoice in doing evil. Then they delight in the perverseness of evil — not in the profit of it, not in what it gets them, but in the wrongness itself.

That last stage is the one to understand, because it explains something readers find baffling in the news and occasionally in people they know. A man does not usually arrive at cruelty by wanting to be cruel. He arrives by doing a wrong thing, surviving it, feeling the odd exhilaration of having got away with something, and finding the next one easier. Conscience is not removed in one operation. It is worn down, and then the wearing down itself begins to feel like freedom.

And the mercy in the verse is where it starts. Every one of these men was once on the path. So the question this passage puts is not whether a reader is capable of ending there — it takes that for granted. It is whether he has begun, in some small and defensible way, to step off.

verseByVerse.quote: men whose paths are crooked, and who are devious in their ways. So you will be delivered from the forbidden woman, from the adulteress with her smooth words, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Men whose paths are crooked, and who are devious in their ways. The word for crooked describes something twisted out of its proper shape, and it is applied here not to their destination but to their method. They do not merely go to the wrong place. They get there dishonestly, and they would be devious about the route to a good place too. Crookedness has become the way the man moves.

Then, with no transition, the second danger of these nine chapters arrives: so you will be delivered from the forbidden woman, from the adulteress with her smooth words. She is a real figure and the danger is real; chapters 5 to 7 will give her three chapters to herself.

And note where the danger is located: smooth words. Not beauty. The weapon named here is speech — flattery, sympathy, the sentence that says you are not appreciated at home, the conversation that keeps going after it should have stopped.

Which explains why the deliverance in this chapter is by discernment rather than by willpower. By the time a man is deciding, he has usually been losing for months. The battle is fought and settled much earlier, in a hundred small exchanges that nobody would have called a temptation, and the man who can hear what is happening in a conversation is already most of the way to being safe.

verseByVerse.quote: who forsakes the companion of her youth and forgets the covenant of her God; for her house sinks down to death, and her paths to the departed; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the woman’s own story, and it is told with more compassion than is usually noticed. She forsakes the companion of her youth and forgets the covenant of her God.

The companion of her youth is her husband, and the phrase carries a whole history: the two of them young, the years since, everything built together. Whatever else is happening in this chapter, a marriage is being described from the inside, and the word for what she does to it is the same word used of the men in v. 13. She forsakes. The adulteress and the violent man are doing the identical thing to two different roads.

Then the phrase that lifts the whole subject out of the merely personal: she forgets the covenant of her God. Her marriage was not a private arrangement between two people who may revise it. God was a party to it, and Malachi says so explicitly — the LORD was witness between a man and the wife of his youth (Malachi 2:14). That is why adultery is treated in Scripture as something more than a broken promise. A third party was standing there when it was made.

And notice the verb: forgets. Not denies, not repudiates. Nobody in this verse has argued herself out of the covenant. She has simply, over time, stopped having it in mind — which is how most vows are broken, and why remembering is treated all through Scripture as a spiritual discipline rather than a mental knack.

Then the geology of it: her house sinks down to death, and her paths to the departed. The house is not stormed. It sinks — the ground under it gives way slowly, while the walls look exactly as they did. That is precisely how this sin works, and it is why the people inside it are so often the last to know.

verseByVerse.quote: none who go to her come back, nor do they regain the paths of life. So you will walk in the way of the good and keep to the paths of the righteous. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
None who go to her come back, nor do they regain the paths of life. That is a severe sentence, and it needs handling carefully, because there are readers who have gone and who will read this line as a door closing behind them.

So say plainly what it is not. It is not a statement that God cannot or will not forgive adultery. He forgives it. The Bible is embarrassingly full of restored adulterers, and one of them wrote half the Psalms; another was told neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more (John 8:11). Anyone in this book who turns is received, and there is no asterisk on the offer.

What the verse describes is the character of the road itself. Proverbs speaks in observations about how things normally run, and the observation here is grim and accurate: this particular path has almost no natural turnings. It entangles. It requires lying, and the lying requires more lying, and each month makes the cost of turning round higher than it was — until men who fully intend to go back discover that intending is not the same as arriving. Left to itself, nobody comes back. That is the honest word, and softening it would be a cruelty to the man standing at the entrance.

But left to itself is the whole qualification, and it is the difference between despair and hope. Nobody walks back up that road under his own power. People are carried back up it, and they are carried by the one who came looking for them. If you are reading this from somewhere on that path, the verse is not telling you it is too late. It is telling you that you will not get out by resolving to, and that you need a rescuer rather than a resolution — which is the truest thing anybody could say to you.

And then v. 20, which is where the chapter has been going all along: so you will walk in the way of the good and keep to the paths of the righteous. Wisdom does not merely pull a man out of something. It puts him on a road. Deliverance that has no destination attached is not what is on offer here, and a man who is only running away from a thing will, in the end, run out of energy and go back.

verseByVerse.quote: For the upright will inhabit the land, and those with integrity will remain in it, but the wicked will be cut off from the land, and the treacherous will be rooted out of it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The long sentence that began in v. 1 finally comes to rest, and it lands on land. The upright will inhabit the land, and those with integrity will remain in it, but the wicked will be cut off from the land.

To an Israelite this was the most concrete promise available. The land was the visible proof of the covenant — actual soil, with boundary stones and olive trees and a family name attached to it, given by God and held from him. To inhabit it was to be at home in the world God had made, in the place he had put you, with nothing outstanding between you and him.

The word that holds the good half together is remain. Not arrive — remain. Anybody can have a good year. What Proverbs is pointing at is the man who is still there in twenty years, still married, still trusted, still recognisably the same person, having weathered the things that removed other people. That is what wisdom is finally for, and it is a slower and less glamorous prize than the young man in ch. 1 was being offered by the gang.

Jesus took this promise and did not shrink it. Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5) — not a strip of Judea but the whole of it, and not for the strong who take it but for the meek who are given it. Every acre the wicked seized in Proverbs 1 by ambush ends up, in the end, belonging to the people who never grasped at anything.

And he is himself the upright man who inhabits the land. He alone kept the covenant that the woman in v. 17 forgot and the men in v. 13 forsook; he alone walked every step of the way of the good; and he was cut off — the word of v. 22, spoken over the only man in history it did not fit — cut off out of the land of the living for the transgression of a people who deserved the uprooting (Isaiah 53:8). The wise man inherits the land because the righteous man was rooted out of it.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>My son, if you receive my words and treasure up my commandments with you,<sup>2</sup>making your ear attentive to wisdom and inclining your heart to understanding;<sup>3</sup>yes, if you call out for insight and raise your voice for understanding,<sup>4</sup>if you seek it like silver and search for it as for hidden treasures,<sup>5</sup>then you will understand the fear of the LORD and find the knowledge of God.<sup>6</sup>For the LORD gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and understanding;<sup>7</sup>he stores up sound wisdom for the upright; he is a shield to those who walk in integrity,<sup>8</sup>guarding the paths of justice and watching over the way of his saints.<sup>9</sup>Then you will understand righteousness and justice and equity, every good path;<sup>10</sup>for wisdom will come into your heart, and knowledge will be pleasant to your soul;<sup>11</sup>discretion will watch over you, understanding will guard you,<sup>12</sup>delivering you from the way of evil, from men of perverted speech,<sup>13</sup>who forsake the paths of uprightness to walk in the ways of darkness,<sup>14</sup>who rejoice in doing evil and delight in the perverseness of evil,<sup>15</sup>men whose paths are crooked, and who are devious in their ways.<sup>16</sup>So you will be delivered from the forbidden woman, from the adulteress with her smooth words,<sup>17</sup>who forsakes the companion of her youth and forgets the covenant of her God;<sup>18</sup>for her house sinks down to death, and her paths to the departed;<sup>19</sup>none who go to her come back, nor do they regain the paths of life.<sup>20</sup>So you will walk in the way of the good and keep to the paths of the righteous.<sup>21</sup>For the upright will inhabit the land, and those with integrity will remain in it,<sup>22</sup>but the wicked will be cut off from the land, and the treacherous will be rooted out of it.

3.title: Proverbs 3 — Trust the LORD; The Protection and Value of Wisdom

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Whole-Life Commands: Trusting God with Everything
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter's first section contains six paired commands, each followed by a promised consequence. Together they form the most comprehensive description of what it looks like to live in dependence on God: keeping his commandments, holding fast to covenant loyalty, trusting him with undivided heart, fearing him and turning from evil, honoring him with firstfruits, and receiving his discipline. The section is the Proverbs equivalent of the Shema: love God with all your heart, soul, and strength.
verseByVerse.theology: The pivotal command is vv. 5–6: 'Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make straight your paths.' This is the anti-thesis of the Proverbs fool, who 'leans on his own understanding' and ends up walking in crooked paths. The command is comprehensive: all your heart (not divided trust), all your ways (not selected domains). God's governance is not partial; neither should human submission be.
verseByVerse.examples: The discipline passage (vv. 11–12) corrects a potential misreading of the preceding blessings: the path of the righteous is not exempt from hardship. God disciplines those he loves—the discipline is itself the evidence of love, not its absence. Hebrews 12:5–6 quotes this passage directly, applying it to the suffering of Christ's followers. The person who receives discipline with faith rather than bitterness is the person who understands the relationship between pain and formation.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, do not forget my teaching, but let your heart keep my commandments, for length of days and years of life and peace they will add to you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
My son, do not forget my teaching, but let your heart keep my commandments. Two dangers, and only one of them is a sin. Forgetting happens to a man; keeping is something he does. The father names both because a life is lost either way, and most lives are lost the first way — nothing repudiated, nothing decided, just a slow evaporation of what was once held.

Then the promise: length of days and years of life and peace they will add to you. Three things — long life, full life, and shalom, which is not calm but wholeness, the state of a life with nothing broken in it and nothing missing.

And here a guard is needed at once, because this promise has been read as a contract and then found to fail. Godly people die young. Job was righteous and lost everything in a fortnight. The wisest man who ever lived was executed at about thirty-three.

Proverbs is not offering a personal guarantee; it is describing the way God has built the world, and the difference is the difference between a climate and a forecast. Say of a country that it is warm and dry, and you have said something true which will not stop you being rained on next Tuesday. Wisdom bends a life toward length and peace. It does not exempt it from a fallen world, and the book itself knows this — it will end up watching the righteous suffer and the wicked prosper and refusing to pretend otherwise.

What is guaranteed, and what the New Testament makes explicit, is that the trajectory is real and it arrives. The long life is longer than this one, and the peace is a peace Christ makes rather than a peace circumstances allow (John 14:27).

verseByVerse.quote: Let not steadfast love and faithfulness forsake you; bind them around your neck; write them on the tablet of your heart. So you will find favor and good success in the sight of God and man. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let not steadfast love and faithfulness forsake you. The two Hebrew words are hesed and emet — loyal covenant love, and dependable truth — and the son should recognise them, because they are the words God used of himself. When God proclaimed his own name to Moses on the mountain, the final phrase was abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (Exodus 34:6).

So the command is more startling than it first appears. The boy is not being told to be nice and honest. He is being told to wear what God is.

Then two images for how. Bind them around your neck — outside, where people can see, the way a man wears something that says whose he is. Write them on the tablet of your heart — inside, cut into the surface, permanent. The pairing is a demand for integrity in the exact sense of the word: one man, not two, with the same thing on the outside and the inside.

And the tablet is not an accidental word. Israel’s covenant was written on tablets of stone, and the tragedy of the Old Testament is that the writing never got any further in than that. Which is why the promise Jeremiah was given is the promise this verse is reaching for and cannot supply: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts (Jeremiah 31:33). Proverbs 3:3 commands the engraving. The gospel performs it.

Then the result: favour and good success in the sight of God and man. Both audiences. It is possible to be well thought of by God and thoroughly disliked by people, and Scripture never promises the crowd’s approval. But the ordinary case is that a man of genuine covenant character is eventually recognised as one, and Proverbs is content to say so.

verseByVerse.quote: Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make straight your paths. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are the best-known words in the book, and familiarity has done them damage. They are quoted on cards and over decisions, and read as a promise that if a man prays hard enough God will tell him which job to take. That is not what they say, and the smaller reading has cost people a great deal of unnecessary anguish.

Start with the verbs. Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding. Lean is the word for putting your weight on something — a stick, a wall, a doorframe. Everybody leans. The question the verse asks is never whether a man will put his weight down, but on what.

And notice what is not being forbidden. Proverbs is a book of thinking; it has just spent two chapters demanding that the reader mine for understanding like silver. It does not say do not use your own understanding. It says do not lean on it — do not make it the thing that takes the load. Use your mind hard, and then put your weight somewhere sturdier than a mind that has been wrong before.

Then in all your ways acknowledge him. The verb is yada, the ordinary Hebrew word for knowing a person, and it is not about consulting God at junctions. It is about the whole road. Most Christians are willing to bring God the two or three large decisions. The verse asks for the ways — plural, all of them, including the ones nobody would think to pray about, which is where a life is actually spent.

And then the promise, which is smaller and better than the one usually claimed. He will make straight your paths. Not: he will show you the route in advance. Straight here means level, made passable, cleared — the word used of preparing a road for a king. He does not hand a man the map. He goes ahead of him and makes the ground walkable.

Which is exactly why the verse cannot be used the way it usually is. It gives no guarantee that a man will be told what to do next, and it gives every guarantee that the road he takes in trust will turn out to have been prepared. Most of the time he will only see the levelling behind him. That is not a defect in the promise. That is what trusting is for.

verseByVerse.quote: Be not wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD, and turn away from evil. It will be healing to your flesh and refreshment to your bones. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be not wise in your own eyes. Of all the ways to fail in this book, this is the one the reader is least likely to detect in himself, because the faculty that would notice it is the faculty that has gone wrong.

The man described here is not arrogant in manner. He may be modest, pleasant and genuinely humble in conversation. What has happened is more interior than that: his own judgment has quietly become the final court. He hears advice and weighs it — against himself. He reads Scripture and assesses it — against himself. Nothing gets in, because everything must first be approved by the thing that needs correcting.

Then the two-part alternative: fear the LORD, and turn away from evil. Those are the same movement seen from two ends, and they are given in this order for a reason. Turning from evil is not the route to fearing God; fearing God is what makes a man turn. Nobody has ever successfully renovated his behaviour while his sense of who God is stayed the same size.

And then a promise that surprises modern readers: it will be healing to your flesh and refreshment to your bones. Not to your soul. Hebrew does not divide a person into a spirit that matters and a body that does not, and it assumes what any doctor now takes for granted — that what a man carries inside him shows up in his body. Bitterness kept for years, fear that never sleeps, a secret that has to be managed daily: these are not merely spiritual conditions.

Which means the fear of the LORD is here presented as, among other things, good for a man. The verse is not embarrassed by that, and neither should the reader be.

verseByVerse.quote: Honor the LORD with your wealth and with the firstfruits of all your produce; then your barns will be filled with plenty, and your vats will be bursting with wine. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Honour the LORD with your wealth and with the firstfruits of all your produce. Money arrives in Proverbs not as a side issue but as a place of worship, and the word that governs it is firstfruits.

The firstfruits were the earliest of the harvest, brought before the rest was in and before anybody knew whether the rest would be any good. That is the whole point of the practice. A man who gives at the end gives out of a known surplus; a man who gives first is making a statement about who he thinks owns the field. And the order is the confession: by the time you have paid everything else and are dividing what is left, you have already said, without meaning to, where God comes in the queue.

Then the promise, and it must be guarded, because it has been turned into an investment scheme. Then your barns will be filled with plenty, and your vats will be bursting with wine.

This is not a mechanism for getting rich, and anyone who preaches it as one has to explain away the apostles, most of the martyrs, and the widow whom Jesus commended for having nothing left (Luke 21:1-4). Proverbs speaks in the language of covenant Israel, where God’s blessing on an obedient nation was visible in barns and vats. The abiding truth underneath is that God is nobody’s debtor and gives back to open-handed people — though he reserves entirely the right to give back something other than money, and he very often does.

The useful test here is not how much a man gives. It is when. Look at the order of payments in an honest month, and the sequence will tell the truth about the heart more accurately than any resolution he has made about generosity.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, do not despise the LORD's discipline or be weary of his reproof, for the LORD reproves him whom he loves, as a father the son in whom he delights. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
My son, do not despise the LORD’s discipline or be weary of his reproof. Two ways of getting this wrong, and they belong to two different sorts of people. To despise is to shrug it off — the hard year meant nothing, God had nothing to do with it, and no lesson was taken. To be weary is the opposite failure: to feel the weight fully and be worn flat by it, until a man stops hoping there is a purpose in it at all.

The second is the more common among people who love God, and the father does not rebuke it harshly. He simply gives a reason to keep going, and the reason is the whole comfort of the passage.

For the LORD reproves him whom he loves, as a father the son in whom he delights. Read that clause slowly, because most sufferers get it exactly backwards. The instinct in hard years is to read pain as evidence of God’s displeasure, or of his absence, or of some fault not yet identified. This verse says the reverse: the discipline is evidence of the love, and — the phrase that does the work — the son in whom he delights. The correction does not interrupt the delight. It comes out of it.

The writer to the Hebrews quotes this passage to a church under real persecution and draws the conclusion the sufferer needs: if you are left entirely alone, that is not a sign of favour (Hebrews 12:5-8). Nobody trains a child who is not theirs.

But say plainly what this does not mean, because it has been used cruelly. It does not mean every hardship is a corrective for a specific sin, and it does not license anybody to inform a suffering person what God is teaching them. Job’s friends took that job and God said they had spoken wrongly of him. The verse is a comfort to be received about oneself, not a diagnosis to be issued about somebody else.

And there is one Son to whom it did not apply, and everything turns on him. He was the Son in whom the Father delighted, publicly and audibly, and what fell on him was not discipline but judgment — not the correction of a beloved child but the punishment of a world. He took the reproof that was not his, so that every stroke falling on the people he died for might be the loving hand of a Father and never again the hand of a judge.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–26 — The Incomparable Value of Wisdom and Its Protection
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter's middle section celebrates wisdom's value (more than silver, gold, or jewels) and its functions (pleasant ways, life, stability, security). Then it grounds wisdom cosmologically: the LORD founded the earth by wisdom; wisdom was the architect of creation. This means that wisdom is not a human invention to be adopted or rejected but the structural principle of reality itself—to be wise is to be aligned with how God made the world to work.
verseByVerse.theology: Verses 19–20 are among the most profound theological statements in Proverbs: God founded the earth by wisdom, established the heavens by understanding, divided the deep by knowledge. Wisdom is not merely useful for navigating life; it is the principle by which God constructed life. This anticipates Proverbs 8:22–31, where Wisdom is present at creation as God's master craftsman. The implication is that rejecting wisdom is not merely impractical; it is working against the grain of the universe itself.
verseByVerse.examples: The security promised in vv. 21–26 is grounded in this cosmic reality. The wise person who trusts God does not need to fear sudden disaster or the ruin of the wicked because they live in alignment with the One who governs all. The LORD is their confidence; his foot will not be caught in a trap. This is not naive optimism but the eschatological confidence of the person who knows the character of the God in whom they trust.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is the one who finds wisdom, and the one who gets understanding, for the gain from her is better than gain from silver and her profit better than gold. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed is the one who finds wisdom. The word is ashre, the same word that opens the Psalter and the Beatitudes — not a wish for someone’s happiness but a verdict on their condition. This is a man to be envied, whatever else is true of him.

And the verb is finds, which sits oddly beside ch. 2’s mining and is meant to. Nobody finds silver without digging, and nobody digs it into existence. Both halves are kept: he worked for it, and it was there to be found, and he did not put it there.

Then the comparison begins, and it runs on for six verses in the language of the market. The gain from her is better than gain from silver and her profit better than gold. Gain and profit — commercial words, chosen deliberately. Wisdom is being priced.

Notice what that does. It refuses to move the argument onto safer ground. The father does not say that money is vulgar and wisdom is spiritual; he says wisdom is the better investment, and invites the comparison on the terms a young man actually uses. Kidner puts it well: Proverbs does not despise money, it relativises it by showing what money cannot do.

And what it cannot do is easy to name once anyone stops to try. It cannot make a family want to be in the room with you. It cannot buy back a reputation, or a decade, or the trust of a son. Every one of those runs on wisdom, and none of them is for sale at any price — which is why the wealthiest man reading this can still be, in the only terms that matter, extremely poor.

verseByVerse.quote: She is more precious than jewels, and nothing you desire can compare with her. Long life is in her right hand; in her left hand are riches and honor. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
She is more precious than jewels, and nothing you desire can compare with her. The comparison has climbed from silver to gold to precious stones, and now it stops comparing and simply closes the door: nothing you desire. Not a category is left out. Whatever it is that a particular reader actually wants — and everybody has one thing he would name if pressed — the verse has already included it and priced it lower.

Then a picture worth seeing clearly. Long life is in her right hand; in her left hand are riches and honour. Wisdom is drawn as a figure with both hands full, approaching the reader.

In the ancient world the right hand was the hand of strength and of the greater gift. So the arrangement is a statement about priority: what Wisdom holds out first and chiefly is life. Riches and honour are in the other hand — genuinely there, genuinely hers to give, and secondary.

That ordering matters, because most people reverse it and then wonder why the trade disappoints. A man will spend the length of his days acquiring what is in the left hand, and discover at the end that he has bought the lesser gift with the greater one. He has paid for riches and honour in years, which is the one currency that does not come back.

And the offer runs the other way round entirely. Take what is in the right hand, and whatever is in the left is thrown in at God’s discretion — which is precisely what Solomon was told when he asked for an understanding mind and was given riches and honour he had not requested (1 Kings 3:13).

verseByVerse.quote: Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace. She is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her; those who hold her fast are called blessed. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace. That sentence has to be defended, because it does not describe how obedience feels on a great many Tuesdays. Doing the right thing is frequently unpleasant, and the peace can be very hard to locate.

The verse is speaking of the road, not the step. Any single stretch of it may be steep. But a man who has walked the way of wisdom for thirty years is living in something the other road cannot produce: nothing hidden, nothing owed, nobody he must avoid, no version of the story he has to keep straight. That is what pleasantness and peace mean here — not an easy day, but a life that is not at war with itself.

And then the image the whole chapter has been building toward. She is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her.

There is only one tree of life in the Bible, and every Israelite knew where it stood. It was in the middle of the garden, and the last thing Genesis says about it is that the way to it was shut and an angel with a flaming sword set to guard the path (Genesis 3:24). That is the human situation in one sentence: the tree is still there, and we are on the outside of it.

So for Proverbs to say that wisdom is a tree of life, and that a man may lay hold of her, is an astonishing claim. Something of what was lost is available again, and available now, to anyone who will take it in both hands.

And Scripture does not leave the picture there. In the last chapter of the Bible the tree stands again, in the middle of the city, its leaves for the healing of the nations, and the way to it is open and never shut (Revelation 22:2, 14). Between the sword at the gate and the open city there stands another tree, on a hill, with a man on it — for cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree (Galatians 3:13). He was hung on the dead tree so that the living one could be given back. The way to it was barred by a sword; it was opened by a spear.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD by wisdom founded the earth; by understanding he established the heavens; by his knowledge the deeps broke open, and the clouds drop down the dew. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD by wisdom founded the earth; by understanding he established the heavens; by his knowledge the deeps broke open, and the clouds drop down the dew.

Suddenly the subject is not personal advice at all. For two verses the father lifts his eyes off his son and looks at the universe, and he does it for a reason that changes how the whole book is read.

The claim is that wisdom is not a human technique for getting through life. It is the thing the world was made with. Foundations, established heavens, springs breaking open, dew forming overnight on cold ground — all of it laid out by the same wisdom being offered here to a young man deciding what to do about his friends.

Which means folly is not merely unwise; it is a collision. A man who lives against wisdom is not breaking an arbitrary rule attached to an otherwise neutral world. He is running across the grain of the actual material of things, and the splintering he experiences is not God intervening to punish him. It is the wood.

And this is where the New Testament takes the passage somewhere Solomon could not see. The wisdom by which the world was founded turned out to be a person. All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made; by him were created all things, and in him all things hold together (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16-17).

So the wisdom that laid the foundations of the earth walked on it. The understanding that established the heavens was carried as a child into Egypt. The knowledge that broke open the deeps slept through a storm on the Sea of Galilee, and stood up, and spoke to the water in the voice that made it. He is the wisdom of God, and the world he holds together was made in his own image of order and beauty — and when it splintered, he did not stand off and let it break. He came down into the grain of it and was broken on it, and put it back together with his own hands.

verseByVerse.quote: My son, do not lose sight of these— keep sound wisdom and discretion, and they will be life for your soul and adornment for your neck. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
My son, do not lose sight of these. The verb is about keeping a thing in view, and it names the danger of the whole chapter. Not rebellion. Losing sight.

Almost nobody abandons wisdom by argument. What happens is that a man gets busy, and the things he once kept in front of him move to the edge of his vision, and then out of it, and he could not tell you which month it happened. He has not changed his mind about anything. He has simply stopped looking at it.

Two things are named for keeping. Sound wisdom is tushiyyah — a word with the flavour of something that works, competence that gets a result. Discretion is mezimmah, the ability to think a thing through to its end before it happens. Between them they describe a man who is both effective and far-sighted, which is a great deal more than being sincere.

Then: they will be life for your soul and adornment for your neck. The necklace is back from 1:9, and the pairing is the same. Inside, they keep him alive; outside, they are the first thing anyone notices. A man properly formed by wisdom does not have to advertise it, any more than a man has to explain the chain around his neck.

verseByVerse.quote: Then you will walk on your way securely, and your foot will not stumble. If you lie down, you will not be afraid; when you lie down, your sleep will be sweet. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the payoff, and it is remarkably ordinary. Then you will walk on your way securely, and your foot will not stumble. If you lie down, you will not be afraid; when you lie down, your sleep will be sweet.

Of all the rewards this chapter has offered — long life, riches, honour, a tree of life — the one it finishes on is a good night’s sleep.

That is not an anticlimax. It may be the most searching test in Proverbs, because sleep is the one part of a man’s life he cannot manage. He can hold himself together all day. He can be competent, pleasant, and entirely convincing about how he is. At two in the morning none of those instruments work, and whatever is actually true about his peace becomes apparent to him, alone, in the dark.

So the diagnostic is simple and nobody else can administer it. What comes for you at two o’clock? A man cannot answer that by deciding what he believes. It answers itself.

And the reason wisdom sleeps is not that it has fewer problems. It is that it has handed the governing of tomorrow to somebody who will be awake. In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety (Psalm 4:8). The only man in the Gospels who is ever recorded sleeping in a crisis was asleep in the stern of a boat that was filling with water, and he was not being careless. He was being Wisdom.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be afraid of sudden terror or of the ruin of the wicked, when it comes, for the LORD will be your confidence and will keep your foot from being caught. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be afraid of sudden terror or of the ruin of the wicked, when it comes. Notice what the verse does not say. It does not say the terror will not come. The clause when it comes sits in the middle of the sentence and concedes the whole thing.

This is characteristic of the Bible’s way with fear, and it is why biblical comfort outlasts the cheerful kind. Scripture almost never reassures by denying the danger. It does not tell a frightened man that the lump is nothing, that the letter will not come, that the marriage will hold. It tells him who will be there when it does.

For the LORD will be your confidence and will keep your foot from being caught. And the word confidence is doing precise work. It is not confidence that something will happen. It is a person occupying the position that self-assurance usually holds — which means the man in this verse is not braver than other men. He is standing somewhere else.

The snare in the second line is a hunter’s trap, hidden under leaves, and it catches by surprise. That is the fear this passage addresses: not the trouble a man can see coming and prepare for, but the one that is already under the path. Wisdom does not promise a path without traps. It promises that the God who founded the earth in v. 19 is watching where a particular foot goes down.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–35 — Wise Treatment of Neighbors: Ethics of Community
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter closes with a series of specific ethical commands governing relationships with neighbors. The commands are concrete and behavioral: do not withhold good when you can give it; do not say 'tomorrow' when you can act today; do not plot against your neighbor; do not envy the violent. Each negative command is matched by the positive reality: God blesses the house of the righteous, graces the humble, and honors the wise.
verseByVerse.theology: The neighbor-ethics of vv. 27–30 show that wisdom is not merely private piety but public ethics. The wise person's relationship with God is inseparable from their treatment of neighbors. This is the Old Testament anticipation of the Great Commandment: love God and love neighbor. The two cannot be separated without distorting both. Waltke: 'The neighbor-ethics of Proverbs are not an appendix to wisdom but its practical expression in the context of community.'
verseByVerse.examples: The contrast between the house of the righteous and the house of the wicked (vv. 33–35) echoes the two-path structure of the whole book. God's curse on the house of the wicked is not arbitrary judgment but the natural consequence of the architecture of moral reality: a house built on wickedness cannot stand. The LORD's blessing and curse are not external impositions but the revelation of what was always structurally true about these respective dwellings.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not withhold good from those to whom it is due, when it is in your power to do it. Do not say to your neighbor, "Go, and come again, tomorrow I will give it"—when you have it with you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter turns from God to the neighbour without a pause, and the first command is uncomfortably concrete. Do not withhold good from those to whom it is due, when it is in your power to do it.

Take the two limits first, because they keep this from being crushing. It concerns good that is due, and only what is in your power. Proverbs is not requiring a man to meet every need in the world, and a person who cannot help is not being accused here.

What is being named is the case where a man can, and the need is real, and it belongs to somebody with a claim on him — and he does not. And the form the failure takes is given in v. 28, which is one of the most exact sentences in Scripture about the human heart: do not say to your neighbour, Go, and come again, tomorrow I will give it — when you have it with you.

Nobody in this verse refuses. That is the whole art of it. He says yes and moves it. Tomorrow is the word doing the damage, because tomorrow costs nothing today, preserves the speaker’s picture of himself as a generous man, and requires him to hand over nothing at all. It is a refusal that feels like an agreement, and both parties can tell — which is why the neighbour goes away knowing something he cannot say.

And the sting is in the last clause: when you have it with you. Not when it would be difficult. When it is in the house.

James says the same thing and gives it a New Testament edge: to a brother without clothes or daily food, saying go in peace, be warmed and filled without giving the things needed for the body is worth precisely nothing (James 2:15-16). The gap between what a man says and what a man hands over is, in both testaments, the place where faith is measured.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not plan evil against your neighbor, who dwells trustingly beside you. Do not contend with a man for no reason, when he has done you no harm. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not plan evil against your neighbour, who dwells trustingly beside you. Everything in that command is carried by the last three words. The sin is not simply harm; it is harm done under cover of trust.

He dwells trustingly beside you. He has no defences up in your direction. He tells you things. He leaves the gate unlocked on that side, because you are not the direction danger comes from — and it is precisely that unguarded side which makes the injury possible, and makes it a betrayal rather than an attack.

Which is why the worst wounds people carry were almost never inflicted by enemies. An enemy has to get past something. Proverbs will come back to this at 18:19, and the psalmist put it best: it was not an enemy, but it is you, a man, my equal, my companion, my familiar friend (Psalm 55:12-13).

Then v. 30: do not contend with a man for no reason, when he has done you no harm. This is aimed at a particular temperament, and every congregation has one — the man who is always in a dispute, and who always has an account of it in which he is responding to something.

The test the verse gives is brutally simple: when he has done you no harm. Not when he was rude, not when you disliked his tone, not when he was wrong on the internet. Actual harm. A man who cannot name the harm has not been provoked into a quarrel; he has gone out and got one, and the honest question underneath is why he wanted it.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not envy a man of violence and do not choose any of his ways, for the devious person is an abomination to the LORD, but the upright are in his confidence. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not envy a man of violence and do not choose any of his ways. Envy is a strange word to use of a thug, and it is exactly the right one. This is the temptation of watching somebody get what he wants by a method you have ruled out.

Very few readers want to be violent. A great many are quietly impressed by people who push. The man who bullies his way through a negotiation, who is unpleasant enough that others give way, who has learned that most people will not stand up to sustained rudeness — he gets results, visibly, and his results sit there while the patient man waits.

Notice that the command comes in two parts, and the second is the one that shows why the first matters. Do not envy, and do not choose any of his ways. Envy is not left alone as a private feeling. It is treated as the first stage of adoption, because a man does not usually decide to become like somebody he despises. He becomes like somebody he has been admiring for a while without meaning to.

Then the reason, and it is the strongest word the book has: the devious person is an abomination to the LORD. To‘ebah is not disapproval. It is the language of revulsion — a thing that cannot be in the room.

And over against it, one of the loveliest phrases in Proverbs: the upright are in his confidence. The Hebrew is sod, and it means the private council, the inner circle where the decision is really made and where a man hears things before the crowd does. It is the word for what friends have. God says of the twisted man that he cannot bear him in the room, and of the straight man that he tells him things.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD's curse is on the house of the wicked, but he blesses the dwelling of the righteous. Toward the scorners he is scornful, but to the humble he gives favor. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD’s curse is on the house of the wicked, but he blesses the dwelling of the righteous. Note that both are houses. This is not a contrast between wealth and poverty; it is a contrast between two homes, either of which might be the larger.

The word house in Hebrew reaches further than a building. It means the household — wife, children, servants, the whole small world a man presides over. So the verse is saying something that ought to sober anybody with a family: a man does not sin privately. Whatever he is, his house is standing inside it.

Then v. 34, which the New Testament reached for twice. Toward the scorners he is scornful, but to the humble he gives favour.

The first half is the principle that God gives a man what he has chosen. The scoffer spent his life declining to take anything seriously; he will find, in the end, that he is not taken seriously either. There is a terrible symmetry to it.

But it is the second half that both James and Peter quote — following the Greek Old Testament, which renders favour as grace: God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble (James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5). It became one of the load-bearing sentences of the New Testament, and it started here.

And what it says is not that humility is a virtue God rewards. It is a statement about plumbing. Grace runs downhill. It cannot be received by a man holding his hands full of his own sufficiency, for the same reason water cannot be poured into a closed vessel — not because the water is unwilling.

Which is why the one who came was born in a stable and washed feet and went to a cross, and why the sentence Paul finally reaches for is that he humbled himself. The God who gives grace to the humble came the whole way down to where the grace runs, so that there is now no one so low that he has fallen out of reach of it, and no one so high that he has not got to come down.

verseByVerse.quote: The wise will inherit honor, but fools get disgrace. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wise will inherit honour, but fools get disgrace. The chapter ends with two men and two destinations, and everything is in the verbs.

Honour is inherited. That is a word about receiving, not achieving — what comes to a man on the strength of whose he is rather than what he seized. The wise man in this book never once sets out to be honoured. He sets out to fear God, and the honour arrives from somewhere else, in somebody else’s hands.

The fool, by contrast, is described with a verb that seems to mean lifting something up — he raises disgrace, carries it aloft, displays it. He is holding his own outcome over his head like a trophy, in front of everybody, and is the only person present who does not know what it is.

Which is the irony the whole chapter has been arguing. Honour is the one thing that cannot be taken; it can only be given, and it is given to the man who was not reaching for it. Every ambitious grasp closes the hand — and an inheritance is received with an open one.
