9.title: Proverbs 9 — Two Invitations: Wisdom's Feast and Folly's Counterfeit

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — Two Women, Two Feasts, Two Destinations
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 9 closes Proverbs 1–9 with a dramatic scene: two women, both issuing invitations from prominent positions, both calling the simple to their respective feasts. Lady Wisdom has built her house (seven pillars), prepared her feast (meat, wine, set her table), and sent out her messengers to invite the simple. Lady Folly sits at the door of her house, calling to those who pass: 'Stolen water is sweet; bread eaten in secret is pleasant.' The contrast is total.
verseByVerse.theology: The seven pillars of Wisdom's house (v. 1) have fascinated interpreters for millennia. Numerical interpretations vary (the seven days of creation, the seven liberal arts, the seven gifts of the Spirit), but the primary point is architectural completeness and stability: a seven-pillared house is built to last, to shelter, to stand against whatever comes. In contrast, Folly's 'house' is never described architecturally—she just sits at its door. She has no building of substance, only a location from which to call.
verseByVerse.examples: The central section (vv. 7–12) contains the most incisive description of the scoffer in Proverbs: correction of a scoffer is futile and brings abuse; correction of a wise man makes him wiser. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom (repeating 1:7); the mocker's days are the mocker's alone to waste. The section draws the sharpest line between the teachable and the unteachable, the wise and the scoffer—and implies that the primary dividing factor is not intelligence but humility.

verseByVerse.quote: Wisdom has built her house; she has hewn her seven pillars. She has slaughtered her beasts; she has mixed her wine; she has also set her table. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first nine chapters have been building to this, and it turns out to be a dinner invitation. Two of them, in fact, from two houses on the same street — and the whole of Proverbs 1 to 9 has been written so that the reader can tell them apart when they arrive.

Wisdom has built her house; she has hewn her seven pillars.

Notice the tense of every verb in these two verses. Built. Hewn. Slaughtered. Mixed. Set. All of it is finished before anybody is invited. Nothing in this house depends on the guests turning up, and nobody who comes will be asked to contribute anything — which is the first difference between the two invitations and, as it happens, the shape of the gospel.

The seven pillars have kept interpreters busy for two thousand years — the seven days of creation, the seven gifts of the Spirit, the seven books of learning. The likeliest meaning is the simplest: seven is the number of completeness, and a house on seven columns is one built to stand. Hold that until v. 14, where Folly is found sitting in a doorway with no house described at all.

Then the menu, and it is not modest. She has slaughtered her beasts; she has mixed her wine; she has also set her table. Meat was rare enough in an Israelite diet to mark an occasion, and to slaughter animals in the plural was a royal gesture — the sort of thing a king does at a coronation.

Which settles something about the tone of this book that a reader nine chapters in may have begun to doubt. After all the warnings and the corners and the darkness, what Wisdom actually wants is to feed people. She is not standing in the street to scold. She has been cooking.

verseByVerse.quote: She has sent out her young women to call from the highest places in the town, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
She has sent out her young women to call from the highest places in the town.

The feast is ready and the house is empty, so she does not wait. She sends servants out to the highest points in the city, where a voice carries furthest, and the invitation goes looking for people who have not asked for it and do not know the meal exists.

That direction of travel is the thing to see. Every other religion in the ancient world ran the other way: a man went up to the temple bringing something, hoping to be received. Here the house is at the top of the hill and the messengers are coming down it.

And the Lord Jesus told this story again, twice, with the detail intensified. A man gave a great banquet, and when the invited would not come he sent the servant out into the streets and lanes for the poor and crippled and blind and lame, and then out again to the highways and hedges with the order to compel people to come in, that my house may be filled (Luke 14:21-23).

The house being filled is what the host is after. Not the worthiness of the guests, of whom nothing at all is said, but the occupancy of the room — and when the church wonders why it should go out to people who are not asking, the answer is here in Proverbs 9:3. The messengers were on the hill before anybody downstairs was hungry.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" To him who lacks sense she says, "Come, eat of my bread and drink of the wine I have mixed. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever is simple, let him turn in here! To him who lacks sense she says, Come, eat of my bread and drink of the wine I have mixed.

Read the guest list. The simple — the man with no lock on his door, who has been in trouble since 1:4. And the one who lacks sense, which in Hebrew is lacks heart: the same phrase used of the boy walking to the wrong house at dusk in 7:7.

Those are the two least promising people in the book, and they are the only two named. There is no invitation in this chapter to the accomplished. If a reader has been working through Proverbs with a growing sense that he is not the sort of person it is written for, this verse is addressed to him specifically, and by name.

And hear the wording of the invitation: turn in here. Not qualify, not prepare, not improve first. Turn. It is a word about a doorway and a direction, and it can be obeyed by somebody standing in the street with nothing in his hands.

Then what is on the table: my bread, and the wine I have mixed. Bread and wine. The staples of the covenant meal, and every Christian reading them here will feel the floor shift a little.

For Wisdom eventually built a house and set a table herself, and what he said when he handed round the bread was this is my body, which is given for you, and of the cup, this cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood (Luke 22:19-20). He had already told them plainly: I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger (John 6:35). The house was built and the beasts were slaughtered and the table was set before a single guest arrived — and what was slaughtered, in the end, was the host.

verseByVerse.quote: Leave your simple ways, and live, and walk in the way of insight." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Leave your simple ways, and live, and walk in the way of insight.

Three imperatives, and the middle one is not an imperative at all but a promise sitting between two: leave, and live, and walk.

The first word is the hard one. Something has to be put down. A man cannot come to this table carrying what he is being invited out of, and Proverbs does not pretend otherwise — which is why this book is finally about repentance and not self-improvement. Nobody keeps his simple ways and adds wisdom to them as an accessory.

And what is being asked for is more painful than it sounds, because the simple ways of this book are not habits. They are a posture: an unwillingness to be told anything, a preference for one’s own account of oneself. Asking a man to leave that is asking him to admit he has been wrong for a long time, in front of somebody, and that is the entrance fee for the whole book.

Then the third word, walk, and it is the one that describes what actually follows. Not arrive at insight. Walk in it — a road, taken at ordinary speed, in the same direction, for years. Nothing in this chapter suggests that the man who turns in at the door becomes wise that evening. He becomes a man going the right way, which is the only sort of wise man there has ever been.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever corrects a scoffer gets himself abuse, and he who reproves a wicked man incurs injury. Do not reprove a scoffer, or he will hate you; reprove a wise man, and he will love you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now, in the middle of the invitation, the chapter says something that sounds almost unkind. Whoever corrects a scoffer gets himself abuse, and he who reproves a wicked man incurs injury. Do not reprove a scoffer, or he will hate you.

Do not reprove. That instruction has troubled sincere Christians, because it appears to excuse them from a duty they know they have. So it needs handling carefully, and the first thing to establish is who is being described.

The scoffer — lets — is a fixed type in this book, and he is not simply someone who disagrees. He is the man who has made contempt his method. He does not answer arguments; he makes the person raising them look ridiculous, and he has found that this works and requires nothing of him. The defining thing about him is not his opinions. It is that correction has stopped being data to him and become an attack to be repelled.

To such a man, Proverbs says, a rebuke does not do nothing — it does harm. It hardens him, it costs you, and it very often makes him worse, because a scoffer who has been corrected now has a grievance to organise around. Jesus said the same with a different picture when he spoke of not giving what is holy to dogs or casting pearls before pigs, who turn to attack you (Matthew 7:6).

Then v. 8 completes it, and the second half is the part to carry away: reprove a wise man, and he will love you.

There is the test, and it works in two directions at once. It shows which man is worth the words — and it shows a man what he is himself. Anybody may discover, in about four seconds, which of these two verses he belongs in. The last time somebody corrected you, was the immediate internal movement gratitude, or the assembling of a defence?

And a guard, because this must not become a licence for silence. Proverbs is not telling anybody to abandon a brother who is going wrong; it is telling him to know the difference between a man who cannot hear yet and a man who will not, and to spend his words where they will do something. It is a rule about wisdom in speaking, not permission to stop caring.

verseByVerse.quote: Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be still wiser; teach a righteous man, and he will increase in learning. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and the knowledge of the Holy One is insight. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be still wiser; teach a righteous man, and he will increase in learning.

This is the other half of the scoffer’s law, and it describes something that compounds. Wisdom accrues to the man who already has some, not because the system is unfair but because the capacity to receive it is itself what wisdom mostly is. The gap between the two men in these verses is not intelligence, and it is not opportunity. They both got the same sentence said to them. One of them added it to himself.

Then v. 10, and the section closes where the book opened: the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom. That sentence stood at 1:7, and its return here closes a bracket around nine chapters. Everything between the two has been an unfolding of it, and the reader who has come this far is being handed back the sentence he was given at the start, to see what it now contains.

And the second line adds something 1:7 did not say: the knowledge of the Holy One is insight.

Notice the parallel. To fear the LORD and to know the Holy One are set side by side as the same thing — which means the fear this book has been requiring is not a distance kept but an acquaintance made. And it means the whole enterprise has a Person at the end of it rather than a skill.

Holiness is the word for what makes God unlike anything else — not merely his purity but his separateness, the fact that he is in a category with no other member. And the promise of this verse is that such a One can be known. Not comprehended; known, the way a person is. He does not stop being the Holy One in order to be knowable, and no one who has come near has ever found him smaller than he feared.

verseByVerse.quote: For by me your days will be multiplied, and years will be added to your life. If you are wise, you are wise for yourself; if you scoff, you alone will bear it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
For by me your days will be multiplied, and years will be added to your life. The covenant promise of 3:2 and 4:10 returns, and it carries the same qualification it carried there: this is how the world normally runs, not a contract enforceable in every individual case.

Then v. 12, which is one of the loneliest verses in Proverbs. If you are wise, you are wise for yourself; if you scoff, you alone will bear it.

Two things are being said. The first is that nobody can be wise on your behalf. A man may have a godly wife, an excellent pastor, a father who prayed for him for forty years — and none of it transfers. Wisdom is not inherited, and there is no arrangement under which somebody else does this part for you.

The second is the harder half: you alone will bear it. The people who talked a man into a course of action are not there when the bill arrives. They are not being unkind; they simply have their own lives, and the consequences of a decision sit with the person who made it, however many voices were in the room at the time.

Which is not a counsel of isolation — this book has spent nine chapters insisting that a man who removes himself from correction is finished. It is a counsel about responsibility. Take all the advice you can get; understand that the account is in your name.

And it is precisely at this point that the gospel does something Proverbs does not do. The verse is entirely right: you alone will bear it, and nobody else can carry the weight of what a man has chosen. That is why the New Testament reaches for the same picture and says that somebody did — he himself bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24). Wisdom tells the truth about the account. The cross is where it was settled by a man to whom none of it belonged.

verseByVerse.quote: The woman Folly is loud; she is seductive and knows nothing. She sits at the door of her house; she takes a seat on the highest places of the town, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now the second invitation, and everything about it is arranged as a mirror. The woman Folly is loud; she is seductive and knows nothing. She sits at the door of her house; she takes a seat on the highest places of the town.

Three descriptions, and the last of them is the diagnosis. She is loud — Wisdom also raises her voice, so volume is not the difference. She is seductive. And she knows nothing, which is what all the noise is for.

Then the physical detail that gives the whole game away, and it is one word. Wisdom built. Folly sits.

Look back at what Wisdom did before she opened her mouth: built, hewn, slaughtered, mixed, set the table, sent out messengers. Six verbs of labour. Folly has one, and it is the verb for doing nothing. There is no house described here, no meal, no preparation and no staff. She has a doorway and a seat and a good position, and that is her whole establishment.

And the position is identical — the highest places of the town, the very words used of Wisdom’s heralds in v. 3. That is deliberate and it is the point of the chapter: the two voices are calling from the same height, to the same people, in the same words, and they are distinguishable only by what is behind them.

Which is the reason Proverbs 1 to 9 exists at all. A man standing in the street at dusk cannot see into either house. He has two invitations and no way to look inside, and what he does next depends entirely on what he already knows.

verseByVerse.quote: calling to those who pass by, who are going straight on their way, "Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" And to him who lacks sense she says, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Calling to those who pass by, who are going straight on their way, Whoever is simple, let him turn in here! And to him who lacks sense she says…

Two details, and both are chilling.

The first is her target. Those who pass by, who are going straight on their way. Not the lost. Not people who have wandered into her part of town looking for something. She calls to men who are on the right road, going in the right direction, at that moment doing nothing wrong at all.

Take that personally, because it corrects a widespread and comfortable assumption. Christians tend to imagine that temptation comes for the drifting and the backslidden, and that a man on a good run is out of range. This verse says the opposite. Going straight on your way is precisely the condition of the people she is shouting at, for the simple reason that they are the ones passing her door.

The second detail is that her invitation is word for word the same as Wisdom’s in v. 4. Whoever is simple, let him turn in here. Not similar. Identical.

So the counterfeit is not a poor imitation, and it does not sound wrong. It uses the same sentence, offers itself to the same people, from the same height, in the same street. A man who is relying on his ability to detect the difference in the moment has nothing to detect it with — which is exactly why the father spent nine chapters filling him with something in advance.

verseByVerse.quote: "Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant." But he does not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant.

This is the whole of Folly’s menu, and it is the most psychologically acute sentence in Proverbs. She is not offering better food. Water and bread are the plainest fare imaginable — the same things anybody has at home. What she is selling is two adjectives: stolen, and in secret.

Her entire case is that the flavour is in the transgression. Not that the thing itself is superior, but that having it in a way you should not is what makes it taste of anything.

And she is telling the truth about how it feels, which is why the verse is so dangerous. There is a real thrill in the illicit, and pretending otherwise has never persuaded anybody who has felt it. The lie is not in the sweetness. The lie is that the sweetness is nourishment.

Then v. 18, and the door swings open on the room: but he does not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol.

The guests are already dead. That is the horror of it, and it is the exact inversion of Wisdom’s house. In v. 2 the beasts were slaughtered so the guests could eat. Here the guests are what has been slaughtered, and the man in the doorway looking in sees a party.

And he does not know is the same clause that ended the young man in 7:23. It is the last thing Proverbs 1 to 9 says about folly, and it is not that folly is wicked. It is that folly is uninformed — that the whole tragedy runs on a piece of missing information which was being shouted from the rooftops the entire time.

So the nine chapters end with two doors on one street. Behind one is a table set by somebody who has paid for everything on it. Behind the other is a room full of people who thought they were coming to a party. And the difference is not discoverable from the street; it is only knowable in advance, from somebody who has been inside, which is what a father has been doing since 1:8.

There is one more feast at the end of the Bible, and it settles which house was which. The marriage supper of the Lamb — with the guests not dead but raised, and the host at the table bearing in his own body the marks of the slaughter that fed them (Revelation 19:9). The invitation still goes out from the highest places of the town, and it still says the same thing to the same people: whoever is simple, let him turn in here.

9.text: <sup>1</sup>Wisdom has built her house; she has hewn her seven pillars.<sup>2</sup>She has slaughtered her beasts; she has mixed her wine; she has also set her table.<sup>3</sup>She has sent out her young women to call from the highest places in the town,<sup>4</sup>"Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" To him who lacks sense she says,<sup>5</sup>"Come, eat of my bread and drink of the wine I have mixed.<sup>6</sup>Leave your simple ways, and live, and walk in the way of insight."<sup>7</sup>Whoever corrects a scoffer gets himself abuse, and he who reproves a wicked man incurs injury.<sup>8</sup>Do not reprove a scoffer, or he will hate you; reprove a wise man, and he will love you.<sup>9</sup>Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be still wiser; teach a righteous man, and he will increase in learning.<sup>10</sup>The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and the knowledge of the Holy One is insight.<sup>11</sup>For by me your days will be multiplied, and years will be added to your life.<sup>12</sup>If you are wise, you are wise for yourself; if you scoff, you alone will bear it.<sup>13</sup>The woman Folly is loud; she is seductive and knows nothing.<sup>14</sup>She sits at the door of her house; she takes a seat on the highest places of the town,<sup>15</sup>calling to those who pass by, who are going straight on their way,<sup>16</sup>"Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" And to him who lacks sense she says,<sup>17</sup>"Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant."<sup>18</sup>But he does not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol.

10.title: Proverbs 10 — The Proverbs of Solomon: Wisdom and Folly in Contrast

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–32 — Antithetical Proverbs: The Shape of the Righteous Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 10 begins the main collection of Solomonic proverbs (chs. 10–22:16), which are primarily antithetical in form: the wise/righteous contrasted with the fool/wicked in tight, memorable couplets. The chapter introduces the major themes that will recur throughout this section: the two ways (wisdom and folly), speech and its consequences, diligence and laziness, wealth and poverty in their proper perspectives, and the LORD's blessing and curse. These are not isolated sayings but a coherent moral vision presented in compressed form.
verseByVerse.theology: The antithetical form of these proverbs is not merely rhetorical but pedagogical: contrast is one of the most powerful tools for forming moral perception. By always presenting the wise option alongside the foolish, the righteous path alongside the wicked, Proverbs trains the reader's moral eye to see clearly—to distinguish between what appears similar but is fundamentally different. The repetition of contrasts across hundreds of proverbs builds a cumulative moral picture that changes how the reader perceives ordinary situations.
verseByVerse.examples: The speech proverbs of this chapter (vv. 10–11, 13–14, 18–21, 31–32) form a mini-collection within the chapter. The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life, silver, nourishment; the mouth of the wicked covers violence, brings trouble, destroys. Speech is the primary social act through which wisdom or folly is most immediately expressed and most concretely consequential. Waltke: 'In Proverbs, speech is the test of character—what comes from the mouth reveals what is in the heart.'

verseByVerse.quote: The proverbs of Solomon. A wise son makes a glad father, but a foolish son is a sorrow to his mother. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The proverbs of Solomon. With those three words the book changes shape. Nine chapters of a father talking to a son end, and what follows is several hundred sentences with no argument running between them — the change from a lecture to a toolbox.

And the first tool is aimed at the same place the lecture was. A wise son makes a glad father, but a foolish son is a sorrow to his mother.

Notice that both parents are named and given different verbs. The father is made glad; the mother is given sorrow — a word for grief that has an edge of vexation in it, the ache of watching something you cannot fix. The pairing is not sentimental padding. It is saying that a young man’s choices land in two particular people, by name, at a kitchen table, and that neither of them can do anything about it once he is grown.

Which is the whole reason the proverb sits here, at the head of the collection. Everything that follows will be about consequences, and this one begins with the consequence nobody factors in. A man weighing a course of action counts what it will cost him. He does not count what it will cost the two people who will hear about it.

verseByVerse.quote: Treasures gained by wickedness do not profit, but righteousness delivers from death. The LORD does not let the righteous go hungry, but he thwarts the craving of the wicked. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Treasures gained by wickedness do not profit, but righteousness delivers from death. The word profit is doing careful work. Money got dishonestly is real money; it buys things. What Proverbs denies is that it ever produces the thing treasure exists to produce — which is not goods but security, and there is no security in a sum a man has to keep quiet about.

Then v. 3: the LORD does not let the righteous go hungry, but he thwarts the craving of the wicked. That needs guarding, because godly people have starved, and saying otherwise would be a lie told to somebody who is currently hungry. Proverbs speaks in the ordinary case, and the ordinary case is that a life lived God’s way does not end in destitution. The book knows about exceptions and will say so.

What it insists on is the second half, which is stranger and rarely noticed: the wicked man’s problem is not that he goes without. It is that God thwarts his craving — he gets the thing and it does not answer. That is a far more accurate account of how a dishonest life actually goes than poverty would be. He is not stopped. He is allowed to arrive, and finds the room empty.

verseByVerse.quote: A slack hand causes poverty, but the hand of the diligent makes rich. He who gathers in summer is a prudent son, but he who sleeps in harvest is a son who brings shame. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A slack hand causes poverty, but the hand of the diligent makes rich. The Hebrew behind slack carries a hint of deceit as well as looseness — the hand that is present but not really applied, which is a description of a great deal of paid work.

Then v. 5 sharpens it into a season: he who gathers in summer is a prudent son, but he who sleeps in harvest is a son who brings shame.

The point is not effort but timing, and it is the ant of 6:8 again. Harvest is short. The grain is ready for a fortnight and then it is on the ground, and no amount of diligence in November recovers a fortnight in August. Every life has these windows — the years when children are still at home and will still talk; the season when a marriage can still be repaired without a third party; the decade when a body will still take training. They do not stay open, and nothing about them announces that they are closing.

So the useful question is not whether a man works hard. It is whether he knows what season he is in. Sleeping is not condemned here; sleeping in harvest is.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessings are on the head of the righteous, but the mouth of the wicked conceals violence. The memory of the righteous is a blessing, but the name of the wicked will rot. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The memory of the righteous is a blessing, but the name of the wicked will rot. Both of these proverbs are about what is left behind, and v. 7 is the more striking.

The verb is decomposition. A name is described as an organic thing that goes off — not attacked, not condemned, simply left out and allowed to decay until nothing is there. And that is what usually happens. Very few wicked men are remembered with hatred; most are not remembered at all, which is worse, and it happens surprisingly fast.

Against it stands a phrase that is easy to read past: the memory of the righteous is a blessing. Not merely pleasant — a blessing, an active good handed on. Everyone knows what this describes. There is a person, probably dead, whose name still does something in a family when it is said; whose way of handling a hard thing is quoted forty years later by people who never met him.

That is the only kind of permanence available to ordinary people, and it is not built at the end. It is built on Tuesdays, in the way a man treats somebody who cannot do anything for him.

verseByVerse.quote: The wise of heart will receive commandments, but a babbling fool will come to ruin. Whoever walks in integrity walks securely, but he who makes his ways crooked will be found out. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever walks in integrity walks securely, but he who makes his ways crooked will be found out.

The word for integrity is tom, and it means wholeness rather than blamelessness — one piece, not two. The security it produces is very specific, and anyone who has lived without it will recognise the description at once. It is the security of having nothing to keep track of.

A crooked life is above all else an administrative burden. It requires remembering which version was told to which person, keeping two accounts of the same events, and a low continuous attention to what might surface. The man of integrity is not braver than that man. He simply has no filing to do, and can therefore answer any question that is asked of him without first working out what he has previously said.

Then the plainest half-verse in the chapter: he who makes his ways crooked will be found out. Proverbs does not say when, and the delay is what makes the thing survivable for years. But a crooked path is held together by continuous effort, and effort lapses; and the odd thing is that men in this position usually experience discovery as a catastrophe arriving from outside, when in fact it was scheduled from the beginning.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever winks the eye causes trouble, and a babbling fool will come to ruin. The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life, but the mouth of the wicked conceals violence. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever winks the eye causes trouble. The winker of 6:13 is back, and the same thing is said about him: he communicates in gestures precisely because a gesture cannot be quoted. Nothing was said, and yet a room has turned against somebody.

Then the counter-image, and it is one of the loveliest in the book: the mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life.

A fountain in that country was not decorative. It was the reason a settlement existed there rather than somewhere else, and people walked to it daily with jars. So the picture is of a man whose speech other people come to on purpose, because they leave carrying something they need.

Which yields a test that is uncomfortable and cannot be answered by intention. Who comes to you to talk, and how do they leave? Not whether your opinions are correct — whether anybody is fed. Some people are a fountain, and some are a tap that mostly runs, and some are a well you have to lower something into. Nobody chooses which he is by deciding.

verseByVerse.quote: Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all offenses. On the lips of him who has understanding, wisdom is found, but a rod is for the back of him who lacks sense. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all offences. That second line was important enough for both Peter and James to quote it (1 Peter 4:8; James 5:20), and it needs handling with care, because it has been badly used.

Covers does not mean conceals, and it does not mean pretends. Hatred works by keeping every offence in view and available; love does the opposite, not by denying that a thing happened but by declining to build the relationship on it. It is what happens when somebody is rude and the matter is genuinely finished by the evening.

And a guard, because this verse has been quoted at people to keep them quiet. Covering an offence against yourself is love. Covering somebody else’s injury — concealing abuse, protecting a man who is doing harm, silencing a person who has been damaged — is not love, and Proverbs elsewhere requires exactly the opposite (31:8-9). The offences a Christian may cover are the ones committed against him.

Which is where the verse finally points. There is one covering of offences that was not a decision to overlook, and it cost everything: blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered (Psalm 32:1). Love covered a multitude, and the covering was a body on a cross.

verseByVerse.quote: The wise lay up knowledge, but the mouth of a fool brings ruin near. A rich man's wealth is his strong city; the poverty of the poor is their ruin. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wise lay up knowledge, but the mouth of a fool brings ruin near. The image is a storeroom. The wise man has things put by that are not currently being used — which is exactly what makes him useful in a crisis, because a crisis never gives time to acquire what should have been stored.

Then v. 15, and it is the flattest observation in the chapter: a rich man’s wealth is his strong city; the poverty of the poor is their ruin.

Note that nothing is being commended here. Proverbs is reporting how the world runs, and it runs like this: money buys options, and the absence of it takes them away. The poor man is not ruined because he is lazy or wicked; he is ruined because a small misfortune that a wealthier man would absorb without noticing takes his house away.

Christians who quote this book about diligence should read that second line slowly. Proverbs says plainly that poverty itself is a destroyer, which is why the same book keeps demanding generosity, and why a reader who concludes from ch. 6 that the poor have brought it on themselves has read one verse and skipped this one.

verseByVerse.quote: The wage of the righteous leads to life, the gain of the wicked to sin. Whoever heeds instruction is on the path to life, but he who rejects reproof leads others astray. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever heeds instruction is on the path to life, but he who rejects reproof leads others astray. The second half is the surprise. A man who refuses correction is not described here as damaging himself — that has been said often enough. He is described as taking other people with him.

See that clearly, because it is the argument that gets past a certain kind of self-sufficiency. A man will accept a great deal of ruin on his own account; there is a bleak satisfaction in it. What he has not usually considered is that somebody is watching how he handles being told he is wrong, and learning from it.

Children learn what to do with correction almost entirely by observation. So do junior colleagues, and younger Christians, and anybody who admires him. He is teaching whether or not he intends to, and the lesson is not what he says about humility. It is what his face does in the four seconds after a criticism.

verseByVerse.quote: The one who conceals hatred has lying lips, and whoever utters slander is a fool. When words are many, transgression is not lacking, but whoever restrains his lips is prudent. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who conceals hatred has lying lips. This is the sin nobody counts, and Proverbs names it as lying. A man says nothing false, holds his tongue, is perfectly civil — and inside there is contempt, so that every pleasant word he speaks is a false statement about where he stands.

Then v. 19, which is the most quotable sentence in the chapter and the least obeyed: when words are many, transgression is not lacking, but whoever restrains his lips is prudent.

The logic is simply arithmetic. Sin is a percentage of output. Nobody in a long evening of talking says only what he meant; the extra sentence gets said, the detail that was not his to share arrives, the joke that would have been fine with two people is made in front of five. The proverb does not say the talkative man is malicious. It says he has increased his exposure.

And the useful form of this is not a resolution to say less, which lasts about a day. It is a question after a conversation: was there anything I said tonight that I would not choose to say again? For most people, on most evenings, there is exactly one — and it was in the part of the evening after the point at which they had said everything they had.

verseByVerse.quote: The tongue of the righteous is choice silver; the heart of the wicked is of little worth. The lips of the righteous feed many, but fools die for lack of sense. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tongue of the righteous is choice silver; the heart of the wicked is of little worth. The parallel is deliberately mismatched — tongue against heart — and that is the teaching. What is valued in the first line is speech, and what is weighed in the second is the source. You cannot get silver out of a heart of little worth, however carefully the words are chosen.

Then v. 21: the lips of the righteous feed many, but fools die for lack of sense.

Feeding is an ordinary, unglamorous business. It is done daily, in small amounts, and nobody thanks anybody for it — but a person who is not fed dies, slowly and for no dramatic reason. That is what the second half describes: fools do not die of catastrophe but of malnutrition, having had food available and declined it.

And there is something quietly enormous in that word many. The righteous man in this verse is not necessarily gifted or prominent. He simply has something true to say and says it, and over a lifetime the number of people who ate at that table is larger than he will ever know.

verseByVerse.quote: The blessing of the LORD makes rich, and he adds no sorrow with it. Doing wrong is like a joke to a fool, but wisdom is pleasure to a man of understanding. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The blessing of the LORD makes rich, and he adds no sorrow with it.

The first half has been badly misused, so take the second half first, because that is where the actual claim lies. Anybody can become wealthy; the market is full of people who did. What is promised here is wealth with nothing attached to it — no sorrow added.

And that is the rarest thing in the world of money. Most fortunes come with something in the box: a marriage that was sacrificed to build it, children who saw very little of their father, a compromise that has to be maintained, or simply the low permanent anxiety of a man who now has something to lose. The verse is not promising a larger figure. It is promising a figure with no freight.

Which is why this is not a prosperity text. It does not say the blessing of the LORD makes everybody rich; it says that what the LORD gives, he gives clean. And the same principle covers the man to whom he gives little — that too arrives without sorrow added, which is a great deal more than can be said for most large sums.

Then v. 23, and it is a diagnosis by amusement: doing wrong is like a joke to a fool. Watch what a man finds funny. It is a more reliable indicator of what he is than anything he would say about himself under questioning, because nobody rehearses a laugh.

verseByVerse.quote: What the wicked dreads will come upon him, but the desire of the righteous will be granted. When the tempest passes, the wicked is no more, but the righteous is established forever. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
What the wicked dreads will come upon him, but the desire of the righteous will be granted. There is a grim symmetry in the first half: the thing he has spent his life arranging not to happen is the thing that happens.

The second half needs a guard, because the desire of the righteous will be granted is not a promise that godly people get what they want. Read with v. 22, and with the whole book, what it describes is a man whose wanting has itself been reshaped — so that what he asks for and what God is doing have converged. That is not a mechanism for obtaining things. It is a description of what happens to a man over thirty years of praying.

Then v. 25, and the image is a storm: when the tempest passes, the wicked is no more, but the righteous is established forever.

Nothing in the verse suggests the righteous man is spared the weather. The tempest passes over both; the difference is what is standing afterwards. Christ told exactly this proverb as a story, with two houses and one storm, and made the whole difference a matter of what was underneath (Matthew 7:24-27). And the word here is forever — which is a large word for a book of practical advice, and it is the right one. What is founded on him outlasts the weather, and then outlasts the world.

verseByVerse.quote: Like vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so is the sluggard to those who send him. The fear of the LORD prolongs life, but the years of the wicked will be short. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so is the sluggard to those who send him. After all the solemnity, a joke — and it is a good one, because both images are exactly right.

Neither vinegar nor smoke is dangerous. Nobody has been killed by either. What they are is continuously unpleasant: the wince, the watering eye, the low irritation that will not resolve while the source is present. That is the sluggard as experienced by the people who depend on him. He is not a villain. He is a man who was asked to do one thing and has not done it, and has an explanation, and will need to be asked again.

And the proverb is written from the point of view of those who send him, which is the part worth noticing. Elsewhere Proverbs shows the sluggard what laziness costs him. Here it shows him what he is like to be around — and that is a piece of information no lazy man has ever had access to on his own.

Then v. 27, the covenant promise again: the fear of the LORD prolongs life. Held with the rest of Scripture it is a statement about the ordinary shape of things, not a guarantee issued to individuals; and the years it finally counts are not the ones on a headstone.

verseByVerse.quote: The hope of the righteous brings joy, but the expectation of the wicked will perish. The way of the LORD is a stronghold to the blameless, but destruction to evildoers. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hope of the righteous brings joy, but the expectation of the wicked will perish. Both men in this verse are hoping. The difference is not that one has hope and the other has none; it is what the hope is fastened to.

And note the tense: the hope brings joy, now, in advance of anything arriving. That is what a well-founded hope does — it pays out early. Anyone who has waited for something certain knows the difference between that and waiting for something possible, and it is the difference between rest and vigilance.

Then v. 29, and one sentence carries both destinies: the way of the LORD is a stronghold to the blameless, but destruction to evildoers.

It is the same way. Not two different arrangements — one structure, experienced two ways depending on which side of the wall a man is standing. That is a hard thing and it is consistently taught: the same rock is a foundation to some and a stone of stumbling to others (1 Peter 2:6-8). Nobody encounters a neutral God. The character that shelters is the character that opposes, and which of the two a man meets is decided by where he is standing.

verseByVerse.quote: The righteous will never be removed, but the wicked will not dwell in the land. The mouth of the righteous brings forth wisdom, but the perverse tongue will be cut off. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The righteous will never be removed, but the wicked will not dwell in the land. The promise of 2:21-22 returns, and the verb in the first half is the important one. Removed is what happens to a boundary stone, or a tent peg, or anything that was fixed and is now not.

The claim is stability rather than comfort. A righteous man may be robbed, disliked, ill or poor; what he cannot be is dislodged, because the thing holding him in place is not any of the things that can be taken.

Then v. 31: the mouth of the righteous brings forth wisdom, but the perverse tongue will be cut off. The verb behind brings forth is agricultural — the word for a tree in fruit. It grows there. It is not manufactured for the occasion, which is why it is available at short notice and under pressure, and why a man cannot fake it in a crisis if it has not been growing for years.

verseByVerse.quote: The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable, but the mouth of the wicked, what is perverse. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable, but the mouth of the wicked, what is perverse. The chapter has spent nineteen verses on speech and ends on the one quality that cannot be acquired directly.

To know what is acceptable is to know what fits — the right thing, to this person, in this room, today. Nobody has ever learned that from a rule, because the rules cancel each other in every real situation: speak the truth, and do not wound; be honest, and be kind; say something, and do not intrude. Wisdom is not a formula for resolving those. It is the capacity a man has when the formula runs out.

And the verse says where it comes from, by putting both halves in the same grammar. Neither man is calculating. Both mouths are simply producing what is in them, which means the whole of this chapter’s teaching about speech finally lands somewhere other than the tongue.

Christ said it without the parallelism and without mercy: out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks (Matthew 12:34). Which is bad news for anybody attempting to manage his words, and very good news indeed for anybody who has been given a new heart to speak out of.

11.overview:
Chapter 11 ranges across the full breadth of social life — business ethics (v. 1), humility and pride (v. 2), political wisdom (v. 14), generosity and its paradoxical rewards (vv. 24–25), the danger of trusting in wealth (v. 28), and the life-giving power of righteousness (v. 30). The unifying thread is the social dimension of wisdom: wise living is not a private achievement but a way of being in community that creates flourishing for oneself and others.

The opening verse — "a false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight" — sets the economic and ethical tone of the chapter. Commercial honesty is not merely a legal or reputational matter; it is a theological one. The LORD is delighted by honest weights and revolted by false ones. This means that the marketplace, the office, and the negotiating table are all places where the character of God is either honoured or dishonoured. There is no sphere of life that is purely secular in Proverbs' view; everything is done before the eyes of the one who founded the earth by wisdom.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 11 — Integrity in Commerce, Righteousness in Community
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 11 opens with the marketplace (the dishonest scale) and radiates outward: pride and shame, the righteousness of the upright, the destructiveness of the wicked, the generosity that leads to abundance. The antithetical form—A but B—drives every comparison toward the reader's decision. Kidner: these are not observations about how the world sometimes works but axioms about how God has ordered it.
verseByVerse.theology: God's moral order is built into creation's fabric; righteousness produces life and wickedness produces death not arbitrarily but necessarily. The fear of the Lord is the invisible foundation beneath every contrast. The generous soul (v.25) mirrors God's own character, and the community that shelters under righteous leadership flourishes.
verseByVerse.examples: Every business transaction is a theological act (v.1). Every act of generosity is an investment in the economy of grace (vv.24-25). The town that rejoices at the righteous (v.10) pictures the peaceable kingdom where God's order is honored.

verseByVerse.quote: A false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight. When pride comes, then comes disgrace, but with the humble is wisdom. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight.

Two words in that sentence are as strong as Hebrew gets, and both are religious words. Abomination is what is said of idols; delight is what is said of acceptable worship. And they are being used about a set of scales.

The picture is concrete. A merchant carried stone weights in a pouch, and a shaved weight was almost impossible to detect and enormously profitable over a year. The law forbids it three times (Leviticus 19:35-36; Deuteronomy 25:13-16), and Amos treats it as oppression of the poor, because that is who it robs — the man buying a day’s grain does not own a second set of scales to check with (Amos 8:5).

What Proverbs adds is where the offence lands. Not on the customer, first, but on God. Which means the marketplace is not a neutral zone with religion applied to it afterwards. The invoice, the estimate, the hours written on the timesheet, the description in the advertisement — every one of those is a set of scales, and God is described as either revolted by them or delighted by them, with nothing in between.

Then v. 2, and the two verses belong together more than they look: when pride comes, then comes disgrace. The false weight and the proud heart share a root, which is a man behaving as though the truth about him is whatever he says it is.

verseByVerse.quote: The integrity of the upright guides them, but the crookedness of the treacherous destroys them. Riches do not profit in the day of wrath, but righteousness delivers from death. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The integrity of the upright guides them, but the crookedness of the treacherous destroys them. Both nouns are given verbs of motion, and the difference is that one of them steers.

Integrity as a guide is a practical claim, not a compliment. The upright man is not endlessly recalculating, because most of his decisions were made years ago in principle and are now only being applied. The crooked man has to work out every situation from the beginning, since he has no fixed position to reason from — and that is exhausting long before it is fatal.

Then v. 4: riches do not profit in the day of wrath, but righteousness delivers from death.

The day of wrath is not defined, and the ambiguity is deliberate: it covers the sudden calamity, the deathbed and the judgment alike. What all three have in common is that money, which is useful in nearly every other circumstance, is simply not admitted.

And that is a sobering thought for anybody who has quietly built his security in one place. A man is not being told that his savings are wicked. He is being told the date on which they stop working, and that he will not be given notice of it.

verseByVerse.quote: The righteousness of the blameless keeps his way straight, but the wicked falls by his own wickedness. The righteousness of the upright delivers them, but the treacherous are taken captive by their lust. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wicked falls by his own wickedness… the treacherous are taken captive by their lust.

Two verses, and neither of them mentions God doing anything. Nobody is struck down here. The wicked man falls over the thing he was carrying, and the treacherous man is taken prisoner by his own appetite — and that second image is the arresting one.

Taken captive. He began by wanting something, which felt like freedom, and by the end of the sentence the wanting has him. That is the ordinary biography of any strong desire that has been fed: it starts as a servant, does excellent work for a while, and finishes as an owner.

And the test of which stage a man is at is not how much pleasure he gets from the thing. It is what happens when he tries to go without it for a fortnight — which is a question a person can answer honestly only by doing it, and the reluctance to try is itself part of the answer.

Against that stands the first half: the righteousness of the blameless keeps his way straight. Kidner puts the alternative exactly. A man who will not be mastered by God does not thereby become his own master; he is mastered by his desires instead.

verseByVerse.quote: When the wicked dies, his hope will perish, and the expectation of wealth perishes too. The righteous is delivered from trouble, and the wicked walks into it instead. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the wicked dies, his hope will perish, and the expectation of wealth perishes too.

Every human being alive is hoping for something, and the whole question this verse asks is whether the hope has a shelf life. Here it is dated to a particular day. Not disappointed on the way — carried the whole distance, faithfully, and then found to expire at the moment it was finally needed.

Which is a test that can be run in advance and by anybody. Name the two or three things that would have to be true for your life to have gone well. Then ask which of them survives your funeral. A man may discover that most of what he is working toward is scheduled to stop working on the one day he cannot postpone.

Then v. 8, which is more difficult: the righteous is delivered from trouble, and the wicked walks into it instead. Read as a rule about individuals it is plainly not always true, and Proverbs elsewhere knows it. What the book insists on is the direction of the current, and a reader in trouble should not conclude from this verse that he has been abandoned — the book of Job exists in the same Bible to stop exactly that conclusion.

verseByVerse.quote: With his mouth the godless man would destroy his neighbor, but by knowledge the righteous are delivered. When it goes well with the righteous, the city rejoices, and when the wicked perish there are shouts of gladness. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
With his mouth the godless man would destroy his neighbour, but by knowledge the righteous are delivered.

Note the rescue mechanism, because it is not what one would expect. The righteous are not delivered by counter-attack, or by influential friends, or by the destruction of the attacker. They are delivered by knowledge — by somebody in the room knowing enough to recognise what is being done.

That is a real and specific service ordinary people can perform for each other. When a person is being quietly dismantled in a community, the thing that stops it is almost never a confrontation. It is one man who has been paying attention and says, mildly, that this is not true, and that he has known him for years.

Then v. 10, and the picture widens: when it goes well with the righteous, the city rejoices. A city is not usually described as having feelings about individuals, and the claim is that a good man’s prospering is a public good. Others are better off because he is doing well — which is precisely what cannot be said about the man in v. 9, whose success requires somebody else’s ruin.

verseByVerse.quote: By the blessing of the upright a city is exalted, but by the mouth of the wicked it is overthrown. Whoever belittles his neighbor lacks sense, but a man of understanding remains silent. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
By the blessing of the upright a city is exalted, but by the mouth of the wicked it is overthrown. A whole town lifted or destroyed by what people say in it — which sounds like exaggeration until you have watched it happen to a church.

Then v. 12, which is one of the most useful proverbs in the book for anybody who is often in rooms with other people. Whoever belittles his neighbour lacks sense, but a man of understanding remains silent.

To belittle is literally to despise — but the English word catches something the Hebrew implies, which is that it is usually done in small amounts. Not denunciation. The diminishing remark, the accurate observation about somebody’s weakness delivered where they cannot hear it, the amused tone that makes a man slightly smaller in the estimation of everyone present.

And what is offered against it is not a better remark. It is silence — and the verse takes the trouble to say that the silence is a mark of understanding, not of timidity. Anybody can be quiet because he has nothing to say. The man being praised here has something to say, and it would probably get a laugh, and he does not say it.

The test is not whether a man ever criticises anybody, since some criticism is a duty. It is whether he can hold an accurate and unflattering opinion of somebody without spending it.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever goes about slandering reveals secrets, but he who is trustworthy in spirit keeps a thing covered. Where there is no guidance, a people falls, but in an abundance of counselors there is safety. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever goes about slandering reveals secrets, but he who is trustworthy in spirit keeps a thing covered. The two halves define each other, and between them they describe the rarest quality in any community.

A confidence is a weight. Somebody has handed a man something heavy and asked him to carry it, and the cost is that he must go on carrying it in every subsequent conversation where mentioning it would have been useful, or interesting, or would have made him look well-informed. Most disclosures are not betrayals of malice. They are a man setting down something heavy because he was tired of holding it.

The phrase trustworthy in spirit is exactly right, because this cannot be managed by rule. It is a settled disposition, and everybody can tell within a year or two who in a congregation has it.

Then v. 14: where there is no guidance, a people falls, but in an abundance of counsellors there is safety. This is the great verse on leadership, and its force is in the plural. Not a counsellor — an abundance.

Anybody who leads anything, at any scale, should feel the warning. The failure is rarely a refusal to take advice. It is the slow assembling of a circle of people who agree, each of whom was chosen for good reasons, until a man is surrounded by his own opinion in several voices and experiences this as confirmation.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever puts up security for a stranger will surely suffer harm, but he who hates striking hands in pledge is secure. A gracious woman gets honor, and violent men get riches. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever puts up security for a stranger will surely suffer harm. The theme of 6:1-5 returns without the drama, and the second half adds a picture: he who hates striking hands in pledge is secure. A handshake was the ancient signature, and the man commended here has a settled reluctance to give one. Not stinginess — the same book demands open-handed generosity — but an unwillingness to make an open-ended promise on somebody else’s behalf.

Then v. 16, which is deliberately lopsided: a gracious woman gets honour, and violent men get riches.

The two halves do not match, and the mismatch is the argument. She gets honour; they get money. Both acquire something real, and the proverb declines to pretend that violence is unprofitable — Proverbs is never naive in that way. It simply sets the two acquisitions side by side and lets the reader notice which of them can be taken away, and which one anybody would actually want said of them at the end.

verseByVerse.quote: A man who is kind benefits himself, but a cruel man hurts himself. The wicked earns deceptive wages, but one who sows righteousness gets a sure reward. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man who is kind benefits himself, but a cruel man hurts himself.

The word for kindness is hesed, which is the great covenant word — the loyal, durable kindness God uses of himself. It is not softness, and it is not a mood. It is the disposition of somebody who has decided in advance to be for you.

And the claim is that this returns to the man who does it, which is not because kind people are rewarded but because of what kindness makes of them. Cruelty is corrosive to the person exercising it: it requires a steady low contempt for other people, and a man cannot hold that posture for twenty years and remain undamaged by it. Nobody arrives at old age hard on the outside and soft within.

Then v. 18, and the phrase is memorable: the wicked earns deceptive wages. Literally wages of falsehood. The pay was real, it arrived on time, and it turns out not to be what the man thought he was working for — which is sin’s consistent business model. It always overpromises, and it always pays in a currency that does not convert.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever is steadfast in righteousness will live, but he who pursues evil will die. Those of crooked heart are an abomination to the LORD, but those of blameless ways are his delight. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those of crooked heart are an abomination to the LORD, but those of blameless ways are his delight.

The pairing of those two words is the whole verse, and the second one deserves far more attention than it usually gets. Christians are generally clear that God is opposed to sin. Very few of them believe the other half of this sentence about themselves.

His delight. Not his tolerance. Not his willingness to overlook. The same word used in v. 1 of honest scales, and it is a word about pleasure taken.

Which is the thing to hold on to, because most people carry a working picture of God in which he is permanently slightly disappointed. Scripture will not have it. The Father who spoke over his Son said he was well pleased, and those who are in Christ are described as accepted in the Beloved — not endured, but received with gladness. He is not putting up with what he is making. He likes it.

verseByVerse.quote: Be assured, an evil person will not go unpunished, but the offspring of the righteous will be delivered. Like a gold ring in a pig's snout is a beautiful woman without discretion. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be assured, an evil person will not go unpunished. The Hebrew behind be assured is hand to hand — the gesture of a bargain struck, which is how you said you have my word on it before there were signatures. Proverbs is not speculating here. It is shaking on it.

And the promise is needed, because the ordinary experience of watching the world is that a great many people get away with a great deal. What the verse insists on is not the timing but the settlement, and a reader who requires the settlement to be visible within his own lifetime is asking for something the book never offered.

Then v. 22, one of the most memorable images in Proverbs: like a gold ring in a pig’s snout is a beautiful woman without discretion.

The ring is genuinely gold, which is the point. Nothing is being said against beauty; the comparison only works because the ring is valuable. What is being said is that a good thing put somewhere unsuitable becomes ridiculous rather than merely wasted, and that it is the location, not the gold, that everybody will remember.

And nobody should read this as aimed at women in particular. The same book says the identical thing about a man’s strength, his wealth, his cleverness and his position — every one of them a real gift, and every one grotesque in somebody with no judgment to hang it on.

verseByVerse.quote: The desire of the righteous ends only in good, the expectation of the wicked in wrath. One gives freely, yet grows all the richer; another withholds what he should give, and only suffers want. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
One gives freely, yet grows all the richer; another withholds what he should give, and only suffers want.

This is the most counter-intuitive economics in the Bible, and Proverbs states it flatly, as observation. The generous man ends up with more. The man who kept it ends up short.

Part of the mechanism is visible to anybody. A generous man is trusted, and trust is the most valuable commodity in any village or trade; people bring things to him, and they warn him about things, and when he is in difficulty a number of them turn up. The hoarder has purchased security and finds, at the moment he needs it, that he is holding it alone.

But the deeper reason is in the shape of the world rather than in social mechanics. This is a universe made by a God who gives — the sun is not diminished by shining, the spring is not exhausted by running, the tree makes more fruit for having borne some. A man who gives is working with the grain of that. A man who hoards is working against it, and hoarding is the only economic behaviour in creation that has no model anywhere in nature.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever brings blessing will be enriched, and one who waters will himself be watered. The people curse him who holds back grain, but a blessing is on the head of him who sells it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever brings blessing will be enriched, and one who waters will himself be watered. The second half is a lovely piece of Hebrew, and the passive is the point: he does not water himself. Somebody else does the watering, and he does not arrange it.

Hold that against the ordinary anxiety about generosity, which is that a person who keeps giving will eventually run out. The verse does not deny the arithmetic. It says that the man in question is not the only party involved.

Then v. 26, which is sharper and more political than it looks: the people curse him who holds back grain, but a blessing is on the head of him who sells it.

This describes a specific and entirely legal practice. In a shortage, a man with a full store does nothing wrong by waiting; he simply sells later, at a much better price. It is good business, and Proverbs says the town curses him for it.

Which establishes something the book will not let go of. There are things a man may do that are lawful, defensible, and commercially sound, and are nevertheless wicked — and the test is not whether he broke a rule but whether his advantage was somebody else’s hunger.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever diligently seeks good seeks favor, but evil comes to him who searches for it. Whoever trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous will flourish like a green leaf. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever diligently seeks good seeks favour, but evil comes to him who searches for it. Both men in this verse are searching. Neither drifts into what he finds. And Proverbs’ observation is that the searching itself does something: a man looking for good becomes the kind of man good things come to, and the same is true in reverse and rather faster.

Then v. 28: whoever trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous will flourish like a green leaf.

Watch what is condemned. Not having riches — trusting them. Proverbs is entirely at ease with the man who has money and rather uneasy about the man who leans on it, which is a distinction most of us apply to other people and rarely to ourselves.

And the test is straightforward, though not comfortable. Imagine the figure gone — not reduced, gone. What exactly is it that would be over? For most people the honest answer is not the possessions. It is the sense of being all right, and that is what the verse means by trust.

Against it, an image with no security in it at all: a green leaf. Leaves are not strong; they are thin, temporary, and destroyed by almost anything. What they are is alive, and supplied continuously by something they are attached to and do not own.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever troubles his own household will inherit the wind, and the fool will be servant to the wise of heart. The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, and whoever captures souls is wise. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever troubles his own household will inherit the wind. The word for trouble is strong — the same root used of Achan, who brought disaster on Israel and on his own family (Joshua 7:25). This is not a man who is difficult to live with. It is a man whose household is being damaged by him.

And what he gets is the wind: not a punishment but an inheritance, which is a bitter joke. He worked for something, and the estate is delivered, and there is nothing in it. Whatever he was pursuing that cost him his home — the career, the grievance, the drinking, the being right — he keeps. It simply turns out to weigh nothing.

Then v. 30, and after all the weighing and selling and inheriting, Eden opens up again: the fruit of the righteous is a tree of life.

The image has already been used of wisdom herself (3:18). Here it is said of a person. A righteous life is described as a tree standing somewhere, which other people eat from — not because he is remarkable, but because that is what trees do, and it happens whether or not he is aware of it.

The last clause is the missionary sentence of the Old Testament: whoever captures souls is wise. The verb is the one for taking a life, turned right way up. And the one who is himself the Tree of Life said it to fishermen in almost the same words, standing on a beach: from now on you will be catching men (Luke 5:10).

verseByVerse.quote: If the righteous is repaid on earth, how much more the wicked and the sinner! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the righteous is repaid on earth, how much more the wicked and the sinner!

The argument runs from the smaller case to the greater, and its force depends on the first half being conceded. The righteous are repaid on earth — that is, God does not let his own people’s sin run unaddressed. He disciplines them, here, in this life, precisely because they are his (3:11-12).

Which is an odd comfort, and Scripture uses it as one. Peter takes this verse up during a persecution, in the form if the righteous is scarcely saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner? (1 Peter 4:18), and he is not trying to frighten the church. He is telling suffering Christians how to read what is happening to them: the fire is in the house of God, and that is not a sign of abandonment.

So the verse asks for two things at once, and they belong together. Sober self-examination — because a man who finds God dealing with him should not be surprised or resentful. And a settled gratitude, because the discipline that falls on a son is not the judgment that falls on a stranger, and the difference between the two was paid for on a hill by somebody who was treated as the sinner so that the sinners could be treated as sons.

11.theology: Generosity as creation ethics. The paradox of verses 24–25 — give freely and grow richer; withhold and suffer want — is not merely social observation but theological claim. It reflects the character of the God who "gives generously to all without reproach" (Jas 1:5) and who does not become less by giving. The created order reflects the Creator's generosity: the sun gives its light and is not diminished; the spring gives its water and is not exhausted; the tree gives its fruit and produces more. The person who lives generously is living in harmony with the grain of a world made by the generous God. The person who hoards is living against that grain, and creation — and its Maker — pushes back. The New Testament makes the theological grounding explicit: "God so loved the world that he gave" (John 3:16). Generosity is Trinitarian ethics applied to human life.
11.examples:
Then: The false balance of verse 1 was not an abstract ethical problem in the ancient world; it was the everyday reality of the marketplace, where the temptation to cheat was constant and the detection of cheating was difficult. Leviticus 19:35–36 and Deuteronomy 25:13–16 prohibit the false weight explicitly; Amos 8:5 condemns it as a form of oppression of the poor. Proverbs frames it not as a violation of law but as an abomination to the LORD himself — which is a stronger and more personal condemnation. The business person who cheats their customers does not merely break a regulation; they revolt God.

Now: "In an abundance of counselors there is safety" (v. 14) is the wisdom text for governance, leadership, and organisational culture. The leader — whether of a family, a business, a church, or a nation — who surrounds themselves with people who agree with them, who dismisses challenge and criticism, who mistakes confidence for competence, is setting themselves up for the fall that pride always brings (v. 2). The cultivating of honest, diverse, wise counsel is not a sign of weakness; it is the most important leadership discipline Proverbs knows.

12.title: The Righteous and the Wicked
12.text: <sup>1</sup>Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge, but he who hates reproof is stupid.<sup>2</sup>A good man obtains favor from the LORD, but a man of evil devices he
