12.overview:
Chapter 12 continues the pattern of antithetical proverbs, with particular attention to two themes: the contrast between the righteous and the wicked (seen in their relationship to discipline, speech, and truthfulness), and the power of words to wound or heal. The chapter opens with the blunt observation that loving discipline is inseparable from loving knowledge (v. 1) — a truth that most people resist — and closes with the beautiful pastoral insight that "a good word makes him glad" (v. 25).

The speech proverbs of this chapter (vv. 17–22) form a cluster of particular moral and pastoral weight. Words are not neutral — they are "like sword thrusts" or they "bring healing"; they are "an abomination to the LORD" (lying) or his "delight" (faithfulness). The God who spoke the world into existence and whose word is truth is the God who holds human words to the highest possible standard. Every lie is a mimicry of the father of lies (John 8:44); every true and healing word is a participation in the truth of the one who is the Word (John 1:1).

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 12 — Wisdom and Folly in Work, Words, and Character
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 12 pairs wisdom and folly in their effects on marriage, work, speech, and reputation. The upright woman (v.4) and the excellent wife contrast with destructive company; the diligent hand (v.24) versus the slack hand; truthful lips versus lying lips. Waltke: Proverbs 12 is a portrait gallery where every portrait is a binary—two paths, two outcomes, one choice.
verseByVerse.theology: Speech is the most prominent theme: truthful lips (v.17), lying tongue (v.19), rash words (v.18), healing words (v.18), the mouth of the righteous (v.6), lips that are the delight of kings (v.22). What we say reveals who we are and shapes who others become. The tongue is the gauge of the heart.
verseByVerse.examples: The excellent wife of v.4 echoes the explicit praise of ch.31. The proverb about the righteous caring for animals (v.10) grounds ethics in a comprehensive view of creation—stewardship of life at every level. The connection between word and deed, character and consequence, runs through every verse.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge, but he who hates reproof is stupid. A good man obtains favor from the LORD, but a man of evil devices he condemns. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever loves discipline loves knowledge, but he who hates reproof is stupid.

Proverbs does not usually call names, and it does here. The word is ba‘ar, and it does not mean unintelligent; it means brutish — from the word for cattle. A man who cannot take correction is being compared to livestock, and the comparison is precise rather than merely rude. An animal can be trained by pain and reward, but it cannot be reasoned with, because there is no way to explain to it why the fence is there.

And the first half is the harder claim: loving discipline and loving knowledge are the same love. Not two virtues that happen to go together — one thing. Which means a man who wants to understand something and is unwilling to be told he is wrong about it wants two incompatible things, and will get neither.

Then v. 2: a good man obtains favour from the LORD, but a man of evil devices he condemns. Note the asymmetry of the verbs. The good man obtains — it comes to him, from outside, unearned. The other man is condemned by a direct act. Grace is described as something received; judgment as something done.

verseByVerse.quote: No one is established by wickedness, but the root of the righteous will never be moved. An excellent wife is the crown of her husband, but she who brings shame is like rottenness in his bones. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one is established by wickedness, but the root of the righteous will never be moved. The image is agricultural and the emphasis is underground. What holds a tree is not the part anybody admires.

Which is the argument against a kind of life that looks, from the outside, extremely successful. A man can be established in every visible sense — position, reputation, property — and have no root at all, and the difference does not show in fair weather. It shows once.

Then v. 4, which is one of the sharpest sentences in the book about marriage: an excellent wife is the crown of her husband, but she who brings shame is like rottenness in his bones.

Excellent is hayil, the word used of soldiers — strength, capability, force of character — and it is the same phrase that opens the great poem of 31:10. She is not called his ornament. She is called his crown, which is the thing that makes a man a king; the honour is hers, and it is placed on him.

The second half is not the mirror image, and the difference matters. A crown is worn outside; rot is in the bones. Trouble in a marriage does not stay in the marriage — it goes into the frame, where it cannot be seen and cannot be set down, and the man carries it into every room he enters. Which is a reason to work at this while it is still an argument rather than a diagnosis.

verseByVerse.quote: The thoughts of the righteous are just; the counsels of the wicked are deceitful. The words of the wicked lie in wait for blood, but the mouth of the upright delivers them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The thoughts of the righteous are just; the counsels of the wicked are deceitful. The comparison is made at the level of what happens before anybody speaks — and this is where Proverbs consistently locates the difference between two men who may behave identically for years.

Both are advising. Both sound reasonable. But one of them is thinking about what is right and the other is thinking about what will work, and the two produce the same sentence often enough that nobody can tell them apart in a single meeting. Over ten years they diverge completely.

Then v. 6, and the picture is an ambush: the words of the wicked lie in wait for blood, but the mouth of the upright delivers them.

That is Proverbs 1:11 again, where the young man was invited to lie in wait — except that here the weapon is not a knife. It is testimony, and the destruction is legal and reputational, which in a small community amounts to the same thing.

And the rescue, once again, is verbal. Somebody speaks and a man is delivered. It costs the speaker something — that is why so few do it — and it is one of the plainest good works available to an ordinary Christian: to be the person in the room who says the true thing when the true thing is inconvenient.

verseByVerse.quote: The wicked are overthrown and are no more, but the house of the righteous will stand. A man is commended according to his good sense, but one of twisted mind is despised. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wicked are overthrown and are no more, but the house of the righteous will stand. Household against household, and the contrast is duration. One of them is still there in three generations.

Then v. 8: a man is commended according to his good sense, but one of twisted mind is despised.

This is a proverb about reputation, and it is more encouraging than it first appears. It says that in the ordinary run of things people are eventually valued for what they actually are — which is not what a young man believes, since at twenty-five it seems obvious that confidence and presentation carry the day.

They do carry the day. They do not carry the decade. Over a long enough period a community works out with considerable accuracy who is reliable, who talks well and delivers little, and whose judgment can be trusted with something that matters — and nobody is ever told the verdict, which is why a man can be the last to learn his own standing.

The application is not to manage the impression. It is to become the thing, and let the estimate look after itself, since the estimate is being formed either way and cannot be hurried.

verseByVerse.quote: Better to be lowly and have a servant than to play the great man and lack bread. Whoever is righteous has regard for the life of his beast, but the mercy of the wicked is cruel. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Better to be lowly and have a servant than to play the great man and lack bread.

There is the whole of social pretence in one sentence, and it is three thousand years old. A man with a modest position and enough to live on, against a man maintaining an appearance and going hungry to do it.

The phrase play the great man is exactly the right translation; the Hebrew is about honouring oneself. And the specific misery it describes has never gone out of fashion — the car that is a stretch, the school fees that are a stretch, the round of drinks bought by the man who cannot afford it, the holiday photographed for people whose opinion he does not even value. He is not deceived about his position. He is spending real money to prevent other people from noticing it.

Then v. 10, which is startling in an ancient text: whoever is righteous has regard for the life of his beast. A man’s treatment of an animal is made a moral index — of an animal that cannot complain, cannot leave, and has no standing anywhere.

And the second half is the sting: the mercy of the wicked is cruel. Even his kindness has something wrong in it. Which is a description anyone will recognise who has been on the receiving end of a favour that had a hook in it.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever works his land will have plenty of bread, but he who follows worthless pursuits lacks sense. Whoever is wicked covets the spoil of evildoers, but the root of the righteous bears fruit. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever works his land will have plenty of bread, but he who follows worthless pursuits lacks sense.

The contrast is not work against idleness. It is work against pursuit — the man in the second half is busy. He is chasing something, and the word for what he chases means empty things, vapour, schemes.

Every generation has its version, and it always looks more intelligent than digging. The scheme, the shortcut, the thing that will change everything, the venture that means he will not have to do the ordinary work any more. And what Proverbs commends against it is the least glamorous sentence available: work his land — the ground he actually has, which is usually small, and which nobody would choose.

Then v. 12 gives the reason, and it is the root image again: the root of the righteous bears fruit. Roots are slow, invisible, and cannot be hurried by wanting fruit sooner. The man with the scheme wants the fruit without the years, and the years are not an obstacle to the fruit. They are how it is made.

verseByVerse.quote: An evil man is ensnared by the transgression of his lips, but the righteous escapes from trouble. From the fruit of his mouth a man is satisfied with good, and the work of a man's hand comes back to him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
An evil man is ensnared by the transgression of his lips, but the righteous escapes from trouble. The trap he falls into is the one his own mouth set — which is 6:2 and 18:7 and a dozen other places, because Proverbs cannot say it often enough.

Then v. 14: from the fruit of his mouth a man is satisfied with good, and the work of a man’s hand comes back to him.

Two halves, and they treat words and work identically. Both are described as things that go out and come back — a harvest, and a boomerang. Nothing a man says or does is spent and gone; it is planted, and it is his own crop that he will be eating.

What makes this useful rather than merely ominous is the timescale. Nobody eats a harvest the week it is sown, which is precisely why the connection is so hard to believe when it matters. The sentence said today and the situation in four years look entirely unrelated, and the whole claim of this book is that they are not.

verseByVerse.quote: The way of a fool is right in his own eyes, but a wise man listens to advice. The vexation of a fool is known at once, but the prudent ignores an insult. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The way of a fool is right in his own eyes, but a wise man listens to advice.

Notice what is not said. The fool is not described as knowing he is wrong and doing it anyway; his way is right in his own eyes, and it feels exactly like being right, because that is what being wrong feels like from inside. There is no internal sensation that distinguishes the two, which is the whole reason advice exists.

So the wise man in the second half is not brighter. He has simply installed an instrument outside himself, and the fool has not — and neither of them can tell the difference from where they are standing.

Then v. 16, one of the most practical verses in the book: the vexation of a fool is known at once, but the prudent ignores an insult.

At once is the diagnosis. Not that the fool is angry — everybody is angry sometimes — but that the interval between the provocation and everyone knowing about it is zero. There is no gap in him.

And the prudent man is not being told to feel nothing. He ignores — the Hebrew is about covering something over, which is a deliberate act performed on a thing that is genuinely there. He felt the insult exactly as sharply. He put something over it, and the room never knew.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever speaks the truth gives honest evidence, but a false witness utters deceit. There is one whose rash words are like sword thrusts, but the tongue of the wise brings healing. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is one whose rash words are like sword thrusts, but the tongue of the wise brings healing.

The word rendered rash means to speak without thinking — babbling, blurting. And the image chosen for it is not a blunt instrument but a sword thrust: something narrow that goes deep, in and out in a second, in a place the speaker never looked at.

Which is exactly how it happens. The remark that took two seconds and is still being carried twenty years later was almost never premeditated. Ask the man who said it and he will not remember the evening. That is the horror of the verse, and it is why the alternative offered is not merely kinder speech but healing — marpe, a medical word, the mending of something injured.

So the wise tongue in this verse is not the one that avoids doing damage. It is the one that repairs damage somebody else did. Every congregation has one or two people like this, and they are almost never the most impressive talkers; they are the ones after whose conversation something in a person is quietly better than it was.

And there is one whose words did that on a scale nobody else could reach. He spoke to a leper and to a woman bent double for eighteen years, and by his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:5) — the sword thrust taken deliberately, once, so that the mending could go the other way.

verseByVerse.quote: Truthful lips endure forever, but a lying tongue is but for a moment. Deceit is in the heart of those who devise evil, but those who plan peace have joy. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truthful lips endure forever, but a lying tongue is but for a moment.

The comparison is duration, and it should be taken literally. A lie has a lifespan. It works now — that is the whole reason it was told — and it is under pressure from the day it is spoken, because the world goes on being what it actually is and the lie has to be maintained against it. Truth needs no maintenance. It simply sits there being the case.

Which is the deepest practical argument for honesty, and it has nothing to do with feeling good. Truth is the cheapest thing to own.

Then v. 20: deceit is in the heart of those who devise evil, but those who plan peace have joy.

Both men are planning; the verse is about what a man is working on when nobody is watching. And the reward attached is not success but joy, which is a strange thing to attach to peacemaking, since peacemaking is thankless work and usually leaves both parties mildly annoyed with the man in the middle.

Yet the promise stands, and Christ made it larger: blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God (Matthew 5:9). Not merely rewarded — named after the Father, because making peace between enemies is the family business.

verseByVerse.quote: No ill befalls the righteous, but the wicked are filled with trouble. Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, but those who act faithfully are his delight. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
No ill befalls the righteous, but the wicked are filled with trouble.

Read flatly, that is false, and pretending otherwise would insult every faithful Christian who has buried a child. So it needs saying plainly what the verse can and cannot mean.

The Hebrew word is aven, and it is not the ordinary word for misfortune; it carries the sense of iniquity, of trouble that is the fruit of wrongdoing. The claim is not that nothing bad happens to good people. It is that the particular species of ruin described all through this book — the self-inflicted kind, the trap a man sets and steps in — is not the righteous man’s inheritance. He may be struck by anything the world can do. He will not be destroyed by himself.

Then v. 22 returns to the two worship words: lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, but those who act faithfully are his delight. Set beside 11:1, and the pattern of the book is plain — false weights and false words are the same offence in two materials, and both are treated as things done to God rather than merely to a neighbour.

verseByVerse.quote: A prudent man conceals knowledge, but the heart of fools proclaims folly. The hand of the diligent will rule, while the slothful will be put to forced labor. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A prudent man conceals knowledge, but the heart of fools proclaims folly.

This is not about secrecy. It is about the fact that knowing something is not by itself a reason to say it, and that a great deal of what people say is said because they know it and would like that to be evident.

The prudent man in this verse has the information and does not produce it. He knows the answer in the meeting and lets somebody else arrive at it. He can see what is wrong in a family and does not diagnose it aloud. He is aware of what a man did in 2009 and the subject does not come up. He is not being coy; he has simply grasped that possessing knowledge and being required to display it are different things.

Then v. 24: the hand of the diligent will rule, while the slothful will be put to forced labour. The end points are the interesting part. Both men end up working. One of them chooses what he does; the other does what he is told, on somebody else’s schedule. Diligence is not presented here as the road to leisure. It is the road to being the one who decides.

verseByVerse.quote: Anxiety in a man's heart weighs him down, but a good word makes him glad. One who is righteous is a guide to his neighbor, but the way of the wicked leads them astray. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anxiety in a man’s heart weighs him down, but a good word makes him glad.

This is the most humane sentence in the chapter and possibly in the book, and the first thing to notice is that Scripture does not scold. Anxiety is not treated here as a sin to be repented of. It is described the way a physical burden is described: it weighs him down — the Hebrew is about being bowed, bent under a load — which is exactly what it does to a body, to a posture, to a face.

Anybody who has carried it knows the accuracy of that. It is not primarily fear. It is weight, carried everywhere, all week, so that ordinary things require an effort nobody else can see.

And then the remedy, and its smallness is the point. Not a solution. Not a resolution of the thing being feared. A good word.

Take that seriously as an instruction, because most people believe they have nothing to offer somebody in trouble and so offer nothing. This verse says the burden is genuinely lifted — the word for glad is the word for rejoicing — by a sentence. Not a clever one. A true, kind, specific one, said out loud, by somebody who bothered.

So there is a concrete thing to do this week, and it costs about a minute: think of the person currently bowed under something, and say the good word rather than intending to. Then v. 26 makes it a way of life — one who is righteous is a guide to his neighbour — a man whose ordinary presence in a street means somebody nearby is less likely to get lost.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever is slothful will not roast his game, but the diligent man will get precious wealth. In the path of righteousness is life, and in its pathway there is no death. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever is slothful will not roast his game, but the diligent man will get precious wealth.

The Hebrew is difficult, but the picture that comes through is comic and devastating. The lazy man has gone hunting. He has been out, he has done the hard part, he has actually caught something — and he will not roast it. The last step, the small one, the one that turns the effort into dinner, does not get done.

Everybody knows this man, and most of us are him somewhere. The course nearly finished. The letter written and not sent. The apology composed and never delivered. The book of the Bible begun in January. The game is in the house, and it is going off, and the only thing missing is a fire.

Then the chapter closes with a line that reaches further than anything else in it: in the path of righteousness is life, and in its pathway there is no death.

That is a startling sentence for the Old Testament, where the grave is usually the horizon of everything. Here is a road with no death on it — not death postponed or made gentler, but a pathway on which the thing is simply absent.

Proverbs says it and cannot explain it. The explanation walks out of a tomb a thousand years later and says it in the first person: whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die (John 11:25-26). The path of righteousness is a person, and there is no death anywhere on him.

12.theology: The image of God and the ethics of speech. Chapter 12's speech proverbs (vv. 17–22) are grounded in the theology of the image of God. Human beings are made in the image of the God who spoke the world into existence, whose word is truth, and whose name is faithful. When human beings speak truly, they reflect their Maker; when they lie, they distort the image and align themselves with the one Jesus calls "a liar and the father of lies" (John 8:44). The seriousness with which Proverbs treats truthfulness — "an abomination to the LORD" for lying, "his delight" for faithfulness — reflects this theological grounding. Speech is not neutral; it is one of the primary arenas in which the image of God is either honoured or defaced.
12.examples:
Then: "Whoever is righteous has regard for the life of his animal" (v. 10) is one of Proverbs' most unexpected ethical observations. Animal welfare is a sign of righteousness — the capacity for care extends beyond the human community to the creatures entrusted to human stewardship. This is creation ethics in miniature: the righteous person treats their animals with the same kind of regard that the Creator has for his creation. The wicked person's "mercy" — even their attempts at kindness — is described as "cruel," because cruelty is what happens when you imitate mercy without the character that makes mercy real.

Now: "A good word makes him glad" (v. 25) is the pastoral charter for encouragement as a spiritual discipline. In a culture of criticism — online and offline — where the easy response to anything is scepticism, cynicism, or complaint, the deliberate cultivation of the encouraging word is an act of wisdom and love. Keller points to this as an application of the gospel: the person who knows they are loved and welcomed by God is freed to give away the good words that others need. Encouragement is not flattery; it is the truthful affirmation of what is genuinely good in a person, offered at the moment when the weight of anxiety needs a word to lift it.

13.title: Hope Deferred
13.text: <sup>1</sup>A wise son hears his father's instruction, but a scoffer does not listen to rebuke.<sup>2</sup>From the fruit of his mouth a man eats what is good, but the desire of the treacherous is for violence.<sup>3</sup>Whoever guards his mouth preserves his life; he who opens wide his lips comes to ruin.<sup>4</sup>The soul of the sluggard craves and gets nothing, while the soul of the diligent is richly supplied.<sup>5</sup>The righteous hates falsehood, but the wicked brings shame and disgrace.<sup>6</sup>Righteousness guards him whose way is blameless, but sin overthrows the wicked.<sup>7</sup>One pretends to be rich, yet has nothing; another pretends to be poor, yet has great wealth.<sup>8</sup>The ransom of a man's life is his wealth, but a poor man hears no threat.<sup>9</sup>The light of the righteous rejoices, but the lamp of the wicked will be put out.<sup>10</sup>By insolence comes nothing but strife, but with those who take advice is wisdom.<sup>11</sup>Wealth gained hastily will dwindle, but whoever gathers little by little will increase it.<sup>12</sup>Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a desire fulfilled is a tree of life.<sup>13</sup>Whoever despises the word brings destruction on himself, but he who reveres the commandment will be rewarded.<sup>14</sup>The teaching of the wise is a fountain of life, that one may turn away from the snares of death.<sup>15</sup>Good sense wins favor, but the way of the treacherous is their ruin.<sup>16</sup>Every prudent man acts with knowledge, but a fool flaunts his folly.<sup>17</sup>A wicked messenger falls into trouble, but a faithful envoy brings healing.<sup>18</sup>Poverty and disgrace come to him who ignores instruction, but whoever heeds reproof is honored.<sup>19</sup>A desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul, but to turn away from evil is an abomination to fools.<sup>20</sup>Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, but the companion of fools will suffer harm.<sup>21</sup>Disaster pursues sinners, but the righteous are rewarded with good.<sup>22</sup>A good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children, but the sinner's wealth is laid up for the righteous.<sup>23</sup>The fallow ground of the poor would yield much food, but it is swept away through injustice.<sup>24</sup>Whoever spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him is diligent to discipline him.<sup>25</sup>The righteous has enough to satisfy his appetite, but the belly of the wicked suffers want.
13.overview:
Chapter 13 touches on themes of wealth and poverty (both real and pretended), the long view of wisdom, the power of association, and the nature of parental love. At its emotional centre is one of the most universally resonant verses in Proverbs: "Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a desire fulfilled is a tree of life" (v. 12). This proverb is not an instruction or a command; it is a diagnosis — a precise and compassionate observation about the inner experience of waiting, disappointment, and eventual fulfilment.

The chapter also contains two of Proverbs' most important social and relational observations: "Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise" (v. 20) — the wisdom of chosen community — and "whoever spares the rod hates his son" (v. 24) — the love that disciplines. Together these proverbs describe the two primary environments in which wisdom is formed: the community of the wise that shapes us by association, and the family of love that shapes us by discipline. Neither is optional; both are forms of love in action.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 13 — Discipline, Hope, and the Intergenerational Stakes of Wisdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 13 is preoccupied with consequences that extend across time: hope deferred and hope fulfilled (v.12), a good man leaving an inheritance (v.22), the rod of discipline and the child's future (v.24). Wealth and poverty appear in multiple angles—honest gain, fraudulent gain, the wealth of the diligent, the ruin of the sluggard. Every proverb is a small window into the long-game nature of wisdom.
verseByVerse.theology: Proverbs 13 insists that parental discipline is an act of love (v.24)—one of the most countercultural claims in the book. The culture says love means giving children what they want; Proverbs says love means shaping children into what they should be. The parent who withholds discipline hates the child; the parent who applies it loves.
verseByVerse.examples: Hope deferred as heart-sickness (v.12) is one of Scripture's most psychologically accurate descriptions. Every counselor recognizes it: the patient who has longed for something good and been repeatedly disappointed. The gospel addresses hope deferred not by promising quick fulfillment but by providing an anchor (Heb. 6:19) that holds even when fulfillment is delayed.

verseByVerse.quote: A wise son hears his father's instruction, but a scoffer does not listen to rebuke. From the fruit of his mouth a man eats what is good, but the desire of the treacherous is for violence. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A wise son hears his father’s instruction, but a scoffer does not listen to rebuke. The Hebrew of the first line has no verb at all — literally a wise son, a father’s instruction — and translators supply hears. The gap is eloquent. The relation between the two is so direct that the sentence does not bother to say what it is.

And the contrast is not son against non-son. It is son against scoffer, which is a description of a stance rather than a stage of life. A man of fifty can be either, and the difference is entirely in what happens when somebody tells him something he did not want to hear.

Then v. 2: from the fruit of his mouth a man eats what is good, but the desire of the treacherous is for violence. The harvest image again — a man eats his own words — and the second half is the sharp part. It does not say the treacherous man commits violence. It says he desires it, which is a statement about what he enjoys thinking about when nothing is happening.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever guards his mouth preserves his life; he who opens wide his lips comes to ruin. The soul of the sluggard craves and gets nothing, while the soul of the diligent is richly supplied. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever guards his mouth preserves his life; he who opens wide his lips comes to ruin. The stakes are set as high as they go, and guards is a military word — a sentry over a gate.

The picture of the second half is a man with his mouth wide open, and what it describes is not malice. It is the absence of a door. Whatever arrives inside goes out, and everyone learns this about him within a fortnight — which means that in time nobody tells him anything, and he is the last to know it.

Then v. 4, which is the best single sentence in Proverbs about laziness: the soul of the sluggard craves and gets nothing, while the soul of the diligent is richly supplied.

Notice that the sluggard is not described as wanting little. He craves. He is not a man of low ambition; his ambitions may be considerably larger than his diligent neighbour’s, because they cost him nothing to hold. That is the thing this book keeps saying and nobody quite believes about himself: laziness is not a failure of desire. The sluggard wants a great deal, and wanting is the only part of the process he ever does.

Which is a test any reader can run. Take the thing you have most wanted for the last three years. What has been done about it this month?

verseByVerse.quote: The righteous hates falsehood, but the wicked brings shame and disgrace. Righteousness guards him whose way is blameless, but sin overthrows the wicked. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The righteous hates falsehood. Not avoids it — hates it, which is a feeling rather than a policy, and it is exactly the definition of the fear of the LORD given at 8:13.

That is a searching thing, because most Christians would say they disapprove of lying and would never claim to hate it. A man who merely disapproves will decline to tell a lie and will listen quite comfortably to somebody else telling one. The revulsion described here is what makes a man uncomfortable in a room where the account being given is not true, even when saying so would cost him.

Then v. 6: righteousness guards him whose way is blameless, but sin overthrows the wicked. Both nouns are agents; neither man is being acted on from outside. This is the structural claim of the whole book in eight words — righteousness is not merely rewarded, it protects, and sin is not merely punished, it trips.

verseByVerse.quote: One pretends to be rich, yet has nothing; another pretends to be poor, yet has great wealth. The ransom of a man's life is his wealth, but a poor man hears no threat. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
One pretends to be rich, yet has nothing; another pretends to be poor, yet has great wealth.

Two men, two performances, opposite directions, and Proverbs declines to say which is worse. The first is 12:9 again, the man financing an appearance. The second is subtler and rather more common among religious people: a man with money who is careful never to look as though he has any, and who thereby escapes both the envy of his neighbours and every appeal for help.

What the verse actually exposes is the pretending, in either direction. Both men have decided that other people should hold a false picture of their circumstances, and both are managing it daily, and neither is free.

Then v. 8, which is bleak and true: the ransom of a man’s life is his wealth, but a poor man hears no threat. A rich man can buy his way out of danger — and is also worth kidnapping. The poor man has neither the ransom nor the risk. Nobody is watching him.

Proverbs is not romanticising poverty; it has already called it a destroyer (10:15). It is noting, drily, that everything valuable comes attached to something, and that the man envying another’s position is usually looking at only one side of the ledger.

verseByVerse.quote: The light of the righteous rejoices, but the lamp of the wicked will be put out. By insolence comes nothing but strife, but with those who take advice is wisdom. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The light of the righteous rejoices, but the lamp of the wicked will be put out. A strange verb for light — it rejoices, which in Hebrew has the sense of shining brightly and gladly at once, the way a fire does. And the other man has a lamp, which is a smaller thing, and it is not said to fade. It is put out, by somebody.

Then v. 10, which repays a slow reading: by insolence comes nothing but strife, but with those who take advice is wisdom.

Nothing but. Proverbs is prepared to concede that most bad things produce a mixed result — the violent man gets rich, the adulteress offers real pleasure. Pride is granted nothing at all. It has never in the history of the world produced a single good outcome, and its entire yield is strife.

And the second half names the cure, which is not humility as a feeling but a habit that can be observed from outside: those who take advice. Not those who seek it, which is easy and flattering to the adviser. Those who take it.

verseByVerse.quote: Wealth gained hastily will dwindle, but whoever gathers little by little will increase it. Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a desire fulfilled is a tree of life. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wealth gained hastily will dwindle, but whoever gathers little by little will increase it. The Hebrew of the first phrase suggests wealth got from vapour — money that came from nowhere, quickly.

And the reason it goes is not that God disapproves of windfalls. It is that money is kept by a set of habits, and habits are built by the same slow process that builds savings. A man who has gathered little by little for fifteen years has, without noticing, become the sort of person who can hold money. A man handed the same sum on a Tuesday has not, and there is nothing in him that the money can rest on.

Then v. 12, and it is one of the most humane sentences in the Bible: hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a desire fulfilled is a tree of life.

Notice what Scripture is prepared to say. Not that a Christian should not be discouraged by long waiting, and not that the sickness is unbelief. It states as a plain fact that hope stretched out over years makes the heart ill — and the word is the ordinary word for being sick, the one used of bodies.

Anybody in a long wait knows how exact that is. The childlessness that is now in its ninth year. The job applications. The prodigal who has still not written. The illness that does not resolve and does not kill. What wears a person down is not the disappointment, which can be absorbed; it is the hoping, again, on a Tuesday, for something that has not come for so long that hoping has itself begun to feel foolish.

Scripture says that is an illness rather than a failing, and it does not scold. And it holds out the other half without pretending the wait is nothing: a desire fulfilled is a tree of life. The tree stands at the end of the Bible with its leaves for the healing of the nations, in a city where God will wipe away every tear and there is nothing left deferred (Revelation 21:4; 22:2). The waiting is real. It is also, and this is the whole of Christian hope, finite.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever despises the word brings destruction on himself, but he who reveres the commandment will be rewarded. The teaching of the wise is a fountain of life, that one may turn away from the snares of death. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever despises the word brings destruction on himself, but he who reveres the commandment will be rewarded. The verbs are opposites at the level of attitude — despising and revering — and neither is about behaviour. This is a proverb about the posture a man takes toward what God has said before he decides anything at all.

Then v. 14: the teaching of the wise is a fountain of life, that one may turn away from the snares of death.

The purpose clause is the useful part. Teaching is not given so that people may know things; it is given that one may turn away. It exists to change a direction of travel, which means instruction that produces admiration and no turning has failed, however good it was.

And the image of a snare is chosen with care. A snare is hidden, and a man walks into it while going about his business, which is why the antidote is not courage but information — somebody who knows where the wire is, telling him in advance.

verseByVerse.quote: Good sense wins favor, but the way of the treacherous is their ruin. Every prudent man acts with knowledge, but a fool flaunts his folly. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Good sense wins favour, but the way of the treacherous is their ruin. Favour here is what other people extend to a man for no reason he can enforce — the benefit of the doubt, the second chance, the recommendation nobody had to make. It cannot be demanded, and this verse says it accrues to good sense rather than to charm.

Then v. 16: every prudent man acts with knowledge, but a fool flaunts his folly.

Flaunts is literally spreads out, the way a merchant lays his goods on a cloth. That is the picture: a man displaying his folly like stock, with evident satisfaction, in the belief that it is doing him credit.

Which is the melancholy comedy of this book. The fool is not hiding anything. He is advertising, and everybody in the market can see what is on the cloth, and he is the only person present who thinks it is impressive.

verseByVerse.quote: A wicked messenger falls into trouble, but a faithful envoy brings healing. Poverty and disgrace come to him who ignores instruction, but whoever heeds reproof is honored. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A wicked messenger falls into trouble, but a faithful envoy brings healing.

Everybody is a messenger. Every day a person carries something from one party to another — what was said in the meeting, how the other side sees it, what a relative actually meant. And the message is never delivered neutrally; there is always a choice about emphasis, about which clause goes first, about the sentence that could be left out.

The faithful envoy is the man who carries it accurately, including the parts that complicate his own position. And the promise is startling for so ordinary a service: he brings healing. A great many broken relationships were broken by a message delivered with a slight lean on it, and a great many are mended by somebody who simply reported what was actually said.

Then v. 18: poverty and disgrace come to him who ignores instruction, but whoever heeds reproof is honoured. The word for ignores is about letting go, releasing a grip. Nothing is refused; something is simply not held on to.

verseByVerse.quote: A desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul, but to turn away from evil is an abomination to fools. Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, but the companion of fools will suffer harm. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul, but to turn away from evil is an abomination to fools. The two halves look unrelated and are not. Both are about the pull of wanting: the sweetness of getting what you want is real, and that is exactly why the fool finds the idea of turning away from something he wants not merely difficult but abominable — a word about revulsion. The suggestion disgusts him.

Then v. 20, which may be the most practically useful verse in Proverbs: whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, but the companion of fools will suffer harm.

The verb is becomes, and it happens by walking. Not by studying the wise, or admiring them, or agreeing with them — by being in their company over time, which is a process nobody directs and nobody notices happening to him.

Which turns the verse into the most searching question in the chapter, and it can be answered in a minute. Name the five people you spend the most hours with. That is a fairly accurate description of the man you will be in ten years, and it is far more accurate than your intentions.

And it comes with a warning against the flattering misreading. Nobody thinks of himself as being formed by his friends; everybody assumes he is the influence. Half the people in any group are wrong about that.

verseByVerse.quote: Disaster pursues sinners, but the righteous are rewarded with good. A good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children, but the sinner's wealth is laid up for the righteous. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Disaster pursues sinners, but the righteous are rewarded with good. The verb is a hunting word. Trouble is not described as arriving; it is described as following, and following implies a scent and no hurry.

Then v. 22: a good man leaves an inheritance to his children’s children, but the sinner’s wealth is laid up for the righteous.

Children’s children is the phrase to sit with, because it names a horizon almost nobody plans to. A man may plan for his own retirement and, if he is thoughtful, for his children. The verse describes a man building for people he will never meet, who will not know his name, and who will have no idea that the reason things were easier for them was decided in a kitchen in 1994.

And the inheritance in view is not primarily money. Money survives to grandchildren only occasionally; what reliably survives three generations is the pattern of a household — how arguments were conducted, whether promises were kept, whether God was spoken of naturally or not at all. Those are inherited whether or not anybody intends to leave them.

verseByVerse.quote: The fallow ground of the poor would yield much food, but it is swept away through injustice. Whoever spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him is diligent to discipline him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fallow ground of the poor would yield much food, but it is swept away through injustice.

This verse is regularly passed over and it should not be, because it is the flat contradiction of a lazy reading of the whole book. Proverbs has said a great deal about diligence and poverty, and it would be easy to leave with the impression that the poor are poor because they did not work. Here the same book says that the ground is good, the yield would be plentiful, and the crop is taken by injustice.

Not by drought. Not by idleness. By somebody — the creditor, the official, the landlord, the man with the shaved weight of 11:1. Poverty in Proverbs has more than one cause, and this is the verse that names the cause nobody in a comfortable congregation wants named.

Then v. 24, and it must be handled carefully: whoever spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him is diligent to discipline him.

Take first what the verse certainly claims, because it is not the part people argue about. It says that failing to correct a child is an act of hatred — that indulgence is not a mild form of love but its opposite, because the child is being left to find out from the world what a father would not tell him, and the world does not care about him. Every parent who has avoided a confrontation because the evening was going well knows this is true.

Then the harder question, on which godly readers differ and have long done so: does the rod require corporal punishment today? Those who say yes point out that the text says rod and means rod, and that Proverbs repeats it (22:15; 29:15). Those who say no point out that shebet is the shepherd’s implement of Psalm 23:4 — an instrument of guidance and protection as much as of striking — and that Proverbs uses vivid concrete language throughout for principles that reach wider than the picture. Both readings are held by people who love Scripture and their children, and the chapter’s own argument sits underneath either one: correction is love, and its absence is not.

What is not open to debate is the line, and it must be said plainly. Nothing in this verse licenses a parent to strike a child in anger, and nothing in it authorises injury, humiliation, or fear as a household atmosphere. That is not discipline; it is the thing Scripture forbids in the same breath as it commands the training — fathers, do not provoke your children to anger (Ephesians 6:4). Discipline in the Bible is the calm, consistent, costly attention of a parent who is entirely for the child, which is precisely why God’s own discipline of his people is offered as proof that they are sons and not strangers (Hebrews 12:7-8). If a reader recognises rage rather than love in his own house — his own, or one he knows of — this verse is not a defence. It is an indictment, and the right response is to get help today.

verseByVerse.quote: The righteous has enough to satisfy his appetite, but the belly of the wicked suffers want. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The righteous has enough to satisfy his appetite, but the belly of the wicked suffers want.

The chapter ends on a small word, and everything is in it: enough.

Not abundance, and not scarcity. The righteous man in this verse is not described as wealthy; he is described as satisfied, which is a different quantity and is not measured in the same units. And the wicked man is not said to have less. He is said to want — which is a condition of the belly rather than of the barn, and no amount of grain has ever cured it.

Which is where this book has been going since ch. 10. Two men may have the same income, the same house and the same salary, and one of them is full and the other is hungry, and the difference is not in what they hold.

The Lord Jesus stood among people who had eaten bread in a wilderness the day before and told them the whole matter in a sentence: I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger (John 6:35). Enough is not a figure that a man arrives at by acquiring. It is what happens when he is finally fed by somebody who does not run out.

13.theology: Hope, eschatology, and the tree of life. Proverbs 13:12 — "hope deferred makes the heart sick, but a desire fulfilled is a tree of life" — carries eschatological weight that the original context only hints at. The "tree of life" is a deliberate echo of Genesis 2–3 and an anticipation of Revelation 22:2. Human longing for the desire finally fulfilled — for the hope that does not defer indefinitely — is the deepest longing of the creature for the Creator, for the restoration of the relationship and the world that sin destroyed. Every earthly experience of a desire fulfilled, every moment when the long-deferred hope finally arrives, is a shadow of the ultimate fulfilment: the face-to-face knowledge of God in the new creation, the tree of life available to all, the heart-sickness of waiting finally resolved. The gospel is the announcement that the desire has been fulfilled in Christ — and that the full experience of that fulfilment awaits the consummation of all things.
13.examples:
Then: "A good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children" (v. 22) sets a multigenerational horizon for wisdom and faithfulness. The wise person does not merely plan for their own flourishing but for the flourishing of their grandchildren — which requires the kind of long-term thinking, patient investment, and deferred gratification that Proverbs consistently commends. The contrast with "the sinner's wealth laid up for the righteous" reflects the reversal of fortunes that Proverbs sees in the long run: the unjust accumulation of the wicked ultimately benefits the righteous, whether through inheritance, restitution, or the simple working of providential justice.

Now: "Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise" (v. 20) is the wisdom text for mentorship, spiritual direction, and the deliberate cultivation of community. Keller observes that the modern tendency toward therapeutic individualism — the assumption that growth is primarily an internal, private process — runs counter to Proverbs' social understanding of wisdom formation. We are shaped by our communities; the question is not whether we will be formed by others but which others will form us. The wise person chooses their community with the same intentionality that they choose their work, their diet, or their reading — because the community is forming them whether they are aware of it or not.

14.title: The Way That Seems Right

14.overview:
Chapter 14 contains one of the most sobering verses in Proverbs — "there is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death" (v. 12) — and one of the most theologically charged — "whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker" (v. 31). Together these two proverbs capture two dimensions of the book's wisdom: epistemological humility (I cannot fully trust my own judgment about what is right) and social theology (how I treat the poor is how I treat the one who made them).

The chapter also contains one of Proverbs' most unsentimental economic observations: "Where there are no oxen, the manger is clean, but abundant crops come by the strength of the ox" (v. 4). Risk, mess, and the management of difficult resources are the price of productivity. The clean manger is the achievement of the person who has avoided all complexity and produced nothing. This is the wisdom of entrepreneurship, leadership, and any endeavour that requires investment: there is no abundant harvest without the ox, and no ox without the mess.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 14 — The Wise Woman, False Witness, and the Fear of the Lord
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 14 opens with the wise woman who builds her house and the fool who tears it down, and closes with the king who honors God by caring for the poor. Between those bookends: the danger of false witness, the deceitfulness of the heart, the fear of the Lord as the only reliable fountain of life. Waltke notes that ch.14 has a particularly high concentration of fool-sayings, as if Proverbs is pressing the reader toward a decision.
verseByVerse.theology: The fear of the LORD appears explicitly in vv.2 and 26-27: it is the foundation of integrity, the fortress of the faithful, and the only reliable protection against the snares of death. Everything else in the chapter—wise speech, honest witness, care for the poor, measured anger—flows from this root. Fear of God is not a feeling but a comprehensive orientation of the person toward the real world as God governs it.
verseByVerse.examples: The poor appear twice (vv.20-21, 31): those who despise the neighbor sin, but those who are kind to the needy honor God. The social ethics of Proverbs are grounded in theology: the poor bear the image of their Maker, and how we treat them reveals how we actually regard him.

verseByVerse.quote: The wisest of women builds her house, but folly with her own hands tears it down. Whoever walks in uprightness fears the LORD, but he who is devious in his ways despises him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wisest of women builds her house, but folly with her own hands tears it down.

The house here is not masonry; it is the household — the whole small world of people and habits and atmosphere that one person can make or unmake. And the arresting phrase is with her own hands. Nobody came in from outside. The demolition is done by the person who lives there, which is the ordinary way households are lost.

And building is the slower verb. A home is made by ten thousand acts nobody will ever list — meals produced, a tone kept when it would have been easier not to, somebody listened to at the end of a long day. It cannot be done in a fortnight, and it can be undone in one.

Then v. 2: whoever walks in uprightness fears the LORD, but he who is devious in his ways despises him. Note the direction of the sentence. It does not say that fearing God produces uprightness, though it does. It reads a man’s walk and tells him what it reveals about his view of God — which means a crooked life is not merely a moral failure but a statement, made with the feet, about whether anybody is watching.

verseByVerse.quote: By the mouth of a fool comes a rod for his back, but the lips of the wise will preserve them. Where there are no oxen, the manger is clean, but abundant crops come by the strength of the ox. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
By the mouth of a fool comes a rod for his back, but the lips of the wise will preserve them. The fool’s mouth is described as manufacturing the instrument of his own beating, which is the picture of 18:6-7 in one clause.

Then v. 4, which is one of the shrewdest verses in the Bible and is almost never preached: where there are no oxen, the manger is clean, but abundant crops come by the strength of the ox.

A clean stable sounds like an achievement, and it is the mark of a farm with no animals. No oxen means no mess, no feed bills, no vet, and no harvest either.

The principle reaches everywhere. Anything that produces also makes a mess, and there is a whole way of living that consists in choosing the empty manger. A church that runs no ministries has no complaints about them. A man with no children has an orderly house. A leader who starts nothing is never blamed for anything, and can point to a clean record made entirely of things he did not attempt.

So the verse asks a question worth asking of any tidy life: is this order, or is it emptiness? Because they look identical from outside, and only one of them will produce anything by autumn.

verseByVerse.quote: A faithful witness does not lie, but a false witness breathes out lies. A scoffer seeks wisdom in vain, but knowledge is easy for a man of understanding. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A faithful witness does not lie, but a false witness breathes out lies. The verb is the one from 6:19 — breathing, not speaking. The lie has become respiration: continuous, unnoticed, and necessary to him.

Then v. 6: a scoffer seeks wisdom in vain, but knowledge is easy for a man of understanding.

Both halves are surprising. The scoffer seeks — he is not indifferent, he is looking, and he does not find. And the man who already has understanding finds knowledge easy, which sounds unfair until the mechanism is clear.

The scoffer’s problem is not access; it is posture. He is looking for wisdom in order to have it, to use it, to be the man who knows — and wisdom in this book will not be acquired by anybody unwilling to be changed by it. He is trying to purchase without the currency.

Whereas the man of understanding has already paid the entrance fee at 9:8, and can therefore receive from anybody, including people beneath him. Nothing is easier than learning when you do not mind who you learn from.

verseByVerse.quote: Leave the presence of a fool, for there you do not meet words of knowledge. The wisdom of the prudent is to discern his way, but the folly of fools is deceiving. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Leave the presence of a fool, for there you do not meet words of knowledge.

The counsel is blunt and it is spatial: get up and go. Not argue, not correct — 9:8 has already explained why that fails — simply be somewhere else.

And the reason given is oddly mild. Not that the fool is dangerous, but that there is nothing there. It is a verse about the value of a man’s hours. A conversation that will not yield anything is a conversation that costs an hour and gives nothing back, and a life has a fixed number of those.

Which needs one guard, because a Christian cannot read this as permission to avoid people he finds tiresome. The fool of Proverbs is a settled type, not a man who is annoying; and Christ was frequently in rooms with people from whom he received nothing at all. The verse concerns where a man goes for counsel and company, not whom he is willing to love.

Then v. 8: the wisdom of the prudent is to discern his way. The whole of wisdom, in one clause, is knowing where you actually are and where this road goes — which is a smaller and more useful definition than most people carry.

verseByVerse.quote: Fools mock at the guilt offering, but the upright enjoy acceptance. The heart knows its own bitterness, and no stranger shares its joy. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fools mock at the guilt offering, but the upright enjoy acceptance.

The guilt offering was the sacrifice a man brought when he had wronged somebody and had to make it right — the animal, the restitution, the public admission that he had been in the wrong. To mock at it is to find the whole business of making amends ridiculous.

And that attitude survives perfectly well in people who have never seen an altar. It is in the man who cannot apologise without an explanation attached, who treats every request for repair as an overreaction, and who genuinely believes that saying sorry is something weaker people do. He is not mocking a ritual. He is mocking the idea that he could need one.

Then v. 10, and it is one of the loneliest and truest sentences in Scripture: the heart knows its own bitterness, and no stranger shares its joy.

There is a floor beneath every human being that nobody else stands on. The grief cannot be fully transmitted; the joy cannot be fully explained. A person can be well loved, well married, surrounded — and still, at the deepest point, unaccompanied. That is not a failure of his friendships. It is the human condition, and Proverbs states it without softening it.

But it is exactly here that the gospel makes a claim nothing else makes. There is one who knew what was in man and needed nobody to tell him (John 2:25); who was himself a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief; and who went down into the one place where no friend could follow, alone, so that no one else would ever have to be. The heart’s bitterness is known to somebody, and he did not learn it from outside.

verseByVerse.quote: The house of the wicked will be destroyed, but the tent of the upright will flourish. There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The house of the wicked will be destroyed, but the tent of the upright will flourish. The mismatch is the argument: house against tent. The wicked man has the better building and the upright man has canvas, and the canvas is what is still standing.

Then v. 12, which is one of the most quoted verses in the book and one of the most necessary: there is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death.

Seems right. Not looks tempting, not feels good — seems right, which is the language of conscience rather than of appetite. This is a man doing what he sincerely believes to be correct.

Which is why the verse is so much more disturbing than a warning about temptation. Everybody knows he can be led astray by wanting something. This says he can be led astray by his own moral judgment, exercised carefully and in good faith. Sincerity is not a safeguard, and a clear conscience is not a verdict — Paul, who had persecuted the church, said he had lived in all good conscience the whole time (Acts 23:1).

So the verse quietly demolishes the age’s favourite maxim, which is to be true to yourself. Proverbs replies that the self is the instrument in question, and it does not come calibrated. The only remedy it offers is the one it has offered all along: something outside the man — a word he did not write, and people who will tell him the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: Even in laughter the heart may ache, and the end of joy may be grief. The backslider in heart will be filled with the fruit of his ways, and a good man will be filled with the fruit of his ways. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even in laughter the heart may ache, and the end of joy may be grief.

Scripture is not usually credited with this kind of observation, and it should be. Here is the Bible noting, without comment, that a man can be laughing and in pain at the same moment, and that the two do not cancel.

Everybody has been in that room. The party where somebody is grieving and laughing on cue. The Sunday morning where a person is genuinely glad to be there and carrying something nobody in the building knows about. And the verse comes immediately after v. 10 — the heart knows its own bitterness — because they belong together: what is hidden is hidden even in the middle of company, and often especially there.

Two things follow. One is for the person doing it: this is not hypocrisy, and Scripture does not name it as such. A man may laugh honestly while something in him is broken, and he is not performing.

The other is for everybody else, and it is the practical use of the verse. The most cheerful person in the room is not thereby accounted for. Proverbs has just told the church, in eight words, that its estimate of who needs attention is unreliable — and the only correction is to ask somebody how he actually is, and to leave enough silence afterwards for the answer.

verseByVerse.quote: The simple believes everything, but the prudent gives thought to his steps. One who is wise is cautious and turns away from evil, but a fool is reckless and careless. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The simple believes everything, but the prudent gives thought to his steps.

The simple of this book is the man with no lock on his door, and here his defining quality is credulity — he believes whatever he was told most recently, and most persuasively.

Scripture treats this as a fault and not as an innocence. There is a kind of Christian who regards being sceptical as unspiritual, and who therefore forwards whatever he was sent, believes whatever was said with confidence, and is a reliable conduit for anything at all. Proverbs is not commending suspicion, which is its own sin. It is asking for a man who checks.

And the alternative it gives is not cleverness but attention: the prudent gives thought to his steps. He looks where his feet are going. That is all.

Then v. 16, and the pairing is exact: one who is wise is cautious and turns away from evil, but a fool is reckless and careless. The word for the fool’s recklessness suggests a man storming through — confident, quick, and entirely unbothered — and the tragedy of it is that from outside, especially to the young, that man looks considerably more impressive than the one who stopped to look.

verseByVerse.quote: A man of quick temper acts foolishly, and a man of evil devices is hated. The simple inherit folly, but the prudent are crowned with knowledge. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man of quick temper acts foolishly, and a man of evil devices is hated. Two men are set side by side, and the pairing is instructive: the hot man and the calculating one. Proverbs puts them in the same verse because both are trouble, and it is not obvious which does more damage. The first is loud and forgiven; the second is quiet and hated.

And note the verb attached to the temper: he acts foolishly. Nothing is said about how he feels. Anger in Scripture is not itself the sin; the speed is. What is condemned here is the absence of any gap between the feeling and the act, which is precisely what makes a hot temper so destructive — not its intensity but its short fuse to the hands and the mouth.

Then v. 18: the simple inherit folly, but the prudent are crowned with knowledge. Inheritance is a passive word. The simple man does not choose folly; he receives it, having done nothing, which is what happens to anybody who makes no decision at all.

verseByVerse.quote: The evil bow down before the good, the wicked at the gates of the righteous. The poor is disliked even by his neighbor, but the rich has many friends. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The evil bow down before the good, the wicked at the gates of the righteous. It is a statement about the end of the story rather than about next Thursday, and Proverbs is content to say it flatly. The current arrangement is not the settled one.

Then v. 20, and the book’s unnerving honesty returns: the poor is disliked even by his neighbour, but the rich has many friends.

That is not advice. Nothing in the sentence commends what it describes. It is Proverbs saying out loud what everybody has observed and nobody says — that poverty costs a man his friendships, that people find the unlucky faintly tiring, and that the man with resources will never lack company and will never be sure why he has it.

And the verse is placed exactly where it is so that v. 21 can land on top of it. The book reports the world as it is, and then tells the reader that he is not permitted to live in it.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever despises his neighbor is a sinner, but blessed is he who is generous to the poor. Do they not go astray who devise evil? Those who devise good meet steadfast love and faithfulness. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever despises his neighbour is a sinner, but blessed is he who is generous to the poor.

This is the reply to v. 20, and it comes immediately. Yes, the poor man is disliked; and the disliking is named a sin, which is a far heavier word than Proverbs usually reaches for in a social observation.

Note also that despising is treated as an action. Nobody in this verse has done anything to the neighbour. A man is condemned here for an attitude he has never voiced and would deny if asked — which is uncomfortable, and is precisely how contempt operates: it lives entirely in the way somebody is regarded, and it leaks anyway.

Then v. 22: those who devise good meet steadfast love and faithfulness. Those are the two great covenant words, hesed and emet — the pair used of God himself on the mountain (Exodus 34:6). A man who spends his life planning good for people does not merely acquire a reputation. He is described as meeting the character of God coming the other way.

verseByVerse.quote: In all toil there is profit, but mere talk tends only to poverty. The crown of the wise is their wealth, but the folly of fools brings folly. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
In all toil there is profit, but mere talk tends only to poverty.

All toil. Not the interesting kind, not the kind that suits a man’s gifts — all of it. That is a word for anybody whose work is dull, unnoticed, and apparently pointless, which is most work that has ever been done. Proverbs says there is profit in it, and it does not qualify the claim.

And the contrast is not idleness but mere talk — literally the word of the lips. The man being warned about is not lying on a sofa. He is discussing it: the plan, the analysis, the things that ought to be done, the meeting about the meeting. Talk feels remarkably like progress, which is why it is so easy to substitute, and Proverbs prices it exactly. It tends only to poverty.

Then v. 24: the crown of the wise is their wealth, but the folly of fools brings folly. The second half is deliberately circular — folly produces more of itself, and that is the whole prospect. It compounds, and nothing else comes out.

verseByVerse.quote: A truthful witness saves lives, but one who breathes out lies is deceitful. In the fear of the LORD one has strong confidence, and his children will have a refuge. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A truthful witness saves lives. Four words, and they are worth more attention than they get. In a legal system without forensics, testimony was everything, and a man who told the truth in court literally kept somebody alive.

The principle outlives the courtroom. Telling the truth about what happened — in a family argument, a disciplinary process, a church dispute — is one of the few things an ordinary person can do that genuinely rescues somebody, and it usually costs him something with the people who would prefer a different account.

Then v. 26, and the promise reaches further than the man himself: in the fear of the LORD one has strong confidence, and his children will have a refuge.

The children are the surprise. A man’s settled trust in God turns out to be a shelter that other people can get inside — and any child raised in a house where the parents were not frightened knows exactly what is being described. The security was not explained to him. He simply grew up in a building that did not shake, and found later that the walls were somebody else’s faith.

verseByVerse.quote: The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life, that one may turn away from the snares of death. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life, that one may turn away from the snares of death.

The same sentence was said of the teaching of the wise at 13:14, word for word in the second half. Here it is said of the fear of the LORD itself, and the substitution is the point: the teaching works because of what it puts a man in front of.

And the two images are chosen against each other. A fountain is out in the open, running, and anybody can see it. A snare is hidden under leaves and catches a man who was not doing anything wrong at the time. So the verse is not offering courage against a visible enemy; it is offering information about ground a man cannot read.

Which is why the whole book keeps insisting that this fear is not a mood but a relation. The one who knows where the wires are is not the traveller. He is the one who set the country out, and who has walked the whole length of that road himself, and came back.

verseByVerse.quote: In a multitude of people is the glory of a king, but without people a prince is ruined. Whoever is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who has a hasty temper exalts folly. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
In a multitude of people is the glory of a king, but without people a prince is ruined. A king with no subjects is a man in a hat. Whatever authority is, it exists in a relation, and the glory of the office is located in the people rather than in the man — which is the flat opposite of how almost every ruler in history has understood it.

Then v. 29: whoever is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who has a hasty temper exalts folly.

Slowness is being called understanding, which is a strange compliment until the mechanics are clear. A man who is slow to anger is not a man with weaker feelings. He is a man who has enough information to wait — who knows that the first account is not the whole account (18:17), that the offence may not have been meant, that he has been wrong before at exactly this point. Speed in anger is a symptom of a small picture.

And the description of God himself, given in his own words, heads the list with this quality: slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love (Exodus 34:6). Not incapable of anger. Slow to it — which is why anybody is still here.

verseByVerse.quote: A tranquil heart gives life to the flesh, but envy makes the bones rot. Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker, but he who is generous to the needy honors him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A tranquil heart gives life to the flesh, but envy makes the bones rot.

Two medical claims, and the Hebrew is entirely comfortable making them. What happens inside a man shows up in his body: peace is described as feeding the flesh, and envy as a disease of the skeleton — the deepest, slowest, least visible part, where nothing can be reached.

And envy deserves the description, because it is the one sin that gives its owner no pleasure whatever. Greed enjoys the money; lust enjoys the moment; pride enjoys itself. Envy is pure ache. It requires the constant contemplation of somebody else’s good, cannot be satisfied by anything happening to the envier, and would be relieved only by another man’s loss — which is why it rots rather than burns.

Then v. 31, which is one of the great social verses of the Old Testament: whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker, but he who is generous to the needy honours him.

Follow the logic, because it is doing something enormous. The poor man is not defended here on the grounds that he is deserving, or innocent, or likely to repay. He is defended on the grounds of who made him — so that treating him with contempt is not primarily an offence against him at all. It is an insult delivered upward, to God, about the quality of his work.

Which means there is no way to be right with God while holding the poor in contempt. The two are the same transaction, and Christ made it explicit and personal: as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me (Matthew 25:40).

verseByVerse.quote: The wicked is overthrown through his evildoing, but the righteous finds refuge in his death. Wisdom rests in the heart of a man of understanding, but it makes itself known even in the midst of fools. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wicked is overthrown through his evildoing, but the righteous finds refuge in his death.

Stop at that last clause, because it is extraordinary and easy to miss. In his death. Not in his life, not before it — the righteous man is described as finding shelter in the very place where shelter runs out.

The Old Testament very rarely says anything like this. Sheol is usually its horizon, and the psalms ask, reasonably, what use a man is to God in the grave. Here is a sentence that steps over the edge and reports that the ground holds.

How, this verse does not say. It could not. But the Christian reading it knows why the sentence was allowed to stand in the book for a thousand years before anybody could explain it, because somebody went into death and made it a place where there is now a refuge. To die is gain (Philippians 1:21) is Proverbs 14:32 with the explanation attached.

Then v. 33: wisdom rests in the heart of a man of understanding. Rests — it is settled there, quietly, not on display. It does not need to be produced in every conversation, which is how you can generally tell it is real.

verseByVerse.quote: Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people. A servant who deals wisely has the king's favor, but his wrath falls on one who acts shamefully. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people.

The chapter has spent thirty-three verses on individuals, and now the same principle is applied to a country — with the significant phrase any people. Not Israel only. Any of them, including the ones that have never heard of the covenant.

Which is Proverbs’ steady assumption and the reason it is such an unusual book. The moral order is not a set of house rules for the people of God. It is the way the world is made, so that a nation with no interest in God at all still rises by honesty and decays by corruption, exactly as this book says, and its own historians will describe the process without once mentioning him.

And the word for reproach means disgrace in the eyes of others — the loss of a nation’s standing. Sin does not merely damage a country internally; it makes it contemptible.

Then v. 35, and the chapter ends with a servant in front of a king: a servant who deals wisely has the king’s favour. After a verse about nations, one man doing his job well. That is the shape of this book. It never lets the reader stay at the level of nations, because righteousness that exalts a country is not enacted by countries. It is enacted on Tuesday, by a servant, in a room.

14.theology: Epistemological humility and the way that seems right. Proverbs 14:12 is the wisdom literature's most explicit warning against the fundamental human epistemological problem: we cannot fully trust our own moral perception. The fall has distorted not only our wills but our minds — we rationalise, justify, and self-deceive with remarkable sophistication. Reformed theology calls this the noetic effects of sin: the corruption of human reason by the fall. The antidote Proverbs prescribes is not the exercise of more careful reason but the submission of reason to the word of God: "trust in the LORD with all your heart and do not lean on your own understanding" (3:5). The way that seems right is diagnosed by the standard of the one whose ways are always right — and that standard is available in Scripture, received by the humble, and applied by the fear of the LORD.
14.examples:
Then: "Whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker" (v. 31) had immediate and specific application in the economic realities of ancient Israel: the wealthy landowner who withheld wages, the merchant who used false weights, the judge who took bribes — all were doing theology, whether they knew it or not. The prophetic tradition (Amos, Isaiah, Micah) hammers on exactly this point: social injustice is theological offence. Proverbs frames it as wisdom: the person who grasps this truth — that the poor person is God's image-bearer — will treat them accordingly, not merely out of compassion but out of reverence.

Now: "The way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death" (v. 12) is the most important verse in Proverbs for an age that has made individual moral intuition the supreme ethical authority. "Seems right to me" has become the clinching argument in contemporary moral discourse. Proverbs' response is not to deny the importance of moral intuition but to insist that it is fallible — fallen, distorted, self-serving — and requires the correction of a standard outside itself. The fear of the LORD, received through Scripture, is that standard. The person who submits their "seems right" to God's word is practising the deepest form of epistemological humility.
