15.overview:
Chapter 15 is rich in speech proverbs, "better than" comparisons, and observations about God's active engagement with human life. It opens with one of the most practically powerful proverbs in the book — "a soft answer turns away wrath" — and closes with the thesis of the entire wisdom tradition: "the fear of the LORD is instruction in wisdom, and humility comes before honor." The chapter consistently chooses quality of life over quantity: a little with the fear of the LORD over great treasure and trouble; a dinner of herbs where love is over a fattened ox with hatred.

The "better than" proverbs of this chapter (vv. 16–17) represent one of Proverbs' most important rhetorical strategies: the deliberate revaluation of what the world considers valuable. Great treasure, fattened oxen, grand feasts — these are the markers of success that every culture celebrates. Proverbs does not deny that they are good; it insists that they are less good than the things that money cannot buy: the fear of the LORD, love, peace, and the presence of God. The person who has learned to prefer the genuinely better over the apparently better has taken a long step toward wisdom.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 15 — Soft Words, Watchful God, and the Discipline That Leads to Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 15 opens with the most famous proverb on speech ('a soft answer turns away wrath') and closes with the fear of the LORD as the path to life. In between: the LORD who watches everywhere (v.3), the glad heart that makes a cheerful face (v.13), the value of the multitude of counselors (v.22), and the discipline that leads to the honored life (v.33). The chapter is a sustained meditation on what it means to live before the watching God.
verseByVerse.theology: God's omniscience (v.3) is not abstract theology but a pastoral reality: the eyes of the LORD are everywhere, watching evil and good. This should produce honest speech, careful conduct, and the joyful sobriety of knowing that you are never unwatched. The person who internalizes this lives differently—not in anxiety but in the freedom that comes from consistent accountability.
verseByVerse.examples: The cheerful heart and glad face (vv.13-15) are not commanded but produced: they are the fruit of wisdom, not its prerequisite. The person who fears God and walks in wisdom acquires a disposition of joy as a byproduct. Discipline (vv.31-33) is the path, not an obstacle—those who receive reproof inhabit wisdom.

verseByVerse.quote: A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger. The tongue of the wise commends knowledge, but the mouths of fools pour out folly. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.

Of all the verses in Proverbs this is the one a person is most likely to have a chance to obey today, and the most likely to fail. It describes a specific moment: somebody has come at you angry, and there is a gap of about two seconds in which the whole thing is decided.

Note that a soft answer is still an answer. This is not the counsel to say nothing, and it is not surrender — the content may be entirely firm. What is soft is the temperature. Anger works by contagion; it is trying to raise yours, and the reason a mild reply works is that it gives the fire nothing to take hold of.

And it is genuinely hard, because a soft answer feels like losing. Everything in a man wants to match what he was given, and to match it slightly higher, and he can produce the sentence that would do it instantly. The two seconds are the whole battle, and nobody watching will ever know that a battle occurred.

Then v. 2: the tongue of the wise commends knowledge, but the mouths of fools pour out folly. Pour out is the word for a spring bubbling over. It requires no decision and it does not stop.

verseByVerse.quote: The eyes of the LORD are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good. A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but perverseness in it breaks the spirit. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eyes of the LORD are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good.

A verse that has been used almost entirely as a threat, and is mostly a comfort. Read the last clause: he keeps watch on the evil and the good. Both. And the good are the ones who usually need to hear it, because the standing complaint of the righteous in Scripture is not that God sees too much but that nobody sees anything.

The faithful woman nursing somebody through a decade of illness with no audience. The man who declined the dishonest arrangement and lost the contract and could not explain why to anybody. The person who has forgiven the same relative eleven times in a room with no witnesses. All of it is watched, and none of it is lost.

Then v. 4: a gentle tongue is a tree of life, but perverseness in it breaks the spirit.

The tree of life is back — and here it is not wisdom or a righteous man but a manner of speaking. Gentleness is being called life-giving on its own terms, quite apart from what is said, which ought to be sobering to anybody who is confident that his content is sound.

And the other half is worse than it sounds: perverseness breaks the spirit. That is the crushed spirit of 18:14, the one nobody can carry — and here it is caused by a tongue. Words can do damage that Proverbs elsewhere describes as unbearable.

verseByVerse.quote: A fool despises his father's instruction, but whoever heeds reproof is prudent. In the house of the righteous there is much treasure, but trouble befalls the income of the wicked. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A fool despises his father’s instruction, but whoever heeds reproof is prudent. The word for despises means to treat as light — not to reject it but to weigh it and find it insubstantial. Nothing is refused. It simply does not register as important enough to act on.

Then v. 6: in the house of the righteous there is much treasure, but trouble befalls the income of the wicked.

The wicked man in this verse is not poor. He has an income, and the trouble arrives with it — attached to the money, travelling in the same envelope. What he gets and what ruins him are not two separate deliveries.

And the treasure in the righteous house is deliberately unspecified. Proverbs will not say it is money, because it very often is not, and everybody has been in a modest house that was plainly full of something.

verseByVerse.quote: The lips of the wise spread knowledge; not so the hearts of fools. The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the LORD, but the prayer of the upright is acceptable to him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lips of the wise spread knowledge; not so the hearts of fools. The mismatch is deliberate — lips against hearts. The problem with the fool is not that he says the wrong thing but that there is nothing to scatter, and a man cannot broadcast what he has not got.

Then v. 8, which is one of the most serious verses in the book: the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the LORD, but the prayer of the upright is acceptable to him.

Set the two halves side by side and the weighting is astonishing. On one side, a sacrifice — an animal, real money, a public act of religion, done correctly. On the other, a prayer, which costs nothing and can be said in a chair. And the expensive one is called an abomination while the free one is acceptable.

This is the great prophetic theme in miniature, the thing Isaiah and Amos and Micah all shouted: God does not accept religious activity as payment for a life. Worship offered by a man who is doing evil is not neutral, and it is not partial credit. It is offensive, precisely because it is an attempt to buy him off with his own property.

And the other half is where the comfort is, and it is enormous. The upright man’s prayer — no altar, no priest, no expense, nothing to bring — is received. What God wants has never been obtainable at a price, which is why the poorest person reading this has exactly the same access as anybody else.

And it should be said why it is received, since the upright man is not sinless either. There is one sacrifice that was never an abomination, offered once by somebody with nothing to buy off, and every prayer that has ever been accepted has been accepted through it.

verseByVerse.quote: The way of the wicked is an abomination to the LORD, but he loves him who pursues righteousness. There is severe discipline for him who forsakes the way; whoever hates reproof will die. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The way of the wicked is an abomination to the LORD, but he loves him who pursues righteousness.

Note the object of the love. Not the man who has attained righteousness — the man who pursues it. That is a participle, an ongoing chase, and it describes somebody who has not arrived and is still going.

Which is a sentence to hold on to for anybody who audits himself honestly and finds the results unimpressive. The verse does not attach God’s love to the score. It attaches it to the direction of travel, and a man who is genuinely after this — falling over, getting up, still after it — is described here as loved while the chase is going on.

Then v. 10, and it is the same truth from the other side: there is severe discipline for him who forsakes the way; whoever hates reproof will die. The severity is not the opposite of the love in v. 9. It is what love does when a man is leaving.

verseByVerse.quote: Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the LORD; how much more the hearts of the children of man! A scoffer does not like to be reproved; he will not go to the wise. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the LORD; how much more the hearts of the children of man!

Sheol is the realm of the dead and Abaddon means Destruction — between them the two most remote and impenetrable places the Hebrew mind could name. They are described as lying open, which in the Hebrew has the sense of being exposed, laid bare, with nothing covering them.

And then the argument, from the greater to the lesser: if that is transparent to him, what about the inside of a man?

Which is the most searching claim in the chapter, because the human heart is the one place everybody assumes is private. A man may be entirely known to his wife in every other respect and still hold the settled conviction that the interior is his own — the thing he actually thought when the news came, the reason underneath the reason he gave, the motive he has never once examined himself.

Proverbs says it is open, and open is a strong word: not inferred, not deduced from behaviour. Open, the way a book is open. And the mercy in that is easily missed. It means that when a man finally comes to God there is nothing to explain, and nothing he could disclose that would change the terms — because he was never being received on the basis of what was known about him.

Then v. 12: a scoffer does not like to be reproved; he will not go to the wise. He does not argue with the wise. He simply does not go where they are, and the arrangement looks from outside like a busy diary.

verseByVerse.quote: A glad heart makes a cheerful face, but by sorrow of heart the spirit is crushed. The heart of him who has understanding seeks knowledge, but the mouths of fools feed on folly. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A glad heart makes a cheerful face, but by sorrow of heart the spirit is crushed.

The first half describes something everybody has seen and nobody can manufacture. A face is not primarily an instrument of communication; it is a readout. What is inside comes up through it without permission, which is why a forced smile is detectable at ten paces by a child.

And the second half is the graver one, and it is anatomically ordered: sorrow is in the heart, and what breaks is the spirit. Grief, held long enough, does not stay where it started. It works downward and outward until the thing that carries a person gives way.

Proverbs states this as a fact about how human beings are built, not as a rebuke — and the practical consequence for a church is direct. A person carrying long sorrow is not failing; he is described here as being under a process. What such a man needs is not exhortation but the removal of some of the weight, which is what the body of Christ is for.

Then v. 14: the mouths of fools feed on folly. A diet, again — chosen daily, in small amounts, and nobody ever notices a single meal.

verseByVerse.quote: All the days of the afflicted are evil, but the cheerful of heart has a continual feast. Better is a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble with it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the days of the afflicted are evil, but the cheerful of heart has a continual feast.

This verse must not be turned into advice to cheer up, and it is regularly used that way. Read the first half carefully: all the days. Proverbs is not scolding the afflicted man; it is reporting, with real sympathy, that affliction colours everything — that the trouble is not confined to the hard hour but tints the whole week, so that even good things arrive through it. Anybody who has been in a long affliction will recognise a description rather than a criticism.

And the second half is not the cure prescribed to the first. It is a separate observation: that a person’s inner condition determines the taste of his circumstances more than his circumstances do. Two men eat the same dinner, and one of them is at a feast.

What the verse does not say is that the afflicted man can simply become the cheerful one by deciding. If he could, he would have. The right use of it is to notice how much of a life is decided in a place that money and events do not reach — and then to ask who has access to that place, which is a question with only one satisfying answer.

Then v. 16, and it belongs with what precedes: better is a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble with it. Proverbs does not say the little is preferable because money is corrupting. It says trouble comes with the treasure — packed in, part of the consignment — and asks the reader to price the whole delivery rather than the headline figure.

verseByVerse.quote: Better is a dinner of herbs where love is than a fattened ox and hatred with it. A hot-tempered man stirs up strife, but he who is slow to anger quiets contention. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Better is a dinner of herbs where love is than a fattened ox and hatred with it.

Two dinner tables, and the comparison is not between poverty and wealth. It is between two rooms.

The first is vegetables — the cheapest meal in the ancient world, what you ate when there was nothing else — and people who are glad to be there. The second is the best meal a household could produce, a whole fattened animal, on a table where somebody is not speaking to somebody.

Everybody has eaten both. And the thing to notice is that the second is not a failure by any external measure. The house is impressive, the food is genuine, and a photograph of it would be enviable. What has gone wrong is not visible in the room; it is in the space between two people sitting four feet apart.

Which is a verse to weigh when a decision is being made about hours, or a move, or a promotion. Households do not usually choose the fattened ox over the love. They choose the ox and assume the love will keep, and it is only years later that anybody notices what the meal is actually costing.

Then v. 18: a hot-tempered man stirs up strife, but he who is slow to anger quiets contention. Note that the second man is not passive. He quiets — an active verb, something done to a situation. Peacemaking is work, and the man doing it is usually the one who had the best grounds for being angry.

verseByVerse.quote: The way of a sluggard is like a hedge of thorns, but the path of the upright is a level highway. A wise son makes a glad father, but a foolish man despises his mother. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The way of a sluggard is like a hedge of thorns, but the path of the upright is a level highway.

This is the most psychologically precise thing Proverbs says about laziness, and it is not what a reader expects. The sluggard’s road is not empty and easy. It is thorns — every step snagged, everything an effort, nothing simple.

And that is exactly right, because the lazy man does not experience his life as restful. He experiences it as uniquely difficult. Everything is complicated: the paperwork he did not do has become a problem, the conversation he avoided has become a crisis, the small job left has grown into a large one, and each new task arrives entangled with three old ones.

The diligent man’s road is not easier because his life is easier. It is a level highway because he has been clearing it as he goes — and the clearing is the small, dull, immediate work that the sluggard skipped, one hour at a time, on the grounds that it was not urgent.

Then v. 20 returns to 10:1, and adds a colder verb: a foolish man despises his mother. Not grieves her now — despises. The sorrow of ch. 10 has hardened into contempt, which is what the passing of years does when nothing is repented of.

verseByVerse.quote: Folly is a joy to him who lacks sense, but a man of understanding walks straight ahead. Without counsel plans fail, but with many advisers they succeed. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Folly is a joy to him who lacks sense, but a man of understanding walks straight ahead. Folly is not described as a temptation he gives in to but as a joy — something he actively enjoys, the way another man enjoys music. That is why argument does not reach him. Nobody has ever been reasoned out of a pleasure.

Then v. 22: without counsel plans fail, but with many advisers they succeed.

Proverbs has said this before (11:14) and says it again, because it is the single most ignored piece of practical wisdom in the book. The verse is not about consulting an expert. It is about plurality — many — because one adviser is very often just a mirror with a different face.

And the practical test is uncomfortable and quick. Think of the last significant decision you made. How many people were consulted before it was settled, as against after? For most people the honest answer is that advice was sought at the point when the decision was already made and what was actually wanted was agreement.

verseByVerse.quote: To make an apt answer is a joy to a man, and a word in season, how good it is! The path of life leads upward for the prudent, that he may turn away from Sheol beneath. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
To make an apt answer is a joy to a man, and a word in season, how good it is!

The exclamation is unusual — Proverbs rarely raises its voice in delight — and it is aimed at something very small: the right thing, said at the right moment.

Everybody has received one. A sentence said to you at nineteen, or on the worst week of your life, that you have never lost, and that the speaker has almost certainly forgotten. It took four seconds and it is still working. That is what a word in season means, and the season is the whole point: the same words a month earlier or a fortnight later would have done nothing.

Which makes this a craft rather than a gift, and it can be pursued. It requires knowing the person, watching for the moment, and — the hardest part — saying nothing on all the other occasions, since a man who is always speaking cannot be in season, only frequent.

Then v. 24: the path of life leads upward for the prudent, that he may turn away from Sheol beneath. The Old Testament almost never draws the map this way, and here it does — one road going up and one going down, and a man on one of them. It is the same reach past the grave as 14:32, and the same silence about how. That would wait for a man who came down first, so that the path could lead up.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD tears down the house of the proud but maintains the widow's boundaries. The thoughts of the wicked are an abomination to the LORD, but gracious words are pure. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD tears down the house of the proud but maintains the widow’s boundaries.

Both halves are about property, and the pairing is the argument. On one side, a house demolished; on the other, boundary stones kept in place.

The widow is named because in Israel she was the standing example of somebody with no way to defend a claim. Her husband is dead, she has no standing at the gate, and boundary stones are easily moved at night by a neighbour who knows perfectly well that nothing will happen to him.

So the verse says something precise about how God works in the world. He is not merely sympathetic to the powerless; he is described as personally doing the job her husband would have done — walking the boundary, keeping the stones where they were put. And on the other side of the sentence he is pulling down a house nobody else could touch.

Then v. 26: gracious words are pure. A short clause with an interesting adjective. Purity is a temple word — what may be brought in — and it is applied here not to a sacrifice but to kindness in ordinary speech.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever is greedy for unjust gain troubles his own household, but he who hates bribes will live. The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer, but the mouth of the wicked pours out evil things. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever is greedy for unjust gain troubles his own household. The victim named is not the man he cheated. It is his family.

That is the connection greed never makes. He is doing it, in his own account of himself, for them — the house, the security, the future — and Proverbs says the arrangement he is building runs straight back into the rooms he is building it for. The word for troubles is the strong one from 11:29: he is not neglecting his household, he is damaging it, and he will be genuinely astonished when this becomes visible.

Then v. 28, and it is the answer to v. 1: the heart of the righteous ponders how to answer, but the mouth of the wicked pours out evil things.

The verb translated ponders is a meditation word — the same root used in the psalms of murmuring over God’s law. It is not calculation. It is the deliberate turning over of something before speaking, and the picture is of a man taking longer than the conversation strictly allows.

Which is the discipline underneath most of this chapter’s teaching, and it is unglamorous. The soft answer of v. 1, the apt word of v. 23, the quieted contention of v. 18 all require the same thing: a gap. Not a better character produced on the spot, but a pause long enough for one to operate.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is far from the wicked, but he hears the prayer of the righteous. The light of the eyes rejoices the heart, and good news refreshes the bones. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD is far from the wicked, but he hears the prayer of the righteous.

That first half will frighten the wrong reader, so say plainly who it describes. The wicked of this book are not people who have sinned; everybody has. They are people settled in a direction, unwilling to be corrected, who have no intention of changing — and the distance is not primarily a punishment but a description of which way they are facing.

A man who is anxious about this verse has already shown he is not the man in it. Nobody in the first half of that sentence is troubled by it.

And the second half needs saying to Christians who suspect they are shouting at a ceiling: he hears. Not he will answer as requested — that is a different promise, and the Bible is careful about it. But heard, every time, without exception, and no prayer offered by somebody who belongs to him has ever failed to arrive.

Then v. 30: the light of the eyes rejoices the heart, and good news refreshes the bones. The light of the eyes is somebody’s face brightening at the sight of you — which costs the giver nothing and is one of the few things in this chapter anybody can do a dozen times before lunch.

verseByVerse.quote: The ear that listens to life-giving reproof will dwell among the wise. Whoever ignores instruction despises himself, but he who listens to reproof gains intelligence. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ear that listens to life-giving reproof will dwell among the wise.

The whole man is reduced to one organ, and the promise attached to it is company. He will dwell among the wise — not become impressive, but end up in a particular room, with particular people, because that is where a man who can take correction eventually finds himself.

Then v. 32, which is the sharpest way this book ever puts it: whoever ignores instruction despises himself.

Not despises the teacher. Himself. The man who will not be told anything believes he is defending his dignity, and Proverbs says he is holding himself cheap — because he has decided that he is not worth the trouble of being improved, and has settled for the version of himself that exists today.

Which turns the whole business of correction round. Taking it is not a humiliation to be endured for the sake of others. It is the only way a man ever treats himself as though he were worth something.

verseByVerse.quote: The fear of the LORD is instruction in wisdom, and humility comes before honor. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fear of the LORD is instruction in wisdom, and humility comes before honour.

The chapter ends where the book began, and the second clause tells the reader why the order cannot be reversed.

Humility comes before honour. Not as a technique — that is the counterfeit, and it is recognisable at once, since a man being humble in order to be exalted has not been humble at any point. The order is structural. It is the way the world is arranged, in the same way that dawn comes before morning.

And the reason it is arranged that way is that honour cannot be held by a proud man. Give it to him and it destroys him, which is a mercy in the sequence: God is not withholding the honour, he is making somebody who can survive receiving it.

The whole of it was demonstrated once, in a life. He was in the form of God and did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, and took the form of a servant, and humbled himself to death on a cross — therefore God has highly exalted him (Philippians 2:6-9). The therefore is Proverbs 15:33 with a name on it. He went down first, and all the way, and the honour that came back to him was the honour of the whole universe.

15.theology: The omniscience of God and the integrated life. Proverbs 15:3 — "the eyes of the LORD are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good" — is the theological foundation for the integrated life that wisdom requires. The person who behaves differently in private than in public has not yet reckoned with the God who sees in every place. The person who has reckoned with this truth is freed from the exhausting performance of virtue before human observers and the covert pursuit of vice in private: they simply live the same life before the one audience that is always present. This is the deepest form of integrity (from Latin integer — whole, undivided): the wholeness of the person who has nothing to hide because they live their entire life before the eyes of the God who sees all things and loves them still.
15.examples:
Then: The "soft answer" of verse 1 was wisdom for every context in the ancient world where honour, shame, and the management of conflict were the constant concerns of daily life — the marketplace, the gate, the household, the court. A harsh response to insult escalated the shame-and-honour spiral; a soft answer broke it. The person who had mastered this discipline was recognised as genuinely wise, and their counsel was sought precisely because they could navigate conflict without inflaming it.

Now: "Better is a dinner of herbs where love is than a fattened ox and hatred with it" (v. 17) is the wisdom text for every family and community that has mistaken prosperity for flourishing. The family that has every material advantage but no love, no peace, no genuine enjoyment of one another, has the fattened ox and the hatred. The family that has modest resources but genuine warmth, laughter, mutual delight, and the fear of the LORD has the dinner of herbs. Proverbs insists that the herbs are better — not because poverty is good, but because love is worth more than any feast that money can buy.

16.title: Plans and Providence

To get understanding is to be chosen rather than silver.<sup>17</sup>The highway of the upright turns aside from evil; whoever guards his way preserves his life.<sup>18</sup>Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.<sup>19</sup>It is better to be of a lowly spirit with the poor than to divide the spoil with the proud.<sup>20</sup>Whoever gives thought to the word will discover good, and blessed is he who trusts in the LORD.<sup>21</sup>The wise of heart is called discerning, and sweetness of speech increases persuasiveness.<sup>22</sup>Good sense is a fountain of life to him who has it, but the instruction of fools is folly.<sup>23</sup>The heart of the wise makes his speech judicious and adds persuasiveness to his lips.<sup>24</sup>Gracious words are like a honeycomb, sweetness to the soul and health to the body.<sup>25</sup>There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death.<sup>26</sup>A worker's appetite works for him; his mouth urges him on.<sup>27</sup>A worthless man plots evil, and his speech is like a scorching fire.<sup>28</sup>A dishonest man spreads strife, and a whisperer separates close friends.<sup>29</sup>A man of violence entices his neighbor and leads him in a way that is not good.<sup>30</sup>Whoever winks his eyes plans dishonest things; he who purses his lips brings evil to pass.<sup>31</sup>Gray hair is a crown of glory; it is gained in a righteous life.<sup>32</sup>Whoever is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city.<sup>33</sup>The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD.
16.overview:
Chapter 16 is the theological centre of the Solomonic collection, containing some of the richest statements of divine sovereignty and human responsibility in the entire Old Testament. The chapter opens with a cluster of proverbs about the relationship between human planning and divine providence (vv. 1–9), and these proverbs have shaped Reformed theology's understanding of that relationship more than almost any other passage outside Paul.

The summary verse is v. 9: "the heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps." Human planning is not dismissed — the heart legitimately plans, and Proverbs consistently commends careful planning. But the outcomes are in the LORD's hands. This is not fatalism (which would eliminate the point of planning) but a profound theological realism: our planning is real and our responsibility is genuine, and the outcomes are ultimately determined by One whose purposes are never frustrated. The chapter also contains the most famous pride proverb in the book: "pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall" (v. 18).

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 16 — God's Sovereignty Over Human Plans and the King's Justice
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 16 is the most theologically dense chapter in the Solomonic collection. Verses 1-9 form a sustained meditation on the relationship between human agency and divine sovereignty—perhaps the most concentrated treatment of providence in Proverbs. The king appears prominently (vv.10-15) as the earthly embodiment of justice and wrath, a type of the divine ruler. The chapter closes with wisdom, gray hair, and patience.
verseByVerse.theology: God's sovereignty and human responsibility coexist without contradiction in ch.16. Humans plan (v.1), commit (v.3), weigh motives (v.2), calculate (v.9)—and God answers, establishes, measures, directs. The Hebrew verb forms suggest ongoing action on both sides. Waltke: the proverbs do not flatten human agency but subordinate it; God's sovereignty is not despite human planning but through and over it.
verseByVerse.examples: The lot (v.33) is the capstone: even chance events are in God's hands. No circumstance is outside his governance. This is either terrifying or the most comforting truth in the world, depending on whether you know and fear the God who governs all things.

verseByVerse.quote: The plans of the heart belong to man, but the answer of the tongue is from the LORD. All the ways of a man are pure in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the spirit. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The plans of the heart belong to man, but the answer of the tongue is from the LORD.

The chapter opens the great theme it will return to five times: what a man decides, and what actually happens. And the division here is drawn in an unexpected place. The planning is granted to him without qualification — Proverbs is not describing a puppet — but the answer, the thing that comes out of his mouth when the moment arrives, is credited elsewhere.

Anybody who has spoken in a difficult situation knows the experience. A man rehearses what he will say, and then he is in the room, and what comes out is not what he prepared — sometimes worse, and often, unaccountably, better. He walks away knowing he did not have that sentence an hour earlier.

Then v. 2: all the ways of a man are pure in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the spirit.

Not some ways. All of them. Every person alive has a running account of himself in which each decision was reasonable given the circumstances, and the remarkable thing is that this survives contact with the evidence. A man can behave badly and produce the justification within the hour.

And against that, one word: God weighs. He does not consult the account; he puts the thing on a scale — the same balance of 11:1, turned round to face the reader.

verseByVerse.quote: Commit your work to the LORD, and your plans will be established. The LORD has made everything for its purpose, even the wicked for the day of trouble. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Commit your work to the LORD, and your plans will be established. The verb behind commit is galal, to roll — the word for shifting something heavy off yourself onto something else. Not entrust in the abstract. Roll it off, the way a man rolls a stone he cannot carry.

And the promise is exact: the plans will be established, which is not a promise that they will happen. To establish something is to make it stand — and a plan rolled onto God is either made to stand or replaced by a better one, and the man who has genuinely handed it over has already accepted both.

Then v. 4, which is one of the hardest verses in the book: the LORD has made everything for its purpose, even the wicked for the day of trouble.

The plainest reading is the one that troubles people, and honesty requires stating it: nothing is outside God’s governance, including the wicked man and including the day his wickedness meets its reckoning. Paul makes the same argument and does not soften it (Romans 9:22). Others, equally reverent, read the Hebrew as saying that God has made everything with its own counterpart or answer, so that the wicked has a day appointed which answers to what he has been. Both readings land in the same place, which is that history is not running loose.

Two things must be held with it, or the verse becomes a monstrosity. God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked and says so under oath (Ezekiel 33:11); and no man in Scripture is ever permitted to plead his destiny as an excuse, because the same Bible holds every person entirely responsible for what he chooses. Scripture never resolves that tension, and neither should anybody. What it does is refuse to let a Christian believe that evil has escaped, or that the present arrangement is the final one.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who is arrogant in heart is an abomination to the LORD; be assured, he will not go unpunished. By steadfast love and faithfulness iniquity is atoned for, and by the fear of the LORD one turns away from evil. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who is arrogant in heart is an abomination to the LORD; be assured, he will not go unpunished. The phrase is hand to hand again (11:21) — the bargain-struck gesture. And the sin is located in the heart, where nobody can see it, which means a man may be an abomination in this verse while being pleasant company.

Then v. 6, and it is a startling sentence to find in the Old Testament: by steadfast love and faithfulness iniquity is atoned for.

Read carelessly it sounds like a man buying off his sins with good behaviour, and that reading must be refused. The two words are hesed and emet — the pair God used of himself when he proclaimed his own name to Moses on the mountain (Exodus 34:6), and the pair the son was told to wear at 3:3. The atoning is being done by the covenant loyalty and truth of God.

Which leaves the second half to do the other work: by the fear of the LORD one turns away from evil. There is the human side, and note its position. It comes after. Turning from evil is not what obtains the atonement; it is what happens in a man who has been atoned for by somebody’s hesed.

And how that could be done without God ceasing to be true, the Old Testament could not say. It waited for a place where the steadfast love and the faithfulness met in one act — where God was shown to be just and the justifier of the man who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). Mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed each other (Psalm 85:10), and they did it on a cross.

verseByVerse.quote: When a man's ways please the LORD, he makes even his enemies to be at peace with him. Better is a little with righteousness than great revenues with injustice. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
When a man’s ways please the LORD, he makes even his enemies to be at peace with him.

Even is doing the work. This is not a promise that a godly man will have no enemies — Proverbs has watched the world too closely for that, and the most righteous man who ever lived was killed by his. It is saying that the reconciliations nobody expected are within God’s reach: Esau running to meet Jacob and falling on his neck, after twenty years of a grudge that had every right to be permanent (Genesis 33:4).

And there is a strategy hidden in it that most people never try. When a relationship has gone wrong, the instinct is to work on the other party — the explanation, the mediator, the message that will finally land. This verse points somewhere else entirely: attend to your own ways before God, and leave the enemy to him.

Then v. 8: better is a little with righteousness than great revenues with injustice. The word is revenues — income, not a lump sum — so this is not about a windfall but about a stream that keeps arriving. Which is why the trade is so hard to refuse, and why so many people who would never steal find themselves, at fifty, unable to explain what they are part of.

verseByVerse.quote: The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps. An oracle is on the lips of a king; his mouth does not sin in judgment. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps.

Here is the theme of the chapter at its plainest, and the scale of the two halves is the point. The man plans a way — the whole route, the long view, the shape of a life. God establishes his steps, one at a time.

So the division is not between his plan and God’s plan, as though there were two competing proposals. It is between the map and the walking. A man may sit down and draw the route as carefully as he likes, and every actual footfall is placed by somebody else.

Which is not a reason to stop planning; the verse assumes he will, and Proverbs elsewhere commends it. It is a reason to hold the plan loosely — and it explains the strange experience, common to most Christians looking back at twenty years, of finding that almost nothing went as designed and yet they arrived somewhere they could not have drawn.

Then v. 10 opens the chapter’s section on kings: an oracle is on the lips of a king; his mouth does not sin in judgment. That is the office described as it ought to be — the ideal, not the record — and Israel’s own history is the long story of kings who fell short of this sentence. It stands here as a job description, and as a hope that would eventually be met by one.

verseByVerse.quote: A just balance and scales are the LORD's; all the weights in the bag are his work. It is an abomination to kings to do evil, for the throne is established by righteousness. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A just balance and scales are the LORD’s; all the weights in the bag are his work.

The false weight of 11:1 is back, and now the claim is enlarged in a way that ought to startle anybody in business. The scales are not merely watched by God. They are his — the instrument itself belongs to him, and the standard weights in the merchant’s pouch are described as something he made.

Which is a claim about the nature of measurement. A kilogram is not a convention that a trade association agreed on and could revise. Behind every honest standard stands the God who fixed it, which is why cheating on it is not a technical infraction but a lie told about reality.

Then v. 12: it is an abomination to kings to do evil, for the throne is established by righteousness.

The reason is the interesting part, and it is structural rather than moral. A throne is established — held up — by righteousness, so a king who does evil is not merely behaving badly; he is removing the thing his own chair is standing on. Every tyrant in history has been sawing at his own legs, and every one of them has believed he was consolidating his position.

verseByVerse.quote: Righteous lips are the delight of a king, and he loves him who speaks what is right. A king's wrath is a messenger of death, and a wise man will appease it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Righteous lips are the delight of a king, and he loves him who speaks what is right. That is the ideal king again, and it names the rarest quality in anybody with power: a genuine appetite for being told the truth.

Turn that round on the reader, since almost nobody in a congregation is a monarch and almost everybody is somebody’s superior. The test of a man’s leadership is not whether he invites honesty — everybody says he does — but what the honest people around him have learned from experience about the cost of it.

Then v. 14: a king’s wrath is a messenger of death, and a wise man will appease it.

Note that the wise man does not stand on his rights. He does not point out that the anger was unjustified, even where it plainly was. He appeases — takes the trouble to defuse a situation he did not cause, because the alternative is a disaster and being right about it will not prevent one.

There is an important limit here, and Proverbs assumes it elsewhere: this is not counsel to flatter power or to stay silent about wrong. Nathan went to David and told him the truth, and Daniel’s friends declined the statue. The verse is about the temper of the exchange, not about the truth of it.

verseByVerse.quote: In the light of a king's face there is life, and his favor is like the clouds that bring the spring rain. How much better to get wisdom than gold! To get understanding is to be chosen rather than silver. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the light of a king’s face there is life, and his favour is like the clouds that bring the spring rain.

Two images, and both are about survival rather than pleasure. In a world where a king’s displeasure could end a man, his approval is life; and the spring rain in Israel was the late rain that filled out the grain before harvest — the difference between a crop and a failure.

Which is why Scripture keeps reaching for a face when it describes God’s favour, and why the Aaronic blessing asks for exactly this: the LORD make his face to shine upon you (Numbers 6:25). It is the oldest human hunger, and every child knows it before he can name it — the look on a face turning toward you and being glad.

Then v. 16: how much better to get wisdom than gold! The book has said this several times and here it says it with an exclamation, and with the word get — the market verb of 4:5. Both are acquired. Both cost. The man reading this is spending his life obtaining one or the other, and generally without having chosen which.

verseByVerse.quote: The highway of the upright turns aside from evil; whoever guards his way preserves his life. Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The highway of the upright turns aside from evil; whoever guards his way preserves his life. A highway is a built road — raised, cleared, maintained. The image is of a route that somebody made, which means the upright man is not picking his way across open country. He is on something constructed, and the construction was not his.

Then v. 18, which everybody knows and most people misquote: pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.

The order is the teaching. Pride is not punished with destruction as a penalty attached afterwards; it goes before it, the way a scout goes before an army. It is the leading edge of the thing, and it arrives first because it is what makes the fall possible.

And the mechanism is not mysterious. Pride removes the instruments a man would need to see the drop: it stops him asking, stops him believing the warning, and stops the people around him troubling to give it twice. By the time he falls, everybody else had known for a year — which is the consistent testimony of anybody who has watched a leader go down.

So the verse is a piece of practical navigation rather than a moral. When a man notices he has begun to find correction tiresome, he has not developed an unattractive trait. He has been given the first sighting of a scout.

verseByVerse.quote: It is better to be of a lowly spirit with the poor than to divide the spoil with the proud. Whoever gives thought to the word will discover good, and blessed is he who trusts in the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is better to be of a lowly spirit with the poor than to divide the spoil with the proud. The word spoil is deliberate: this is the winning side, dividing the takings, and the invitation is to be in the room. What is being turned down is not money. It is belonging.

Then v. 20: whoever gives thought to the word will discover good, and blessed is he who trusts in the LORD.

The two halves are the whole Christian life in one sentence, and they are in the right order. Gives thought is the verb for paying close attention to something — real work, done with the mind, over a text. And it is followed immediately by trust, which is not work at all.

Neither can substitute for the other. Attention without trust produces a man who knows a great deal about God and is not resting in any of it; trust without attention produces a warmth with nothing under it that will not survive a hard year. The verse puts them in one breath and calls the result blessed.

verseByVerse.quote: The wise of heart is called discerning, and sweetness of speech increases persuasiveness. Good sense is a fountain of life to him who has it, but the instruction of fools is folly. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wise of heart is called discerning, and sweetness of speech increases persuasiveness.

That is a more interesting claim than it looks, because it says that how a thing is said changes whether it is received — and Christians are often suspicious of this, as though caring about the manner were a compromise of the matter.

Proverbs does not agree. Sweetness of speech is presented as a genuine addition to the truth, not a coating on it. A true thing said harshly has been made harder to receive, and the person who said it has not thereby been more faithful; he has been less effective, and often more comfortable.

Then v. 22: good sense is a fountain of life to him who has it, but the instruction of fools is folly. Note who drinks from the fountain in this verse — him who has it. Wisdom feeds its owner first. A man who is being changed by what he knows will feed other people almost automatically, and a man who is not will feed nobody however much he says.

verseByVerse.quote: The heart of the wise makes his speech judicious and adds persuasiveness to his lips. Gracious words are like a honeycomb, sweetness to the soul and health to the body. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heart of the wise makes his speech judicious and adds persuasiveness to his lips. The direction of causation is the point, and it is the reverse of how people try to improve their speaking. The heart teaches the mouth. Not the other way round, and never the other way round.

Which is why every attempt to fix a speech problem at the level of the tongue fails within a month. A man may resolve to stop being sharp, and the resolution is genuine, and it holds until he is tired — because the sharpness was never in the mouth. It was being supplied.

Then v. 24: gracious words are like a honeycomb, sweetness to the soul and health to the body.

Honey was the ancient world’s picture of both pleasure and medicine, and both are claimed here. The word for health is the healing word of 12:18. So gracious speech is being described as something that tastes good and does good — and the two are not usually found together, which is what makes the comparison worth making.

And there is a plain application in it that costs nothing. Somebody in reach of every reader is short of this, has been for months, and would be measurably better by Friday for one true kind sentence. It is the cheapest medicine in the world and almost nobody dispenses it.

verseByVerse.quote: There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death. A worker's appetite works for him; his mouth urges him on. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death.

This is 14:12, repeated word for word. Proverbs does not often do that, and when it does the repetition is the emphasis — the same device as the two printings of the gossip proverb at 18:8 and 26:22. Somebody thought it needed saying twice.

And the reason is that it is the one warning a man cannot generate for himself. Every other danger in this book can be spotted from inside: he can notice that he is angry, or lazy, or tempted. He cannot notice that his own judgment is the thing that has gone wrong, because the faculty he would use to notice is the faculty in question.

Then v. 26, which is startlingly modern: a worker’s appetite works for him; his mouth urges him on. Hunger is described as a colleague. The man does not have to be inspired or motivated; he has to eat, and the need does the driving.

Proverbs is not being cynical about vocation. It is noticing, without embarrassment, that a great deal of the world’s honest work has been done by people who got up because there was a bill, and that this is a legitimate and God-given engine and not a lesser one.

verseByVerse.quote: A worthless man plots evil, and his speech is like a scorching fire. A dishonest man spreads strife, and a whisperer separates close friends. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A worthless man plots evil, and his speech is like a scorching fire. The beliyya‘al of 6:12 returns, and the image for his talk is a fire in a dry season — which spreads without being carried, needs no help once started, and consumes things that had nothing to do with the original quarrel.

Then v. 28, and the second half is one of the saddest lines in the book: a dishonest man spreads strife, and a whisperer separates close friends.

Look at the target. Not enemies, not strangers — close friends. And that is the specialism, because two men who barely know each other cannot be separated; there is nothing there to break. The whisperer’s work requires an existing bond, and the closer it is the more effective the small remark becomes, since a sentence about somebody you love goes in further and stays longer.

And nothing in the verse suggests he is lying. The whisperer’s stock in trade is very often the truth, delivered in a lowered voice, with regret in the face — which is why it is so hard to confront and why he is so often thought of as a thoughtful man.

God puts him last on the list of the seven things he hates (6:19), in the position of climax, because he is undoing the one thing God is doing in the world.

verseByVerse.quote: A man of violence entices his neighbor and leads him in a way that is not good. Whoever winks his eyes plans dishonest things; he who purses his lips brings evil to pass. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man of violence entices his neighbour and leads him in a way that is not good. The verb is the enticement of 1:10, and the victim is his neighbour — somebody who lives close enough to trust him. Every recruitment in this book happens between people who already know each other.

Then v. 30: whoever winks his eyes plans dishonest things; he who purses his lips brings evil to pass.

The winker of 6:13 and 10:10 appears for the third time, and Proverbs adds a detail: the pursed lips, the compressed mouth. Both are the face of a man deciding something and giving nothing away — which is what makes them worth recording. The book has now spent three separate passages on gestures rather than words, because the damage that is done with a face cannot be quoted, cannot be answered, and cannot be proved.

And there is one honest use of these verses that is easily missed. They are usually read as a description of somebody else. They are also a warning about a habit anybody can fall into — the significant look across a table, the little movement of the eyebrows that tells the room what to think and leaves the speaker with nothing to retract.

verseByVerse.quote: Gray hair is a crown of glory; it is gained in a righteous life. Whoever is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gray hair is a crown of glory; it is gained in a righteous life.

In a culture organised around youth this sentence is almost unintelligible, and it should be allowed to land. Age is described as a crown — not a decline to be managed, disguised, or apologised for, but the visible mark of something achieved.

And the second clause keeps it honest. It is gained in a righteous life. The crown is not conferred by the calendar; anybody can grow old. What is being honoured is the accumulation — forty years of decisions, most of them small, that have made a person into someone worth consulting.

Which puts an obligation on both ends of a congregation. The old are not owed deference for having survived; and the young are being told plainly that the most valuable resource in the room is sitting near the back and is not being asked anything.

Then v. 32, one of the great sentences of the Old Testament: whoever is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city.

Taking a city was the highest thing a man could do — the achievement that got a name into a chronicle. And Proverbs sets against it a man in a kitchen who did not say the thing he wanted to say. It does not call the second man equal. It calls him better, and nobody will ever hear about it.

verseByVerse.quote: The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD.

The chapter that began with a man’s plans ends with a pair of dice, and the sovereignty theme closes over the whole of it. The lot was Israel’s way of referring a matter to God when human judgment could not settle it (18:18) — stones shaken in a fold of cloth, as random a procedure as they could devise.

And the verse says there is no such thing as random. Not that God usually intervenes, or that he oversees the general direction: its every decision. The one place in the ancient world deliberately designed to be outside anybody’s control is described as entirely inside his.

Which reaches a long way past dice. If the lot is his, then so is the interview that went to somebody else, and the scan result, and the fact that of all the houses in that street the family who would change everything lived in the one next door. Nothing in a Christian’s life is accidental, not because coincidence is denied but because it is claimed.

And the whole chapter has to be read together or this becomes cold. The God who governs every throw is the God of v. 6, whose steadfast love and faithfulness atone for iniquity — and the sharpest illustration in Scripture is a group of soldiers casting lots for a coat at the foot of a cross, not knowing that they were fulfilling a psalm written a thousand years earlier (Psalm 22:18; John 19:24). Even there, at the worst hour in the history of the world, with men gambling over the clothes of the Son of God, the decision was from the LORD.

16.theology: Divine sovereignty and human responsibility. Proverbs 16 holds together, without tension or apology, the full weight of both human responsibility and divine sovereignty. The heart plans — genuinely, freely, responsibly. The LORD establishes the steps — sovereignly, purposefully, without eliminating the reality of the planning. This is the biblical teaching on providence in its wisdom-literature form. Reformed theology has always insisted that these two truths are not contradictory but complementary: the God who ordains all things also ordains the means — including the decisions, plans, and choices of his creatures. The person who understands this is freed from both anxiety (my plans must succeed or my life will fail) and fatalism (my plans do not matter because God controls everything). They plan wisely and trust completely.
16.examples:
Then: "Pride goes before destruction" (v. 18) was immediately recognisable to ancient readers familiar with the stories of the great empires — Egypt, Assyria, Babylon — whose rulers' pride preceded their catastrophic falls. The pattern is theological as much as historical: the tower of Babel, Pharaoh's hardened heart, Nebuchadnezzar's madness — pride is always the prelude to the humiliation that God sends to the proud. Israel's own kings (Saul, Uzziah, Hezekiah in part) confirm the pattern. Pride does not merely risk destruction; it goes before it, predictably and reliably.

Now: "Commit your work to the LORD, and your plans will be established" (v. 3) is the wisdom text for every Christian engaged in long-term projects — raising children, building a career, planting a church, writing a book, starting a business. The invitation is to hold the plans loosely, to work diligently, and to trust the outcome to the one who establishes steps. Keller observes that the person who cannot commit their work to the LORD — who must control the outcome — has made the work an idol: it is too important to be surrendered, which means it has become more important than the God whose establishment is more reliable than any plan.

17.title: A Friend Who Sticks Closer Than a Brother
17.text: <sup>1</sup>Better is a dry morsel with quiet than a house full of feasting with strife.<sup>2</sup>A servant who deals wisely will rule over a son who acts shamefully and will share the inheritance as one of the brothers.<sup>3</sup>The crucible is for silver, and the furnace is for gold, and the LORD tests hearts.<sup>4</sup>An evildoer listens to wicked lips, and a liar gives ear to a mischievous tongue.<sup>5</sup>Whoever mocks the poor insults his Maker; he who is glad at calamity will not go unpunished.<sup>6</sup>Grandchildren are the crown of the aged, and the glory of children is their fathers.<sup>7</sup>Fine speech is not becoming to a fool; still less is false speech to a prince.<sup>8</sup>A bribe is like a magic stone in the eyes of the one who gives it; he who makes his door high seeks destruction.<sup>20</sup>A man of crooked heart does not discover good, and one with a dishonest tongue falls into calamity.<sup>21</sup>He who sires a fool gets himself sorrow, and the father of a fool has no joy.<sup>22</sup>A joyful heart is good medicine, but a crushed spirit dries up the bones.<sup>23</sup>The wicked accepts a bribe in secret to pervert the ways of justice.<sup>24</sup>The discerning sets his face toward wisdom, but the eyes of a fool are on the ends of the earth.<sup>25</sup>A foolish son is a grief to his father and bitterness to her who bore him.<sup>26</sup>To impose a fine on a righteous man is not good, nor to strike the noble for their uprightness.<sup>27</sup>Whoever restrains his words has knowledge, and he who has a cool spirit is a man of understanding.<sup>28</sup>Even a fool who keeps silent is considered wise; when he closes his lips, he is deemed intelligent.
17.overview:
Chapter 17 is one of Proverbs' most humanly warm chapters, with its reflections on friendship, family, the management of conflict, and the surprising power of silence and joy. At its heart is the famous definition of friendship: "a friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for a time of adversity" (v. 17). This is not a sentimental description of pleasant companionship but a definition of the friend who will be there when things go wrong — which is the only test of friendship that ultimately matters.

The chapter also contains Proverbs' most memorable observation about silence: "even a fool who keeps silent is considered wise" (v. 28). This is both humorous and profound: the discipline of not speaking what one is thinking is so rare, and its results so positive, that even the fool who practices it is credited with wisdom he does not have. The chapter consistently commends the restraint, patience, and long-suffering that are the social expression of the wisdom that chapter 16 grounds in the sovereignty of God.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 17 — The Merry Heart, True Friendship, and the Silence of the Wise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 17 is rich in social observation: the peacefulness of a dry crust versus strife-filled feasting (v.1), the refining work of affliction (v.3), the friend who loves at all times (v.17), the merry heart as medicine (v.22). Silence is commended (vv.27-28) as one of wisdom's most surprising gifts. Waltke: Proverbs 17 is a sustained argument for social intelligence—understanding people, managing conflict, maintaining loyalty.
verseByVerse.theology: The friend who loves at all times (v.17) is one of Proverbs' most searching tests of relationship: friendship is not fair-weather mutual benefit but committed loyalty through adversity. 'A brother is born for a time of adversity' refines this: the kinship bond proves itself exactly when everything is going wrong. Christ is the fulfillment of this friendship—the friend who loved not in fair weather but at the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: The merry heart (v.22) as good medicine is psychologically accurate: positive affect has measurable physiological effects. But Proverbs goes deeper than health psychology—the merry heart is the fruit of wisdom and trust in God, not a technique for wellbeing. It is the overflow of a heart rightly ordered toward God and neighbor.

verseByVerse.quote: Better is a dry morsel with quiet than a house full of feasting with strife. A servant who deals wisely will rule over a son who acts shamefully and will share the inheritance as one of the brothers. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Better is a dry morsel with quiet than a house full of feasting with strife.

15:17 said this with vegetables; here it is a dry morsel — a crust, with nothing on it — and the improvement is in the other half of the sentence. There the alternative was hatred. Here it is only strife, which is a much lower bar and therefore a far more common house.

Nobody in the second half of this verse hates anybody. It is a household with an atmosphere: the argument that resumes every few days, the subject that cannot be raised, the tone at the table. And what Proverbs values against it is not love, or peace, or reconciliation — it is quiet. A crust and no noise.

That is a low and honest standard, and the reason it is set so low should be said. Some people reading this are not in a position to obtain a happy home. They can sometimes obtain a quiet one, and Scripture says that is genuinely better than a full table with a fight in it.

Then v. 2: a servant who deals wisely will rule over a son who acts shamefully. Blood gives a man a claim; it does not preserve it. In the end things end up with whoever can handle them, which is a warning to families that assume the next generation is entitled and a considerable encouragement to anybody who arrived with nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: The crucible is for silver, and the furnace is for gold, and the LORD tests hearts. An evildoer listens to wicked lips, and a liar gives ear to a mischievous tongue. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crucible is for silver, and the furnace is for gold, and the LORD tests hearts.

The comparison controls the verse, so the metallurgy matters. A crucible does not damage silver and a furnace does not destroy gold. Heat is applied for one purpose only: everything in the mixture that is not the metal comes to the surface, where it can be lifted off. The refiner is not attacking the silver. He is removing what was never silver.

And that is what is being said about God and a human heart. The heat is not punishment and it is not a test in the sense of an examination he needs the result of — he already knows. It is a process with an output, and the output is a man with less in him that is not gold.

Which is the only account of suffering that survives contact with a hard year. It does not explain why this particular trouble came, and Scripture rarely does. It says what the trouble is for, and that the man holding the tongs is not indifferent, and that he is watching the surface the whole time.

Then v. 4: an evildoer listens to wicked lips, and a liar gives ear to a mischievous tongue. Both halves are about the audience, not the speaker. Slander requires a market, and this verse says the buyer is as implicated as the seller — which is 18:8 from the other side, and the reason a whisperer never runs out of custom.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever mocks the poor insults his Maker; he who is glad at calamity will not go unpunished. Grandchildren are the crown of the aged, and the glory of children is their fathers. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever mocks the poor insults his Maker; he who is glad at calamity will not go unpunished.

14:31 said that oppressing the poor insults God. This goes further and lowers the bar considerably: not oppressing — mocking. A man need not have taken anything from anybody. The joke is enough, and the joke is described as an insult delivered upward about the quality of God’s workmanship.

Then the second half, which names a sin almost nobody confesses: being glad at calamity. Not causing it. Being pleased about it — the small lift when a man who did well out of something loses it, the interest in the downfall of somebody successful, the satisfaction in hearing that a person one disliked has been found out.

Everybody has felt it, and it is the exact opposite of the love that does not rejoice at wrongdoing (1 Corinthians 13:6). Proverbs does not treat it as a minor blemish. It attaches the guarantee formula: he will not go unpunished.

Then v. 6, and after two hard sentences a warm one: grandchildren are the crown of the aged, and the glory of children is their fathers. The traffic runs both ways. The old are crowned by the young, and the young are given standing by the old — which is a description of a society that is not currently common, and a rebuke to a church arranged so that the two never meet.

verseByVerse.quote: Fine speech is not becoming to a fool; still less is false speech to a prince. A bribe is like a magic stone in the eyes of the one who gives it; wherever he turns he prospers. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fine speech is not becoming to a fool; still less is false speech to a prince. The argument moves upward. Eloquence in a fool is merely incongruous; lying in a man with power is worse, because the higher the office the more damage an untrue word does on its way down.

Then v. 8, which is one of the most misread verses in Proverbs: a bribe is like a magic stone in the eyes of the one who gives it; wherever he turns he prospers.

Note the qualification, because it is the whole verse: in the eyes of the one who gives it. This is not Proverbs commending bribery — the same book calls it a perversion of justice fifteen verses later. It is Proverbs reporting, with a slightly raised eyebrow, what bribery feels like from the inside to the man doing it.

And it feels like magic. That is exactly right. A door that would not open opens; a process that should have taken months takes a week; obstacles that stop other people are simply not there. The man begins to believe he has found how the world actually works, and everyone else is a fool for queuing.

Which is why bribery is so hard to give up once started. It is not merely profitable; it is enchanting, and a man under an enchantment does not experience himself as corrupt. He experiences himself as effective.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever covers an offense seeks love, but he who repeats a matter separates close friends. A rebuke goes deeper into a man of understanding than a hundred blows into a fool. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever covers an offence seeks love, but he who repeats a matter separates close friends.

10:12 said that love covers offences. This adds the direction of travel: covering an offence is how a man seeks love — it is not the fruit of a relationship already secure, it is the thing that builds one.

And the opposite is defined with unusual precision. Not slandering. Not lying. Repeating a matter — saying, accurately, a thing that happened. The offence is real, the account is true, and the retelling is what does the damage.

Which catches a great deal of talk that would never be called sin. Bringing it up again in an argument. Mentioning it to a third party who has no need to know. Referring to it in a joke two years later. Every repetition renews an injury that was healing, and the man doing it can defend each instance individually.

Then v. 10, and it is one of the sharpest sentences in the book: a rebuke goes deeper into a man of understanding than a hundred blows into a fool.

A hundred blows. That is the measure of how little correction reaches a man who has decided not to receive it, and it explains why some people never change despite consequences that would have altered anybody else. The consequences arrived; they did not go in.

And the useful half is the first. A word — one word, mildly said — goes deep into the right man. Which means the person who has to correct somebody teachable does not need force, and should be careful how hard he speaks, because a light blow to that man lands like a heavy one.

verseByVerse.quote: An evil man seeks only rebellion, and a cruel messenger will be sent against him. Let a man meet a she-bear robbed of her cubs rather than a fool in his folly. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
An evil man seeks only rebellion, and a cruel messenger will be sent against him. The word only is the diagnosis. Not that he sometimes rebels — that rebellion is the thing itself, sought for its own sake, with no particular object.

Then v. 12, and Proverbs makes a joke that is not really a joke: let a man meet a she-bear robbed of her cubs rather than a fool in his folly.

A bear that has lost her cubs is the most dangerous animal an Israelite could imagine — and Proverbs says take your chances with the bear.

The comparison rewards a moment’s thought, because the bear is in some ways the safer proposition. She is predictable: she will do exactly what a bereaved bear does, and a man who knows anything about bears knows what is coming. A fool in his folly is not predictable. There is no calculating what he will do, because he is not calculating either — and he can be reasoned with even less than she can, since she at least is responding to something real.

Which is why the counsel of 14:7 was to leave. There is no technique for the situation described here. There is only distance.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone returns evil for good, evil will not depart from his house. The beginning of strife is like letting out water, so quit before the quarrel breaks out. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone returns evil for good, evil will not depart from his house. A permanent resident. The verse does not say he will be punished; it says the thing takes up residence, and house means household — so the wrong done to a benefactor settles into a family and is still there when the man who did it is not.

Then v. 14, which is the best sentence in Scripture about how arguments actually start: the beginning of strife is like letting out water, so quit before the quarrel breaks out.

The image is an earth dam or an irrigation channel — a wall of packed soil holding back water. Make a small opening and the water does the rest: it widens what it runs through, and it widens it faster the more of it gets past, and there is a point about four seconds in when nothing anybody does will close it.

Anybody who has been in a marriage or a church meeting knows the accuracy of that. There is a moment — before the raised voice, before the sentence that cannot be taken back — when the whole thing could be stopped by one person simply not continuing. It costs almost nothing at that moment. Ten minutes later it cannot be bought at any price.

And the counsel is not to win the argument or resolve it. It is quit — walk away, drop it, leave the last word unsaid. Which feels like weakness, and is the single most useful skill in any household, and requires the man who is right to be the one who stops.

verseByVerse.quote: He who justifies the wicked and he who condemns the righteous are both alike an abomination to the LORD. Why should a fool have money in his hand to buy wisdom when he has no sense? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who justifies the wicked and he who condemns the righteous are both alike an abomination to the LORD.

This is a courtroom verse, and its plain sense is not difficult. Justice is destroyed as thoroughly by acquitting the guilty as by convicting the innocent, and both are called abomination — the strongest word the book has, and it is applied to a judge going soft quite as much as to a judge being cruel.

But the Christian reader ought to stop here, because there is a collision, and it is the most important one in the Bible. Paul writes that God justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5) — and he uses the same legal word. Proverbs says that a judge who acquits the guilty is an abomination to God. Paul says God acquits the guilty. Both are Scripture.

The tension is not a puzzle to be dissolved. It is the exact problem the gospel exists to solve, and Paul knew precisely what he was doing when he wrote that sentence. If God simply overlooks guilt, he is the corrupt judge of Proverbs 17:15 — and no one who has been genuinely wronged wants a universe run by a God who does not care what was done to them.

So Romans 3 answers it, and the answer is not that God relaxed the standard. It is that the penalty was paid, in full, by somebody else, in public, so that God might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). The wicked man is acquitted, and the courtroom is not corrupted, because the sentence was carried out. He condemned sin in the flesh (Romans 8:3) — and the one condemned in that court was the only righteous man who has ever stood in one.

Both halves of this proverb met at Calvary. The wicked were justified, and the righteous was condemned, and God was not an abomination but glorified — because the judge came down from the bench and stood in the dock.

verseByVerse.quote: A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity. One who lacks sense gives a pledge and puts up security in the presence of his neighbor. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.

At all times is the whole verse. Not most times, not when it is convenient, not while things are going well. And the phrase carries a particular weight because friendship is the one relationship with no structure holding it in place — no vow, no blood, no contract. It continues only while both parties keep choosing it, which is precisely why the qualifier is needed.

Then the second half turns to the other kind: a brother is born for adversity. Not a brother is useful in adversity — born for it. The relationship exists, in this reading, for the bad day, and everything before it was preparation.

Put that question to anybody with siblings, and to any church that calls its members brothers. If a family exists for the hard time, then the ordinary years are not the point of it; they are the years in which the thing is built that will be needed later. A great many people discover at a funeral that they have spent thirty years not building it.

And there is one for whom both halves are literally true. He loved his own to the end (John 13:1) — at all times, including the hours when every one of them had left. And he is called the firstborn among many brothers, born for our adversity, born for nothing else: he came to a world at its worst hour and was not ashamed to call us his family.

Then v. 18 returns to standing surety in the presence of a neighbour — the public handshake of 6:1, made worse by an audience, since it is very hard to decline in front of a room.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever loves transgression loves strife; he who makes his door high seeks destruction. A man of crooked heart does not discover good, and one with a dishonest tongue falls into calamity. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever loves transgression loves strife; he who makes his door high seeks destruction.

The second image is unusual and worth having. A high doorway in an ancient town was a boast — grander than the neighbours, visible from the street, a statement about the man inside. And Proverbs says such a door seeks destruction, partly because it advertises to anybody who might be looking for a house worth robbing, and partly because a man who builds his door to be looked at has told the world where his heart is.

Everybody has a high door somewhere. It is whatever a person has built taller than it needed to be so that it would be noticed — and the test is not the size of the thing but what happens inside him when nobody remarks on it.

Then v. 20: a man of crooked heart does not discover good. Not is denied good — does not discover it. He is looking at the same world as everybody else and the good in it is invisible to him, because a bent instrument reads everything bent (8:9). He genuinely believes he lives among people who are all working an angle, and he can produce evidence, and the evidence is real, and he is the reason he is finding it.

verseByVerse.quote: He who sires a fool gets himself sorrow, and the father of a fool has no joy. A joyful heart is good medicine, but a crushed spirit dries up the bones. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
