verseByVerse.quote: A man of great wrath will pay the penalty, for if you deliver him, you will only have to do it again. Listen to advice and accept instruction, that you may gain wisdom in the future. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man of great wrath will pay the penalty, for if you deliver him, you will only have to do it again.

Here is a verse the church badly needs and rarely preaches, because it sets a limit on rescue.

The man in question has a temper, and his temper has produced a consequence — a lost job, a broken relationship, a debt, a legal difficulty. And somebody who loves him is about to step in and absorb it. Proverbs says: you will be doing this again.

The reason is not that the man is beyond help. It is that the consequence is the only teacher currently able to reach him, and removing it removes the lesson while leaving the temper. The rescuer is not being kind; he is paying for the privilege of being needed, and the arrangement will run for years.

Which requires a careful line, because Scripture commands mercy and does not permit anybody to use this verse as a reason to abandon a difficult relative. The distinction is between bearing somebody’s burden, which Galatians commands, and carrying his load, which Galatians says every man must carry himself (Galatians 6:2, 5). Help him. Do not stand between him and the outcome of what he keeps doing.

Then v. 20: listen to advice and accept instruction, that you may gain wisdom in the future. The horizon is the point — in the future, in your latter end. Advice taken today pays out in a decade, which is exactly why so little of it is taken.

verseByVerse.quote: Many are the plans in the mind of a man, but it is the purpose of the LORD that will stand. What is desired in a man is steadfast love, and a poor man is better than a liar. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many are the plans in the mind of a man, but it is the purpose of the LORD that will stand.

The asymmetry is deliberate, and the numbers are the point. The man has many plans; God has one purpose. And the verb applied to it is not wins or overrules but stands — it is simply still there when everything else has been tried.

Anybody looking back over twenty years knows the experience. Not usually a dramatic collision between what he wanted and what God wanted, but a great many intentions that came to nothing for ordinary reasons, and one line running through it all that he could not have drawn and can now partly see.

Then v. 22: what is desired in a man is steadfast love, and a poor man is better than a liar. The word is hesed again. Of all the qualities a person could want in another — competence, intelligence, charm, success — the one named here as most desirable is loyal kindness that does not stop. Ask anybody who has been ill for a long time which of those they wanted from the people around them.

verseByVerse.quote: The fear of the LORD leads to life, and whoever has it rests satisfied; he will not be visited by harm. The sluggard buries his hand in the dish and will not even bring it back to his mouth. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fear of the LORD leads to life, and whoever has it rests satisfied; he will not be visited by harm.

The middle clause is the loveliest in the chapter: rests satisfied. In Hebrew it is literally spending the night full — the picture of a man who has eaten and lies down, and there is nothing outstanding.

That is what the fear of the LORD finally produces, and it is the opposite of what the phrase sounds like. Not a man on edge before God. A man who has stopped needing to secure his own position, because the question of where he stands has been settled by somebody else, and he can therefore sleep.

Then v. 24, and Proverbs makes a joke: the sluggard buries his hand in the dish and will not even bring it back to his mouth.

The comedy is precise. He has got as far as the food. The effort of reaching, the decision, the hand in the bowl — all done. What defeats him is the return journey, which is the shortest distance in the whole operation and the one that would have fed him.

Everybody has a version of this: the thing carried to within one small step of completion and left there. Proverbs finds it funny, and the laughter is a kindness, because the man in the joke is one movement away from dinner.

verseByVerse.quote: Strike a scoffer, and the simple will learn prudence; reprove a man of understanding, and he will gain knowledge. He who does violence to his father and chases away his mother is a son who brings shame and reproach. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Strike a scoffer, and the simple will learn prudence; reprove a man of understanding, and he will gain knowledge.

Three men in one verse, and the arithmetic repays following. The scoffer is struck and learns nothing — 9:8 has already said so. But the blow is not wasted, because somebody else is watching: the simple, who cannot yet tell where a road goes, sees a consequence land and learns from it what he could not have been told.

That is the honest case for public accountability in a church, and it is uncomfortable. When somebody is disciplined and it is seen, the person disciplined may be unmoved, and the young Christians watching will have learned something they will not forget. That is not the reason to do it, and it is a real effect of doing it.

And the man of understanding needs none of it. A reproof — words, quietly — and he gains. Three men, three treatments, and the difference between them is entirely in what they are willing to receive.

Then v. 26: he who does violence to his father and chases away his mother is a son who brings shame and reproach. The verb is active and physical. This is not neglect; it is a son turning on the people who raised him — and Proverbs, having spent nine chapters on a father speaking to a son, records that this happens.

verseByVerse.quote: Cease to hear instruction, my son, and you will stray from the words of knowledge. A worthless witness mocks at justice, and the mouth of the wicked devours iniquity. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cease to hear instruction, my son, and you will stray from the words of knowledge.

The form is ironic — an instruction to stop taking instruction — and the sting is in the consequence. Not: you will rebel. You will stray, which is the sheep word again, the verb of no decision at all.

So the mechanism is set out with complete simplicity. Nobody has to be argued out of the faith. It is enough to stop listening, and the drifting looks after itself. Which is why the ordinary disciplines — the Sunday, the page, the friend who is allowed to ask — are not the maintenance of a spiritual life but the whole of it, and their absence needs no other cause to be fatal.

Then v. 28: a worthless witness mocks at justice, and the mouth of the wicked devours iniquity. That second image is the arresting one. He does not commit iniquity; he devours it, swallows it down — which puts it beside the delicacies of 18:8. Wickedness has become food, and a man who eats it will be hungry again tomorrow.

verseByVerse.quote: Condemnation is ready for scoffers, and beating for the backs of fools. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Condemnation is ready for scoffers, and beating for the backs of fools.

The chapter closes on a single word: ready. Not threatened, not coming eventually — prepared, waiting, already in position.

Which is the settled answer of this book to the observation everybody makes, that the scoffer appears to be doing rather well. Proverbs does not dispute the observation; it has spent this very chapter noting that money attracts friends and that poverty ends them. What it denies is that the present arrangement is the finished one. Nothing has been overlooked. The account is not closed because it has not yet been called.

And for the Christian this is not a chapter to end on grimly, because the whole force of the gospel is that the condemnation which was ready did not stay unclaimed. It was ready, and somebody came and took it — there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). The scoffer’s sentence is real and it is waiting; and the one thing this book could never have imagined is that the Judge would walk into the dock and receive it in the place of scoffers, so that men who deserved v. 29 might be given v. 23 instead, and lie down satisfied.

19.theology: The poor, the LORD, and the economics of grace. Proverbs 19:17 — "whoever is generous to the poor lends to the LORD" — is the wisdom literature's most direct statement of what might be called the economics of grace: the system of exchange that operates in the kingdom of God, where generosity to the vulnerable is generosity to God himself. This is consistent with the theology of the image of God (14:31 — oppressing the poor insults the Maker) and with the prophetic tradition (Amos, Micah, Isaiah — care for the poor is the litmus test of genuine covenant faithfulness). And it is confirmed by Jesus, who in Matthew 25 makes the treatment of the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the naked, and the imprisoned the criterion by which the nations are judged: what is done or not done to the least is done or not done to him. Generosity to the poor is not optional philanthropy; it is covenantal faithfulness to the LORD who identifies himself with them.
19.examples:
Then: "When a man's folly brings his way to ruin, his heart rages against the LORD" (v. 3) was recognisable to every ancient Israelite who had seen the pattern in their own community: the person who made bad decisions (foolish financial risks, sexual unfaithfulness, dishonest dealings) and then, when the consequences arrived, complained that God was being unfair. This is not a modern phenomenon; it is the timeless human instinct to attribute to God what we ourselves have caused. The wisdom tradition's insistence on honest self-examination is the antidote.

Now: "A prudent wife is from the LORD" (v. 14) is the wisdom perspective on the pursuit of a spouse. In a culture that approaches marriage as a matter of personal preference, strategic compatibility, and market dynamics, Proverbs insists that the most important qualities in a spouse — wisdom, character, prudence, faithfulness — are ultimately gifts of God rather than achievements of searching. This does not mean passivity in the search but a posture of dependence and gratitude: the wisdom to recognise a genuine gift when it is offered, and the humility to receive it as from the LORD rather than as a personal achievement.

20.title: Wine Is a Mocker

strokes make clean the innermost parts.
20.overview:
Chapter 20 is one of the more theologically reflective chapters in the Solomonic collection, with several proverbs that press beneath the surface of behaviour to the deeper questions of human nature and divine governance. "Who can say, 'I have made my heart clean; I have been pure from my sin'?" (v. 9) is one of the most important rhetorical questions in the Old Testament — an implicit answer that anticipates the universal sinfulness that Paul will articulate in Romans 3. And "the spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD, searching all his innermost parts" (v. 27) is a remarkable statement about divine omniscience and human self-knowledge.

The chapter also contains an important observation about deep motivation: "the purpose in a man's heart is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out" (v. 5). Human motivation is rarely transparent — people do not always know why they do what they do, and neither do the people around them. The person of understanding has the patient, empathetic skill to draw out what is hidden — to hear beneath the stated reason to the actual reason, to see beneath the presenting behaviour to the deeper desire or fear that drives it.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 20 — Sobriety, Integrity, and the Lamp That Searches the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 20 begins with wine as a mocker (v.1) and ends with the human spirit as a lamp of the LORD (v.27). Between those poles: the lazy man at harvest (v.4), the mystery of who is truly pure (v.9), the divine sovereignty over hearing and sight (v.12), the danger of hasty vows (v.25), and the sanctity of honest weights. The chapter is a sustained call to self-examination before a God who sees everything.
verseByVerse.theology: The lamp of the LORD searches the spirit (v.27)—one of the most searching statements in Proverbs about divine knowledge of the inner life. God does not observe behavior from the outside but illuminates the innermost person. Nothing is hidden from this light. This should produce both awe and freedom: awe because all pretense is futile; freedom because we need not pretend.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 9 ('Who can say, I have made my heart pure?') is one of Proverbs' most honest moments: even after wisdom's formation, no one can claim moral purity. The awareness of remaining corruption is itself a mark of wisdom; only the fool thinks himself clean. This humility drives the believer back to the gospel, the only true cleansing.

verseByVerse.quote: Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise. The terror of a king is like the growling of a lion; whoever provokes him to anger forfeits his life. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wine is a mocker, strong drink a brawler, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise.

The two nouns are people, not substances. Proverbs does not say wine causes mockery; it says wine is a mocker — a character in the room, with a personality, doing something to whoever is with it.

And the two words chosen describe exactly what alcohol does at its two stages. First it mocks: it makes a man funnier than he is, louder than he is, and finally ridiculous, and he is the only person present who does not know which stage he has reached. Then it brawls.

Note carefully what the verse does not say. It does not forbid wine. Scripture blesses it — the psalm says God gives wine to gladden the heart of man (Psalm 104:15), and the Lord Jesus made a great deal of it at a wedding. What Proverbs warns against is the man led astray by it, and the tell in that phrase is the passive: he is being taken somewhere.

So the honest question is not whether a Christian may drink. It is whether the thing is leading. And that has a simple test which anybody can run and few want to: go without it for a month, and notice not whether you can, but what you feel on the second evening.

Then v. 2 sets the terror of a king beside the mocker of v. 1 — two powers a man is unwise to provoke, one of them outside him and one in his hand.

verseByVerse.quote: It is an honor for a man to keep aloof from strife, but every fool will be quarreling. The sluggard does not plow in the autumn; he will seek at harvest and have nothing. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is an honour for a man to keep aloof from strife, but every fool will be quarrelling.

An honour. The same claim as 19:11, and the same reversal of instinct: walking away from a fight is presented not as the loss of face it feels like but as the thing that gives a man standing.

And the second half explains why. Every fool will be quarrelling — so quarrelling is not a distinction. Anybody can do it; it requires nothing, and the room is full of people willing. What is rare, and therefore honourable, is the man who could have engaged and did not.

Then v. 4, and it is the sluggard again with a new and better picture: the sluggard does not plough in the autumn; he will seek at harvest and have nothing.

Ploughing in autumn is cold, wet, and entirely unrewarding. Nothing grows for months. There is no way to feel productive doing it, and no visible difference at the end of the day between a field ploughed and a field not.

Which is the whole difficulty, and it is not laziness in the ordinary sense. The sluggard is defeated by work whose reward is invisible and distant — and that describes most of the important work anybody does: prayer, marriage, the slow raising of a child, study, saving. He is not unwilling to work. He is unwilling to work in November.

verseByVerse.quote: The purpose in a man's heart is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out. Many a man proclaims his own steadfast love, but a faithful man who can find? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The purpose in a man’s heart is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out.

This is the counselling verse of the Old Testament, and both halves matter.

The first is a warning against a common and confident error. What a man says he wants is very often not what he wants. He himself may not know; the real purpose is deep water, unlit, and he has no more access to the bottom of it than anybody else. Which is why arguments about the stated reason so rarely settle anything — the stated reason was never the reason.

And the second half is a job description. The man of understanding draws it out, and the verb is the one for hauling a bucket up a well. Slowly, hand over hand, and by asking rather than by telling.

Anybody can learn this and almost nobody practises it, because it requires the two hardest things in conversation: a question that is not disguised advice, and then silence long enough to be uncomfortable. Most people, offered thirty seconds of quiet, will say the true thing they did not intend to say — and the friend who can wait through those thirty seconds is worth more than the one with the better answer.

Then v. 6, and it is a sigh: many a man proclaims his own steadfast love, but a faithful man who can find? Everybody advertises loyalty. Almost nobody delivers it over twenty years — and the question mark at the end is left open, because Proverbs cannot answer it, and there is finally only one place the answer is found.

verseByVerse.quote: The righteous who walks in his integrity— blessed are his children after him! A king who sits on the throne of judgment winnows all evil with his eyes. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The righteous who walks in his integrity — blessed are his children after him!

The exclamation is on the children, and the phrase is after him. This is not a promise that a good man’s children will be converted; Scripture and experience both refuse that. It is a statement about inheritance of a different kind: a father who was one person, consistently, for thirty years leaves his children something they will be drawing on when he is gone.

And it is the walking that does it rather than the teaching. Children retain almost nothing that was said and almost everything that was done — which ought to relieve a parent of the pressure to be eloquent, and terrify him about Tuesday.

Then v. 8: a king who sits on the throne of judgment winnows all evil with his eyes. Winnowing is throwing threshed grain into the air so the wind carries the chaff away — a separating work, done by lifting everything up where the air can get at it.

And the instrument here is his eyes. Not an investigation. A good judge separates largely by looking, because most deceit is visible to a man who has seen a great deal of it and is not in a hurry.

verseByVerse.quote: Who can say, "I have made my heart pure; I am clean from my sin"? Unequal weights and unequal measures are both alike an abomination to the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who can say, I have made my heart pure; I am clean from my sin?

The question is rhetorical and the answer is nobody, and this is one of the most important verses in the book.

Notice how it is framed. Not who is pure — who can say. The challenge is to stand up and make the claim, and the whole force of it is that everybody reading knows he cannot, and knows it instantly, without needing to review the evidence.

And the verb is even more searching: I have MADE my heart pure. It is not primarily asking whether a man is clean but whether he has cleaned himself — and that is the thing every religion in the world exists to attempt, and this book, at the summit of the wisdom tradition, says plainly that it cannot be done. Proverbs has spent nineteen chapters on how to live well, and now stops and says that nobody who has followed it perfectly has arrived at a pure heart, because nobody has followed it perfectly.

Which leaves a book of wisdom with a problem it cannot solve, and it does not pretend to. It asks the question and leaves it standing.

The answer came a thousand years later, and it came in the form the question demanded. Not a technique, and not a better effort. The blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7) — and it is a passive: he is cleansed, by somebody else, from the outside. Nobody has ever made his own heart pure. A great many have had it done to them.

Then v. 10 — unequal weights and unequal measures are both alike an abomination — and the placing is not accidental. Immediately after a verse about a man’s inability to see himself clearly comes a verse about carrying two sets of scales.

verseByVerse.quote: Even a child makes himself known by his acts, by whether his conduct is pure and upright. The hearing ear and the seeing eye, the LORD has made them both. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even a child makes himself known by his acts, by whether his conduct is pure and upright.

The word even is doing the work. If it is true of a child — who has no strategy, no reputation to manage, and no capacity for the long deception adults are capable of — how much more plainly is a grown man readable by what he does.

And the verse is a gift to parents, who spend a good deal of energy wondering what is going on inside a child who will not say. It says: watch what he does. Not the declared feelings, not the answers to direct questions, which children are as poor at as adults. The conduct is the disclosure.

Then v. 12: the hearing ear and the seeing eye, the LORD has made them both.

A quiet sentence with a great deal under it. In a book obsessed with listening and looking — with hearing instruction, with where a man’s eyes go — this stops and observes that the equipment itself was issued.

Which cuts two ways. It makes hearing an accountable act: the ear was given for something, and a man who will not use it is misusing property. And it offers hope to anybody who has concluded that he simply cannot hear — because if the LORD made the ear, he can open one, and the prophets say he does exactly that (Isaiah 50:5).

verseByVerse.quote: Love not sleep, lest you come to poverty; open your eyes, and you will have plenty of bread. "Bad, bad," says the buyer, but when he goes away, then he boasts. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love not sleep, lest you come to poverty. Not do not sleep — Scripture is warm about sleep and calls it a gift (Psalm 127:2). What is forbidden is loving it, which is a different relation entirely: the man who is not resting but retreating, and for whom bed has become the place where the day’s difficulties do not have to be met.

Then v. 14, and Proverbs turns comic: Bad, bad, says the buyer, but when he goes away, then he boasts.

Anybody who has haggled knows this man and has been him. He stands in front of the thing he intends to buy, running it down — the condition, the age, the flaw nobody else noticed — and every word is aimed at the price. Then he walks off down the road delighted with what he has got.

Proverbs finds it funny, and the humour is not the whole point. Nothing he said was technically a lie; every criticism was arguable. But the words were not about the object at all, and both parties knew it — which makes this the most ordinary and least confessed form of dishonesty there is. It is the sin of speech aimed at an effect rather than at the truth, and it is committed a dozen times a day by people who have never told an outright lie in their lives.

verseByVerse.quote: There is gold and abundance of costly stones, but the lips of knowledge are a precious jewel. Take a man's garment when he has put up security for a stranger, and hold it in pledge when he puts up security for foreigners. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is gold and abundance of costly stones, but the lips of knowledge are a precious jewel. The first half concedes the market: gold exists, jewels exist, and there is a great deal of both. What is rare is not the treasure. It is somebody who says something worth hearing.

Then v. 16: take a man’s garment when he has put up security for a stranger.

The instruction is directed at the lender, and it sounds harsh until the situation is seen. Somebody has guaranteed a stranger’s debt — the folly of 6:1 — and the counsel is: take his coat. Hold real security, because this man has demonstrated that he does not understand what he has agreed to.

The law limited it — a poor man’s cloak had to be returned by sundown, because he slept in it (Exodus 22:26-27) — so this is not licence for hardness. It is Proverbs being practical about a man who has made a promise he cannot cover, and refusing to let sentiment build the transaction on nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be full of gravel. Plans are established by counsel; by wise guidance wage war. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be full of gravel.

The image is one of the best in the book because it happens in one mouth, in two stages.

First the sweetness, and Proverbs never denies it. Dishonest gain tastes better than honest gain — it is the same bread with the additional flavour of having got away with something. Anybody who pretends otherwise has not been listened to by a single person who has done it.

Then the second stage, and the horror is that nothing has been swapped. The bread does not become something else; it turns to gravel in the mouth that is eating it — dry, gritty, impossible to swallow, and there is a great deal of it. The man is left chewing the same meal he enjoyed.

Which is exactly how it is described by people years afterwards. Not that the money went — often it did not. That the enjoyment of it stopped, permanently, and could not be recovered, and every subsequent good thing bought with it arrived with grit in it.

Then v. 18: plans are established by counsel; by wise guidance wage war. The subject is the largest, most irreversible decision an ancient society could make — and the counsel is the same as for everything else: do not do it alone.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever goes about slandering reveals secrets; therefore do not associate with a simple babbler. If one curses his father or his mother, his lamp will be put out in utter darkness. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever goes about slandering reveals secrets; therefore do not associate with a simple babbler.

The therefore carries a piece of reasoning most people never complete. Everybody knows that talking to a gossip is unwise because of what he might say about you. Proverbs draws a different conclusion: do not associate with him at all — not because of the risk to your reputation, but because of what association does to you.

A man cannot spend regular time with somebody who trades in other people’s private business and remain unaffected. He begins to hear news as currency. He starts to know things he has no business knowing, and the knowing feels like being close to the centre. Nobody in that friendship is only receiving.

Then v. 20: if one curses his father or his mother, his lamp will be put out in utter darkness.

The sentence is severe, and it belongs to a world where the family was the whole social order — so contempt for a parent was an assault on the structure everything else stood on. The image is a lamp going out at night in a house, and the phrase for the darkness is the deepest one Hebrew has.

And a word is needed here for readers whose parents were not good ones. The verse concerns cursing — the deliberate invocation of harm, the settled contempt — and it is not addressed to somebody who is grieving what he did not receive, or who has had to put distance between himself and a person who hurt him. Honouring a parent is commanded; pretending is not.

verseByVerse.quote: An inheritance gained hastily in the beginning will not be blessed in the end. Do not say, "I will repay evil"; wait for the LORD, and he will deliver you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
An inheritance gained hastily in the beginning will not be blessed in the end. The same principle as 13:11, applied to money that arrives rather than money that is made — and hastily may carry the sense of grasped at, taken before it was due.

Then v. 22, and it is one of the great verses of the Old Testament: do not say, I will repay evil; wait for the LORD, and he will deliver you.

Notice that the verse forbids the saying. Not merely the act — the sentence a man rehearses, silently, on the drive home. That is where revenge lives, and most of it never gets any further, and Proverbs still says do not.

And what is offered instead is not forgetting and it is not pretending nothing happened. It is wait for the LORD, which assumes the wrong is real, assumes it deserves an answer, and assigns the answer to somebody else. The reason is not that vengeance is too strong a thing but that it is too big a thing for the man holding it — he cannot see well enough to measure it, and he is not neutral.

Paul quotes exactly this instinct and gives it the settled New Testament form: never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, Vengeance is mine, I will repay (Romans 12:19). The comfort in that is easily missed. It does not say the matter will be dropped. It says it has been transferred to a court with better information and no personal stake.

verseByVerse.quote: Unequal weights are an abomination to the LORD, and false scales are not good. A man's steps are from the LORD; how then can man understand his way? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unequal weights are an abomination to the LORD, and false scales are not good. The third time in this book (11:1; 20:10), and the repetition is the emphasis. If Proverbs says anything three times about business, that is where the reader should look.

Then v. 24, which is the deepest sentence in the chapter: a man’s steps are from the LORD; how then can man understand his way?

The first half is 16:9. The second half is new, and it is a question — and the logic in it is the reason so many Christians are confused about their own lives.

If God is placing the steps, then the pattern being walked out is his, and a man in the middle of it is the one person least able to read it. He can see where he has been and cannot see the shape. Which means the frustration of not understanding one’s own life is not a failure of faith or of attention. It is structural, and this verse says so with a shrug.

That is more freeing than it sounds. A great deal of Christian anxiety consists of trying to work out what God is doing — as though a man could, and as though he must before he can rest. The verse quietly removes the obligation. The steps are his. The understanding was never issued.

verseByVerse.quote: It is a snare to say rashly, "It is holy," and to reflect only after making vows. A wise king winnows the wicked and drives the wheel over them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is a snare to say rashly, It is holy, and to reflect only after making vows.

The picture is a man declaring something dedicated to God in a moment of feeling — an amount, a possession, a commitment — and doing his thinking afterwards. Ecclesiastes gives the same warning and tells him not to let his mouth lead him into sin (Ecclesiastes 5:2-6).

And this is a live danger for anybody in a warm meeting. Something is said from the front, the music is right, a man feels the whole thing keenly, and he promises — the money, the year abroad, the ministry — and on Wednesday he is a man with an obligation he made in a state he cannot now reproduce.

Proverbs does not tell him to feel less. It tells him to do his reflecting first, and it calls the alternative a snare — a trap he built and baited himself, out of genuine devotion.

Then v. 26: a wise king winnows the wicked and drives the wheel over them. The threshing wheel was a weighted sledge dragged over the harvest to break the grain from the husk. The image is brutal and its function is separation: leadership includes the unpleasant work of not letting everything stay mixed together.

verseByVerse.quote: The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD, searching all his innermost parts. Steadfast love and faithfulness preserve the king, and by steadfast love his throne is upheld. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD, searching all his innermost parts.

A remarkable sentence, and the Hebrew should be had exactly. God is described as carrying a lamp through the inside of a man, and the lamp he carries is the man’s own spirit.

This is the Old Testament’s account of conscience, and it explains something everybody has experienced and few can name. There is a faculty in a person that reports on him against his own interest. It wakes him at four in the morning with a thing he did in 1998. It refuses to accept the explanation he has successfully given everybody else. He would switch it off if he could, and he cannot — because it is not finally his instrument. It is being held by somebody, and the searching is being done.

Which is a terror and a mercy in the same sentence. A man whose conscience still troubles him has not been abandoned; the lamp is still lit and still moving. It is the ones who feel nothing at all, whose consciences are seared (1 Timothy 4:2), who are in the dark.

Then v. 28: steadfast love and faithfulness preserve the king, and by steadfast love his throne is upheld. Hesed and emet again — the pair from 16:6 and Exodus 34:6. A throne is held up not by force but by the two qualities that describe God’s own character, which is why the only king whose throne is finally secure is the one who is those things.

verseByVerse.quote: The glory of young men is their strength, but the splendor of old men is their gray hair. Blows that wound cleanse away evil; strokes make clean the innermost parts. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The glory of young men is their strength, but the splendour of old men is their grey hair.

Two words for magnificence, one given to each end of a life, and neither is disparaged. The young are not told that their strength is vanity, and the old are not consoled with the idea that what they have lost did not matter. Both are called glorious, and they are different glories.

What the verse quietly forbids is either one attempting the other’s. An old man performing youth is not splendid, and a young man affecting the gravity of age is not either. Each has been given something the other cannot have, and the entire arrangement only works if they are in the same room.

Then v. 30, and the chapter closes on a hard sentence: blows that wound cleanse away evil; strokes make clean the innermost parts.

The claim is that some things in a man do not come out by any gentler method — that there is a kind of evil which is not reasoned away, or gradually outgrown, but only ever removed by something that hurts. Anybody who has actually changed in a deep way knows this is true, and knows it was not a book that did it. It was a loss, or a failure, or a public humiliation, or an illness.

And the verse must not become a licence, since Proverbs has already forbidden violence in anger and God’s own discipline is the discipline of a father who delights (3:11-12). What it is doing is naming the cost of real cleansing, honestly, so that a man in the middle of a painful year is not left thinking that the pain means nothing is happening.

And there is one place where this proverb was fulfilled to the letter and the arrangement was reversed. The wounds went into somebody who had no evil in him to cleanse. With his stripes we are healed (Isaiah 53:5) — the strokes fell on him, and the innermost parts made clean were ours.

20.theology: Universal sinfulness and the need for divine cleansing. Proverbs 20:9 — "who can say, 'I have made my heart clean; I have been pure from my sin'?" — is the wisdom literature's contribution to the biblical theology of universal human sinfulness. The rhetorical question's implied answer (no one) is the foundation for the entire New Testament soteriology: if no one can clean their own heart, then the gospel's offer of cleansing through Christ is not a luxury for the morally sensitive but a necessity for every human being. Keller reads Proverbs 20:9 as the point at which the wisdom tradition's self-knowledge leads inevitably to the need for grace: the wise person, who has genuinely attended to the reality of their own heart, discovers what Jeremiah 17:9 states explicitly ("the heart is deceitful above all things and desperately sick — who can understand it?") — and this discovery is the beginning of the openness to the gospel.
20.examples:
Then: "The righteous who walks in his integrity — blessed are his children after him!" (v. 7) is the multigenerational vision of wisdom: the blessing of integrity is not merely personal but propagates to the next generation. The children of the person of integrity grow up in an environment shaped by that integrity — they observe it, absorb it, are formed by it. This is not a guarantee of their own righteousness (each person must make their own choices) but a recognition that the environment of integrity is itself a gift to the next generation, one of the most important things a parent can provide.

Now: "The purpose in a man's heart is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out" (v. 5) is the wisdom text for all pastoral and counselling ministry. The presenting question is rarely the real question; the stated reason for the decision is rarely the deepest reason; the surface behaviour is rarely the whole story. The person of understanding — who has learned to listen patiently, to ask the question beneath the question, to create the trust that allows the deep water to surface — is one of the most valuable people any community can have. This is pastoral wisdom as Proverbs understands it: not the rapid dispensing of advice but the patient, empathetic drawing out of what is genuinely there.

21.title: The King's Heart

how much more when he brings it with evil intent.<sup>28</sup>A false witness will perish, but the word of a man who hears will endure.<sup>29</sup>A wicked man puts on a bold face, but the upright gives thought to his ways.<sup>30</sup>No wisdom, no understanding, no counsel can avail against the LORD.<sup>31</sup>The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD.
21.overview:
Chapter 21 opens with the most striking statement of divine sovereignty in the book: "the king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will" (v. 1). If the most powerful human being — the king, whose word is law — is in the LORD's hands as easily as a stream of water, then no human power or human plan can ultimately resist the purposes of God. The chapter closes with the companion proverb: "the horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD" (v. 31). Between the king's heart and the battle horse, human agency and divine sovereignty bracket the entire chapter.

The chapter also contains one of Proverbs' most important social ethics proverbs: "whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself call out and not be answered" (v. 13). The connection between our response to others' need and God's response to our need is stated here with stark symmetry: those who do not hear the cry of the poor will not be heard when they cry. This is the justice principle of reciprocity that runs through the entire wisdom tradition and that Jesus will make explicit: "with the measure you use it will be measured to you" (Matt 7:2).

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 21 — God's Sovereignty Over the King, and the Character of the Wise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 21 opens with one of the most powerful sovereignty statements in Proverbs ('The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD') and moves through justice, sacrifice without righteousness, the contentious wife, and the ultimate futility of planning against God. The chapter closes with the war-horse—powerful, prepared, impressive—and the declaration that victory belongs to the LORD alone.
verseByVerse.theology: Justice and righteousness (v.3) is more acceptable to God than sacrifice—a prophetic note inside the wisdom literature (cf. 1 Sam. 15:22; Amos 5:21-24). Religious performance without ethical conformity is rejected. The God of Proverbs is the God of the prophets: he cannot be honored with ritual while his image-bearers are oppressed.
verseByVerse.examples: The verse about giving to the poor (v.13) and the verse about the righteous giving and not sparing (v.26) together create a picture of generosity as a defining characteristic of the righteous. The contrast with the wicked who crave all day long is the contrast between desire governed by love and desire governed by appetite.

verseByVerse.quote: The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will. Every way of a man is right in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the heart. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king’s heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will.

The picture is irrigation. In a dry country a farmer directed water by opening and closing small channels with his foot or his hand, and the water went where the channel went. It did not argue and it did not know.

And the subject chosen is not an ordinary man but a king — the least directable person in the ancient world, answerable to nobody, whose decisions could not be appealed. Proverbs picks the hardest case on purpose. If the king’s heart is a channel in God’s hand, everybody else’s is.

It is the single most steadying verse in Scripture for anybody who has watched a decision made above him that he could do nothing about. The board, the government, the consultant, the man who would not take the call. None of them is outside the hand, and none of them will feel a thing — because the king in this verse is not aware of being turned. He experiences himself as deciding, and he is deciding, and the water still goes where the channel goes.

Then v. 2: every way of a man is right in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the heart. The near-twin of 16:2, with one word changed. There God weighed the spirit; here the heart. Between them nothing is left unweighed.

verseByVerse.quote: To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice. Haughty eyes and a proud heart, the lamp of the wicked, are sin. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice.

This is 15:8 sharpened. There the sacrifice of the wicked was an abomination; here even the ordinary, proper, commanded sacrifice is ranked below plain right dealing.

And that is a startling thing to find in the Old Testament, since the sacrifices were God’s own appointment. He commanded them. Proverbs is not attacking them — it is refusing to let them be used as a substitute, which is exactly what Samuel told Saul (1 Samuel 15:22) and what the prophets spent their lives shouting.

The reason it needs saying in every generation is that religious activity is so much easier than justice. A man can attend, give, serve on a rota and be visibly devout, and all of it is more comfortable than paying a bill he could delay, or telling the truth about what happened in the meeting, or treating an employee the way he would want his son treated. Worship is public and finite. Righteousness is daily and nobody applauds it.

Then v. 4: haughty eyes and a proud heart, the lamp of the wicked, are sin. The Hebrew is compressed and the striking thing is the last word. Not lead to sin, not produce it. The proud look and the proud heart are sin — before anything has been done with them.

verseByVerse.quote: The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance, but everyone who is hasty comes only to poverty. The getting of treasures by a lying tongue is a fleeting vapor and a snare of death. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance, but everyone who is hasty comes only to poverty.

The contrast is not diligence against laziness — it is diligence against haste, and the hasty man in this verse is working extremely hard. He is simply working fast, and the two are being set against each other as though they were opposites, which in practice they are.

Diligence in this book is a slow quality. It has plans; it accumulates; it is prepared to spend three years on something. Haste wants the same result and is unwilling to spend the time, so it takes the route that skips a stage — and the skipped stage is nearly always the one that would have made the thing hold.

Then v. 6: the getting of treasures by a lying tongue is a fleeting vapour and a snare of death. The word for vapour is hevel — the word Ecclesiastes uses forty times for everything under the sun. Breath on a cold morning: visibly there, and gone, and nothing to hold.

And the two halves of the image do not agree, which is the point. It is a vapour, so there is nothing to it; and it is a snare, so it holds a man fast. That is precisely the condition of the person who has money he should not have. There is nothing in his hands, and he cannot get free.

verseByVerse.quote: The violence of the wicked will sweep them away, because they refuse to do what is just. The way of the guilty is crooked, but the conduct of the pure is upright. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The violence of the wicked will sweep them away, because they refuse to do what is just. The verb is a flood word. Their own violence is the water, and it takes them — which is 1:18 again, the ambush that catches the men who set it.

And the reason given is worth noticing: because they refuse. Not because they do not know. This book is careful about that distinction all the way through, and it is why Proverbs is finally a moral book rather than an educational one. The wicked man in this verse has the information.

Then v. 8: the way of the guilty is crooked, but the conduct of the pure is upright.

Two roads and one word doing the work in each. Crooked here is a rare word meaning twisted back on itself, and it describes something anybody can verify by listening to a dishonest man explain himself: the account doubles back, qualifies, produces a second version of a detail already given, and takes four minutes to say what a straight answer says in six words.

verseByVerse.quote: It is better to live in a corner of the housetop than in a house shared with a quarrelsome wife. The soul of the wicked desires evil; his neighbor finds no mercy in his eyes. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is better to live in a corner of the housetop than in a house shared with a quarrelsome wife.

The roof of an Israelite house was flat and used for sleeping in hot weather, and a corner of it means exposed on all sides, with no shelter, in whatever the night brings. Proverbs says: that, rather than the house.

Two things must be said, and the first is that the same book knows the other side of this exactly. It says at 12:4 that a contentious spouse is rottenness in the bones, and it says at 19:13 that quarrelling is a dripping that never stops — and it also says, three times over, that the same fault in a man kindles strife like charcoal on a fire (26:21; 15:18; 29:22). The sin has no sex. The proverb speaks from the angle of the household it was written in.

The second is that this verse is not counsel to leave. It is a measurement — of how much misery a permanent low-level conflict actually causes, set against how little most people think it matters. A couple who would never consider divorce may well be living in the second half of this verse, and the verse exists to say out loud that it is a serious condition and not a temperament to be endured indefinitely without anybody naming it.

Then v. 10: the soul of the wicked desires evil; his neighbour finds no mercy in his eyes. The appetite is named first and the effect on the neighbour second, in that order, because that is the order it happens in.

verseByVerse.quote: When a scoffer is punished, the simple becomes wise; when a wise man is instructed, he gains knowledge. The Righteous One observes the house of the wicked; he throws the wicked down to ruin. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
When a scoffer is punished, the simple becomes wise; when a wise man is instructed, he gains knowledge.

This is 19:25 again, and the arrangement of the two halves is the teaching: three men, and the one being dealt with is the only one who learns nothing. The simple learns by watching, the wise man learns by being told, and the scoffer is the occasion of both lessons and the recipient of neither.

Then v. 12: the Righteous One observes the house of the wicked; he throws the wicked down to ruin.

Most translations capitalise the Righteous One, and the reason matters. This is not a good man watching his neighbour. It is God, and the verb is a watching verb — considering, attending, taking the measure of a household from outside.

And that is the answer this book keeps returning to when the accounts do not balance. The question in every reader’s mind, all through Proverbs, is why the wicked house is standing and looks so well appointed. The answer given here is not that it will fall soon. It is that somebody is looking at it, and has been for years, and has not yet said anything.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself call out and not be answered. A gift in secret averts anger, and a concealed bribe, strong wrath. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself call out and not be answered.

The symmetry is exact and it is frightening. Not a general warning about judgment — the punishment is the crime, done back. The verb is the same on both sides: he did not hear a call, and his own call will not be heard.

And closes his ear describes something active. Nobody in this verse failed to notice the poor man. He heard, and then did something with the hearing — changed the subject, moved the thought on, produced the reason why this particular case was not his to deal with. Everybody has a mechanism for this and it operates in about two seconds.

Which is why the verse cannot be answered by a direct debit, useful as one is. What is being described is not a failure to give but a trained deafness — and the way it is unlearned is by letting a specific cry in, from a specific person, and not immediately deciding what to do about it.

Then v. 14: a gift in secret averts anger, and a concealed bribe, strong wrath. Proverbs is observing again rather than commending — the same dry realism as 17:8. It reports that this works, and it has already said three times where it comes out.

verseByVerse.quote: When justice is done, it is a joy to the righteous but terror to evildoers. One who wanders from the way of good sense will rest in the assembly of the dead. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
When justice is done, it is a joy to the righteous but terror to evildoers.

One event, two reactions, and the reactions sort the room — which applies to a good deal more than courtrooms.

Everybody is in favour of justice in the abstract. What this verse says is that when it actually lands — when the thing is investigated, when the accounts are examined, when the person who has been getting away with it is finally named — a man’s response is a disclosure. Relief is one answer. Anxiety is another.

And the application closest to home is the second coming, which the New Testament describes in exactly these two registers: the day is a hope to be longed for and a terror to be fled, and which of the two it is depends entirely on where a man stands.

Then v. 16: one who wanders from the way of good sense will rest in the assembly of the dead. Wanders again — the sheep verb, no decision anywhere in it. And the phrase assembly of the dead has a chill in it that death alone does not: he does not merely die, he joins a company. He was never as individual as he thought; a great crowd went the same way, one small step at a time, and he is with them.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever loves pleasure will be a poor man; he who loves wine and oil will not be rich. The wicked is a ransom for the righteous, and the traitor for the upright. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever loves pleasure will be a poor man; he who loves wine and oil will not be rich.

The word is loves, and the verse is not against pleasure. Wine and oil are good things in Scripture, given by God to gladden and to anoint. What is named here is a man who has organised his life around them, and the observation is economic rather than moral: this is expensive, and it does not stop being expensive.

And there is a modern edge to it. Wine and oil were the ancient world’s luxuries — the small, frequent, entirely legitimate comforts. Not vice. Nobody goes bankrupt on one bottle, and a great many people are quietly poor from a hundred small pleasant things bought without ever making a decision.

Then v. 18, which is difficult: the wicked is a ransom for the righteous, and the traitor for the upright.

The plainest sense is an observation about how things come out in the end: the trouble the wicked man prepared for the righteous falls on him instead, so that he ends up, as it were, paying the price the other man was going to pay. Haman on his own gallows is the Bible’s clearest illustration.

But a Christian cannot read the word ransom in that sentence without feeling the ground move, because the gospel runs the transaction the other way. Proverbs describes the wicked substituting for the righteous by the ordinary working of justice. At the cross the righteous substituted for the wicked, by nothing but love — the Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). The word is the same. Everything else is reversed.

verseByVerse.quote: It is better to live in a desert land than with a quarrelsome and fretful woman. Precious treasure and oil are in a wise man's dwelling, but a foolish man devours it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is better to live in a desert land than with a quarrelsome and fretful woman. The roof of v. 9 has become a wilderness — the same complaint, escalated. And fretful adds something the earlier verse did not have: not only anger but a continuous low agitation that has no particular object and cannot be resolved by fixing anything.

That is the honest thing this verse contributes, and it applies to whoever in a household is the one carrying it. Some conflict is about the subject under discussion and can be settled. Some is not about anything, and the attempt to settle it by addressing the stated issue will fail repeatedly until somebody realises that the stated issue was never it.

Then v. 20: precious treasure and oil are in a wise man’s dwelling, but a foolish man devours it.

The contrast is storing against devouring, and the fool is not described as poor. He has had the same treasure. The difference is that in the wise man’s house it is in the house — present, kept, available when needed — and in the fool’s it went through him.

Anybody who has seen two households on identical incomes knows this is real, and knows it is not about arithmetic. One of them has something put by and the other cannot say where it went, and neither could tell you the decision that separated them, because there was not one.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever pursues righteousness and kindness will find life, righteousness, and honor. A wise man scales the city of the mighty and brings down the stronghold in which they trust. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever pursues righteousness and kindness will find life, righteousness, and honour.

There is a small joke in that sentence and it carries the whole verse. He pursues two things and finds three — and one of the three is the thing he was already chasing. He went after righteousness, and righteousness is listed among what he found.

Which is the paradox at the centre of the moral life. The man who sets out to obtain a quality by aiming at it directly generally does not get it; the man who pursues it as a way of living discovers he has it, and is the last to notice. Nobody has ever become humble by trying to be humble. Righteousness is found by people who were going after it for its own sake and were not watching themselves acquire it.

Then v. 22: a wise man scales the city of the mighty and brings down the stronghold in which they trust.

One man, on foot, against fortifications — and he wins. Which is the same claim as 24:5 and the reason Proverbs keeps returning to it: strength is impressive and wisdom is decisive. Ecclesiastes tells the story with a poor wise man who saved a city and was forgotten immediately afterwards (Ecclesiastes 9:14-15), and the forgetting is part of the point. Wisdom takes the city and nobody writes it down.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever keeps his mouth and his tongue keeps himself out of trouble. "Scoffer" is the name of the arrogant, haughty man who acts with arrogant pride. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever keeps his mouth and his tongue keeps himself out of trouble. The same verb twice — keeps, and keeps — as at 19:16. Guard the mouth and it turns out you were guarding yourself, and the man who does it will never know which specific disasters did not happen.

That is the difficulty with this kind of obedience, and it should be said plainly. Restraint has no visible reward. Nobody thanks a man for a sentence he did not say, and he gets no story out of it; the whole benefit is a series of catastrophes that quietly failed to occur.

Then v. 24 does something unusual: it defines a word. Scoffer is the name of the arrogant, haughty man who acts with arrogant pride.

Proverbs has used scoffer for twenty chapters and now stops to say who he is, and the definition is entirely about pride. Not cynicism, not humour, not intelligence. The scoffer mocks because mockery is what contempt sounds like when it is spoken — and mockery is his method precisely because it never requires him to be answerable for a claim. A man who argues can be shown to be wrong. A man who sneers has said nothing that can be examined, which is the whole appeal.

verseByVerse.quote: The desire of the sluggard kills him, for his hands refuse to labor. All day long he craves and craves, but the righteous gives and does not hold back. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The desire of the sluggard kills him, for his hands refuse to labour.

Not his laziness kills him — his desire. That is the most acute thing this book says about the subject, and it is the diagnosis of 13:4 driven all the way home.

What destroys the sluggard is the gap. He is not a man without appetite; he wants a great deal, and the wanting is vivid and continuous and costs nothing. And it kills him because it produces the sensation of a life being lived while nothing whatever is happening — so that a man may spend twenty years in a state of permanent intention and experience it, from inside, as almost the same thing as effort.

Then v. 26 sets the picture beside its opposite: all day long he craves and craves, but the righteous gives and does not hold back.

The comparison is not the one a reader expects. The opposite of the man who craves is not the man who works. It is the man who gives — because craving and giving are the two directions a life can face, and the sluggard’s problem is finally not idleness but a hand that is always turned upward.

verseByVerse.quote: The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination; how much more when he brings it with evil intent. A false witness will perish, but the word of a man who hears will endure. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination; how much more when he brings it with evil intent.

15:8 said the first half. This adds a stage, and the stage is worse than most readers notice. The baseline is a wicked man bringing a proper offering with no particular scheme in mind — and that is already an abomination. Then Proverbs says: how much more when the worship is itself a tool.

Which describes a real and common thing. Religion used to build a reputation that will be useful. Attendance maintained to keep access to people. Generosity given publicly to purchase standing in a congregation. Prayer offered aloud that is aimed sideways at whoever is listening.

Nobody in that description is a hypocrite in the crude sense; most of it is done half-knowingly by people who would be appalled at the accusation. And this verse says God has watched the whole transaction and knows the difference between an offering and an instrument.

Then v. 28: a false witness will perish, but the word of a man who hears will endure. The contrast is unexpected — not a truthful witness, but a man who hears. What makes testimony durable is not sincerity in the speaking; it is accuracy in the listening, and a man who listened carefully will still be right in ten years.

verseByVerse.quote: A wicked man puts on a bold face, but the upright gives thought to his ways. No wisdom, no understanding, no counsel can avail against the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A wicked man puts on a bold face, but the upright gives thought to his ways.

The phrase is literally that he makes his face strong, and it names a technique that works extremely well in most rooms. Confidence is treated by human beings as evidence, and a man who looks certain is believed over a man who is thinking.

And the contrast is exactly right. What the upright man does is invisible: he gives thought to his ways, which produces no expression at all and reads, at a meeting, as hesitation. Two men, one composing his face and one composing his conduct — and in the short run the first one carries the room.

Then vv. 30 and 31 close the chapter and return to where it opened: no wisdom, no understanding, no counsel can avail against the LORD.

Three nouns, and they are the three things this entire book has been telling the reader to acquire. Twenty-one chapters urging a man to get wisdom, understanding and counsel — and then a sentence saying that all three of them are nothing if they are set against God.

Which is not a contradiction; it is the frame the whole book has always been sitting in. Wisdom is not a power a man acquires and then possesses independently. It is alignment. Used with the grain of God it does everything Proverbs has promised; turned against him it is not merely wrong but weightless, and the cleverest men in every generation have discovered this at their own expense.

verseByVerse.quote: The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD.

The chapter ends on a sentence that has kept a great many people sane, and its balance is perfect.

The horse is made ready. That is a real job and it is the man’s. In an ancient army it meant everything — the animal fed, trained, shod, harnessed, brought to the field on the right morning. The verse does not sneer at any of it, and Proverbs has spent twenty-one chapters insisting on exactly this kind of preparation.

And then the second half removes the one thing the preparation was for. The victory is not produced by the horse, however well prepared, and no amount of readiness converts into an outcome. The two clauses do not compete; they simply belong to different parties.

Which is the settled Christian posture toward every serious thing a person does. Prepare the sermon properly, and God gives the effect. Do the treatment, and the healing is his. Raise the children as carefully as you know how, and their souls are not in your hands. The refusal to prepare is presumption; the belief that the preparation secures the outcome is a different presumption, and it is the one that breaks people when the outcome does not come.

And so the chapter that began with a king’s heart as a channel of water ends with the whole apparatus of human power drawn up on a field and waiting. The horses are ready. The LORD gives the victory — and the day it was finally given, there was no cavalry anywhere in sight, only a man on a borrowed donkey riding into a city to die, and coming out of a tomb having won.

21.theology: Divine sovereignty over history and the limits of human power. Proverbs 21:1 and 21:30–31 together form the book's most comprehensive statement of divine sovereignty over history. The king's heart, the counsellor's wisdom, the warrior's horse — all are in the LORD's hands. This is not a counsel of fatalism but of faith: the person who knows that the LORD governs the king's heart and secures the victory is freed from the anxiety of ultimate responsibility. They plan, they prepare, they fight — but they hold the outcome loosely, because they know who holds the outcome. This is the Calvinist tradition's "God controls and we are responsible" applied to the full range of human endeavour: political, intellectual, and military. Human agency is real and matters; but it operates within a governance that ensures the LORD's purposes will stand (19:21).
21.examples:
Then: "To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice" (v. 3) was a prophetic challenge to a culture that had learned to separate religious observance from social ethics. The person who offered elaborate sacrifices at the temple while oppressing workers, cheating in business, and ignoring the poor had not understood either sacrifice or justice. The sacrifice is the expression of a life; when the life contradicts the sacrifice, the sacrifice is worse than useless — it is an insult to the God whose character it claims to honour.

Now: "The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD" (v. 31) is the wisdom text for every leader, strategist, and planner who has done everything right and still found the outcome out of their hands. Prepare thoroughly — this is wisdom's consistent counsel. But hold the preparation with an open hand, knowing that the victory is the LORD's to give or withhold according to purposes that exceed your strategy. The leader who has internalised this is both more diligent (because preparation is real responsibility) and more peaceful (because the outcome is not ultimately their burden to carry).

22.title: A Good Name
22.text: <sup>1</sup>A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches, and favor is better than silver or gold.<sup>2</sup>The rich and the poor meet together; the LORD is the Maker of them all.<sup>3</sup>The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it.<sup>4</sup>The reward for humility and fear of the LORD is riches and honor and life.<sup>5</sup>Thorns and snares are in the way of the crooked; whoever guards his soul will keep far from them.<sup>6</sup>Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it.<sup>7</sup>The rich rules over the poor, and the borrower is the slave of the lender.<sup>8</sup>Whoever sows injustice will reap calamity, and the rod of his fury will fail.<sup>9</sup>Whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor.<sup>10</sup>Drive out a scoffer, and strife will go out, and quarreling and abuse will cease.<sup>11</sup>He who loves purity of heart, and whose speech is gracious, will have the king as his friend.<sup>12</sup>The eyes of the LORD keep watch over knowledge, but he overthrows the words of the traitor.<sup>13</sup>The sluggard says, "There is a lion outside! I shall be killed in the streets!"<sup>14</sup>The mouth of forbidden women is a deep pit; he with whom the LORD is angry will fall into it.<sup>15</sup>Folly is bound up in the heart of a child, but the rod of discipline drives it far from him.<sup>16</sup>Whoever oppresses the poor to increase his own wealth, or gives to the rich, will only come to poverty.<sup>17</sup>Incline your ear, and hear the words of the wise, and apply your heart to my knowledge,<sup>18</sup>for it will be pleasant if you keep them within you, if all of them are ready on your lips.<sup>19</sup>That your trust may be in the LORD, I have made them known to you today, even to you.<sup>20</sup>Have I not written for you thirty sayings of counsel and knowledge,<sup>21</sup>to make you know what is right and true, that you may give a true answer to those who sent you?<sup>22</sup>Do not rob the poor, because he is poor, or crush the afflicted at the gate,<sup>23</sup>for the LORD will plead their cause and rob of life those who rob them.<sup>24</sup>Make no friendship with a man given to anger, nor go with a wrathful man,<sup>25</sup>lest you learn his ways and entangle yourself in a snare.<sup>26</sup>Be not one of those who give pledges, who put up security for debts.<sup>27</sup>If you have nothing with which to pay, why should your bed be taken from under you?<sup>28</sup>Do not move the ancient landmark that your fathers have set.<sup>29</sup>Do you see a man skillful in his work? He will stand before kings; he will not stand before obscure men.
22.overview:
Chapter 22 opens the collection's most famous verse — "a good name is to be chosen rather than great riches" (v.1) — and then pivots to "the thirty sayings of the wise" (vv.17–24:22), a section with remarkable parallels to the Egyptian wisdom text Instruction of Amenemope. That such wisdom appeared across cultures does not diminish Scripture; it shows that general revelation seeds wisdom broadly, while special revelation perfects and redeems it.

The chapter holds together two great themes: reputation rightly ordered (vv.1–9) and instruction rightly received (vv.17–29). A good name is not a brand to manage but a life poured out in integrity before God. The rich and poor alike bear the LORD's image (v.2) — a leveling that should dismantle both pride and contempt.

Timothy Keller notes that "fear of the LORD" (v.4) is the engine beneath all genuine wisdom. Humility before God produces the kind of person whose name becomes, almost accidentally, a good one. The one who grasps for reputation loses it; the one who fears God gains it freely.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 22 — A Good Name, Train Up a Child, and the Thirty Sayings of the Wise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 22 is transitional: vv.1-16 continue the Solomonic antithetical proverbs, then v.17 introduces 'The Words of the Wise' (22:17-24:22), which bears resemblance to the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope. This section is more extended and instructional in form, addressed directly to the son. The thirty sayings (v.20) are a distinct literary unit within this section.
verseByVerse.theology: The opening verse—a good name chosen over riches—is one of Proverbs' most foundational value statements. Reputation built on integrity is more valuable than wealth. The training of children (v.6) is a call to individualized formation: 'the way he should go' may carry the sense of 'the way suited to him.' The promise is covenantal: faithful formation has reliable results over the long arc of a life.
verseByVerse.examples: The thirty sayings begin with the most urgent social ethics (v.22: do not rob the poor; v.24: avoid the angry man) before moving toward financial wisdom and the skill of the craftsman (v.29). The pedagogy is practical and urgent: these are not theoretical principles but survival wisdom for a young man entering public life.

verseByVerse.quote: A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches, and favor is better than silver or gold. The rich and the poor meet together; the LORD is the Maker of them all. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches, and favour is better than silver or gold.

The verb is chosen, which means the two are being offered as alternatives. Proverbs is not saying a man may have both; it is putting them on a table and telling him to pick, because in practice there are moments when he must.

And the reason a name is worth more is in its economics. Money can be replaced — men have lost everything at fifty and rebuilt it. A name cannot. It is assembled over decades out of small consistencies and can be spent in a single afternoon, and the man who spends it discovers that there is no market in which to buy another.

Then v. 2, which is one of the great levelling sentences of the Old Testament: the rich and the poor meet together; the LORD is the Maker of them all.

They meet. In a village they could not avoid each other — the same well, the same gate, the same road — and Proverbs says the meeting itself is instructive, because the one thing that is true of both of them is the thing neither arranged.

And it is the deepest ground there is for how a Christian treats people. Not that the poor man is virtuous, and not that the rich man is guilty. Both were made, by the same hand, and neither had any say in which of the two he turned out to be — which is why contempt in either direction is finally a remark about the Maker.

verseByVerse.quote: The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it. The reward for humility and fear of the LORD is riches and honor and life. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it.

Two men and one hazard, and the difference is entirely in the first verb: one of them sees. Everything else follows from that, and it is why this book spends so much time on perception rather than on courage.

And note that the prudent man’s response is not to confront the danger or to prepare for it. He hides. There is no heroism anywhere in the verse — Proverbs regards getting out of the way as an entirely respectable outcome, which is a useful corrective in a Christian culture that often mistakes exposure for faith.

The simple, meanwhile, does the most natural thing in the world. He goes on. He does not decide to walk into it; he simply continues, because continuing requires no decision, and the verse says he pays for it.

Then v. 4: the reward for humility and fear of the LORD is riches and honour and life. Read with the whole book this is the ordinary shape of things rather than a contract — and note which qualities are named. Not competence. Humility, and the fear of God, which are the two things a man cannot fake for long and cannot acquire by wanting the reward.

verseByVerse.quote: Thorns and snares are in the way of the crooked; whoever guards his soul will keep far from them. Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thorns and snares are in the way of the crooked; whoever guards his soul will keep far from them. The crooked road is not merely wrong, it is unpleasant — snagged and trapped, the hedge of thorns of 15:19. And the counsel is distance again: not vigilance on that road, but staying off it.

Then v. 6, and this verse has done more damage to more godly parents than any other sentence in Proverbs: train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it.

Take the promise first and take it seriously, because it is real. The years of a childhood are formative in a way nothing later is; what a child absorbs before he can evaluate it goes in deeper than anything argued into him at thirty. Proverbs is telling parents that the work repays doing and that it lasts, and that is true and ought to be believed.

And take the word train. The Hebrew root has to do with dedicating something — the same root as the word for the dedication of a house or the temple. It is not primarily instruction. It is the setting apart of a child for a purpose, which is a much larger and more patient activity than teaching him things.

Now the pastoral matter, and it must be said plainly, because a great many people reading this verse are reading it with a grown child in mind who has walked away.

This is a proverb. It is not a promise with God’s name attached and it never was. Everything in this book speaks of how life generally runs, and every reader has already accepted that elsewhere — that the diligent generally prosper, that the righteous are generally delivered — while knowing Job exists. It is only at this verse that people suddenly demand it be a guarantee, and then conclude, when it fails, that the fault must have been theirs.

Consider what that conclusion actually requires. It requires that no child raised well ever rebels, which the Bible itself contradicts on nearly every page. God is the perfect Father. His instruction was flawless, his household was Eden, and his children walked out of it — I have reared and brought up children, and they have rebelled against me (Isaiah 1:2). Whatever Proverbs 22:6 means, it cannot mean that a departed child proves a failed parent, or the charge lands first on God.

Some readers take the Hebrew to say according to his way — according to the child’s own bent, his particular making — and that reading has a long history and a good deal to commend it. Either way the verse stands as it always did: an encouragement to do the work, not a receipt issued in advance.

And to the parent whose child is gone: the training was not wasted, and it is not finished. What was put in early does not evaporate; it waits. There is a long list in Scripture of people who came back much later, and the man who wrote the parable of a son who went into a far country was not describing a father who had failed.

verseByVerse.quote: The rich rules over the poor, and the borrower is the slave of the lender. Whoever sows injustice will reap calamity, and the rod of his fury will fail. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rich rules over the poor, and the borrower is the slave of the lender.

No comment is attached. Proverbs simply states the mechanics of debt in the plainest language available and lets the word slave sit there.

And it is not an exaggeration, as anybody in real debt will confirm. What is lost is not money — the money was spent and enjoyed. What is lost is the ability to decide. A man in debt cannot leave the job, cannot take the risk, cannot say no to the client, cannot move, cannot give what he wants to give. Somebody else’s schedule now governs a large part of his life, and it will do so for a determined number of years.

Note that borrowing is not called sin here. Scripture regulates lending rather than forbidding borrowing, and there are debts a wise man takes on with his eyes open. What the verse insists on is that the transaction has a second half that is never printed on the advertisement: the money arrives now, and a portion of his freedom leaves with the same post.

Then v. 8: whoever sows injustice will reap calamity, and the rod of his fury will fail. The image is a man whose weapon breaks in his hand — which is the whole doctrine of this book about violence, delivered in one clause.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor. Drive out a scoffer, and strife will go out, and quarreling and abuse will cease. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
