Four verbs, and they describe an activity almost nobody performs. He saw — anybody would have. Then he considered, and looked, and received instruction. He stopped at a broken wall and let it teach him something.

Which is where a great deal of wisdom actually comes from, and it is available to everybody. Not from books, and not from having a remarkable life. From noticing what is in front of you — the marriage that failed, the man who was ruined, the department that fell apart — and being willing to stand at the wall long enough to be instructed by it, instead of walking on.

verseByVerse.quote: A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest, and poverty will come upon you like a robber, and want like an armed man. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest, and poverty will come upon you like a robber, and want like an armed man.

The chapter ends by quoting 6:10-11 word for word — and the quotation is the punchline of the story.

The man at the wall has been looking at a ruined vineyard, and the instruction he received from it turns out to be a sentence he already knew. He did not learn a new principle. He learned that an old one was true, and he learned it by standing in front of what it looks like.

Which is the difference between knowing something and having received instruction, and it is why this chapter troubles itself to tell the story at all. Everybody reading has heard that laziness leads to poverty. Nobody is changed by hearing it again. What changes a man is one afternoon looking over a wall at a field that used to be somebody’s living, and doing the arithmetic backwards from the nettles to the mornings.

And the repeated a little is the whole mechanism, printed twice in this book because once was not enough. Nothing in the ruin of that vineyard ever looked like a decision. There was no morning on which the man decided to lose it. There were only mornings, each of which he could reasonably have spent otherwise, and the arithmetic did the rest.

24.theology:
Resurrection Anthropology. Verse 16 embeds a proto-resurrection hope in Proverbs' account of the righteous life. The righteous are not those who are immune to falling but those who are constitutionally oriented toward rising — because the God they fear is the God who raises the dead. Paul develops this in 2 Cor. 4:9: "struck down, but not destroyed." The wicked have no such resource; their stumble in calamity is final because they have no one to raise them.

The Ethics of Rescue. Verses 11–12 establish that wisdom is not passive. Knowing and not acting is its own form of guilt. This anticipates the prophetic tradition (Isa. 1:17; Micah 6:8) and the New Testament (James 1:27). The God who weighs hearts is not fooled by performative ignorance. The church that knows about injustice and does nothing has not yet grasped the wisdom of God.
24.examples:
Then: The "rescue" command (vv.11–12) likely referred to specific situations: wrongful capital punishment at the gate, debt slavery, or unjust judicial proceedings. Witnesses could intervene, elders could speak. "Pleading ignorance" was already a known excuse. The honey metaphor (v.13) connected wisdom to the agricultural bounty of Canaan — wisdom is as Israelite as the honey of the promised land.

Now: Verse 16 is a lifeline for any Christian in a season of repeated failure — addiction recovery, pastoral burnout, protracted grief, marital crisis. The righteous person is not the one who falls least but the one who keeps getting up. Verses 11–12 speak to every generation that faces systemic injustice: the question is always whether those who know will act. And verse 17 confronts social-media culture's delight in public shaming and the downfall of enemies — wisdom calls for a different emotional posture toward those who fail, even those who harmed us.

25.title: A Word Fitly Spoken
25.text: <sup>1</sup>These also are proverbs of Solomon which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied.<sup>2</sup>It is the glory of God to conceal things, but the glory of kings is to search things out.<sup>3</sup>As the heavens for height, and the earth for depth, so the heart of kings is unsearchable.<sup>4</sup>Take away the dross from the silver, and the smith has material for a vessel;<sup>5</sup>take away the wicked from the presence of the king, and his throne will be established in righteousness.<sup>6</sup>Do not put yourself forward in the king's presence or stand in the place of the great,<sup>7</sup>for it is better to be told, "Come up here," than to be put lower in the presence of a noble. What your eyes have seen<sup>8</sup>do not hastily bring into court, for what will you do in the end, when your neighbor puts you to shame?<sup>9</sup>Argue your case with your neighbor himself, and do not reveal another's secret,<sup>10</sup>lest he who hears you bring shame upon you, and your ill repute have no end.<sup>11</sup>A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in a setting of silver.<sup>12</sup>Like a gold ring or an ornament of gold is a wise reprover to a listening ear.<sup>13</sup>Like the cold of snow in the time of harvest is a faithful messenger to those who send him; he refreshes the soul of his masters.<sup>14</sup>Like clouds and wind without rain is a man who boasts of a gift he does not give.<sup>15</sup>With patience a ruler may be persuaded, and a soft tongue will break a bone.<sup>16</sup>If you have found honey, eat only enough for you, lest you have your fill of it and vomit it.<sup>17</sup>Let your foot be seldom in your neighbor's house, lest he have his fill of you and hate you.<sup>18</sup>A man who bears false witness against his neighbor is like a war club, or a sword, or a sharp arrow.<sup>19</sup>Trusting in a treacherous man in time of trouble is like a bad tooth or a foot that slips.<sup>20</sup>Whoever sings songs to a heavy heart is like one who takes off a garment on a cold day, and like vinegar on soda.<sup>21</sup>If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat, and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink,<sup>22</sup>for you will heap burning coals on his head, and the LORD will reward you.<sup>23</sup>The north wind brings forth rain, and a backbiting tongue, angry looks.<sup>24</sup>It is better to live in a corner of the housetop than in a house shared with a quarrelsome wife.<sup>25</sup>Like cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country.<sup>26</sup>Like a muddied spring or a polluted fountain is a righteous man who gives way before the wicked.<sup>27</sup>It is not good to eat much honey, nor is it glorious to seek one's own glory.<sup>28</sup>A man without self-control is like a city broken into and left without walls.
25.overview:
Chapter 25 opens the Hezekiah collection (chapters 25–29), proverbs copied and arranged by the scribes of King Hezekiah around 700 B.C. The chapter is particularly rich in extended similes — a literary hallmark. Where many proverbs state a truth flatly, chapter 25 paints it: apples of gold, cold snow in harvest, a soft tongue breaking bone.

The organizing theme is speech — what it is, what it can do, and how precious it is when used well. A word fitly spoken (v.11) is not merely pleasant; it is a work of art that reflects the beauty of wisdom itself. Speech is also powerful: a soft tongue breaks bone (v.15), meaning patient persuasion accomplishes what force cannot.

The ethical climax is verses 21–22: give bread to your enemy. Paul quotes this in Romans 12:20, embedding it in his great vision of non-retaliation and love. What Proverbs presents as wisdom, Paul presents as the shape of cruciform love — the pattern of a community that does not overcome evil with evil but with good.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 25 — Glory, Restraint, Enemies, and the Right Word at the Right Time
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 25 opens a new collection: 'These also are proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied.' This section (25-29) has a slightly different character: more extended metaphors, more poetic development of a single theme, more explicit use of comparison. Chapter 25 includes royal sayings, social wisdom (don't overstay your welcome, don't brag), and the famous 'coals of fire' proverb about treating enemies with kindness.
verseByVerse.theology: The glory of God is to conceal things; the glory of kings is to search things out (v.2)—one of the most provocative epistemological statements in Proverbs. Mystery is not a failure of knowledge but a divine choice. The king who investigates is imitating the divine character in his search for truth. Investigation is royal; humility before mystery is divine.
verseByVerse.examples: The word fitly spoken (v.11) and the coals of fire on an enemy's head (vv.21-22) are among the most quoted verses in Proverbs. Both concern the social power of the right action at the right moment. Paul quotes the coals-of-fire proverb in Romans 12:20 as the summary of Christian social ethics.

verseByVerse.quote: These also are proverbs of Solomon which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied. It is the glory of God to conceal things, but the glory of kings is to search things out. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
These also are proverbs of Solomon which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied.

A small historical note with a great deal in it. Solomon reigned in the tenth century; Hezekiah some two hundred and fifty years later — and in his reign a group of men sat down and copied out proverbs that had been in circulation since before their grandfathers were born.

Pause over that, because it is a glimpse of how the Bible reached anybody. Hezekiah was a reforming king in a bad century, and among the things his reformation produced was a scriptorium: men doing slow, unglamorous, entirely unmemorable work, copying old sayings so that they would still exist. Nobody knows their names. Everybody who has ever read Proverbs 25 to 29 has read what they preserved.

Then v. 2, and it is one of the most interesting sentences in the Old Testament: it is the glory of God to conceal things, but the glory of kings is to search things out.

Two glories, and they are not in conflict. God’s greatness shows in what he does not explain; a king’s shows in his patient digging into what has been hidden. Which means investigation is a kingly activity rather than an impious one — and every scientist, historian, doctor and judge who has ever gone looking for something buried has been doing what this verse commends.

And the first half is the comfort. That God conceals is not a failure of communication or a reluctance to be known. It is described as his glory — so a man who finds that a great deal about God’s dealings is not explained to him has not encountered a problem. He has encountered God.

verseByVerse.quote: As the heavens for height, and the earth for depth, so the heart of kings is unsearchable. Take away the dross from the silver, and the smith has material for a vessel; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the heavens for height, and the earth for depth, so the heart of kings is unsearchable.

The two measurements are the largest available, and they are unmeasurable on purpose. Nobody has the height of the sky or the depth of the ground, and the point of naming them is that neither figure is obtainable.

And the application is to anybody who deals with people who hold power. What is actually going on in the mind of the man deciding cannot be worked out from outside, and a great deal of energy is spent by subordinates in every organisation attempting exactly that — reading the tone of an email, interpreting a silence, constructing the reasoning behind a decision. Proverbs says the depth is not readable, and the honest consequence is to stop trying and do the work.

Then vv. 4 and 5 are a single image in two halves: take away the dross from the silver, and the smith has material for a vessel; take away the wicked from the presence of the king, and his throne will be established.

The silver is not improved by the refining. It was always there — what changes is that the dross has gone, and only then can anything be made of it. Which is a precise picture of what removing one person from a room does. Nothing new is added to the organisation. What was already there becomes workable.

verseByVerse.quote: take away the wicked from the presence of the king, and his throne will be established in righteousness. Do not put yourself forward in the king's presence or stand in the place of the great, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take away the wicked from the presence of the king, and his throne will be established in righteousness. The second half of the refining image, and the phrase from the presence of matters. Not from the kingdom — from the room. It is the men closest to power who determine what a reign becomes, and every leader is finally the average of the five people who have his ear.

Then v. 6, and the chapter turns to a scene: do not put yourself forward in the king’s presence or stand in the place of the great.

The setting is a banquet with assigned seating and everybody watching, and the counsel is entirely about where a man puts himself when he arrives — which is a decision people make in every gathering, at speed, and mostly without admitting they are making it.

And what is being described is not modesty as a feeling. It is a piece of practical wisdom about where to sit, and the reason is given in the next verse: there are two ways this can go and only one of them is survivable.

verseByVerse.quote: for it is better to be told, "Come up here," than to be put lower in the presence of a noble. What your eyes have seen do not hastily bring into court, for what will you do in the end, when your neighbor puts you to shame? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it is better to be told, Come up here, than to be put lower in the presence of a noble.

This is the proverb the Lord Jesus took and turned into a parable, almost word for word, at a dinner where he had been watching the guests choose the best places (Luke 14:7-11) — and he added the sentence that makes it more than etiquette: everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.

What both the proverb and the parable notice is the asymmetry. Being moved up is a pleasure; being moved down is a humiliation performed in front of everybody who watched you sit. And they are not equally likely to be survived, which is why the lower seat is simply the better bet even for a man with no humility at all.

Then v. 8 begins a run of three verses on quarrels, and the counsel is legal: what your eyes have seen do not hastily bring into court, for what will you do in the end, when your neighbour puts you to shame?

Note what your eyes have seen. He is not making it up. He saw it, and he is right about what he saw — and Proverbs still says do not hurry it into a formal process, because being right about the incident is not the same as being right about the whole matter, and the neighbour has a second half of the story that has not been heard.

verseByVerse.quote: Argue your case with your neighbor himself, and do not reveal another's secret, lest he who hears you bring shame upon you, and your ill repute have no end. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Argue your case with your neighbour himself, and do not reveal another’s secret.

Two instructions and both are about who is in the room. Take it to him — the person concerned, first, directly, before anybody else has heard of it. And do not, in the course of making your case, spend somebody else’s private business as evidence.

The first is the procedure the Lord Jesus laid down for the church, in the same order and for the same reason: go and tell him his fault, between you and him alone (Matthew 18:15). The reason it comes first is that most disputes die there, and a dispute that dies there has cost nobody a reputation.

The second instruction addresses what actually happens instead, and it is the more penetrating. A man in a dispute reaches for material. He wants to be believed, and there is a thing he knows about the other party, or about somebody else, which would help — and it is true, and it is not his to use.

Then v. 10: lest he who hears you bring shame upon you, and your ill repute have no end. The judgment falls on the man who was right about the facts. He wins the argument and acquires a reputation, and the phrase is no end: people forget the dispute entirely and remember, permanently, that he is somebody who will use what he knows.

verseByVerse.quote: A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in a setting of silver. Like a gold ring or an ornament of gold is a wise reprover to a listening ear. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in a setting of silver.

Nobody is sure exactly what the object was — golden fruit in a silver dish, or carved work, or an ornament — and the uncertainty does not matter, because every reading gives the same two qualities. It is beautiful, and it is set. Somebody arranged the one thing inside the other, and the arrangement is a large part of the effect.

Which is the whole force of fitly spoken. The Hebrew suggests something spoken on its wheels, at its proper turning — the right word, in the right place, at the right moment. And every element is required. The same sentence a month early is intrusive; a month late it is useless; said to the wrong person it is gossip.

And the comparison to a made object says something about how it is achieved. Apples of gold in a setting of silver are not found lying about. Somebody worked on them. The people who say the right thing at the right moment are almost never spontaneous; they have thought about that person during the week.

Then v. 12: like a gold ring or an ornament of gold is a wise reprover to a listening ear. Note that the jewellery requires both. A wise reprover speaking into an unwilling ear is not an ornament; he is an irritation, and 9:8 has already said so. It takes the two of them to make the thing valuable — which means the man being corrected is contributing half the gold.

verseByVerse.quote: Like the cold of snow in the time of harvest is a faithful messenger to those who send him; he refreshes the soul of his masters. Like clouds and wind without rain is a man who boasts of a gift he does not give. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like the cold of snow in the time of harvest is a faithful messenger to those who send him.

Harvest in Israel was the hottest work of the year, and there was no snow anywhere near it — so the image is of something impossible and exquisite: cold, in August, in a field. Probably snow brought down from the heights of Hermon and packed for a great man’s table, which was the ancient world’s ultimate luxury.

And that is what a reliable person is like to whoever depends on him. Not merely useful — a relief, and slightly astonishing, because most people are not.

Which is an encouragement to anybody whose contribution is faithfulness rather than brilliance. The man who does what he said he would do, on the day he said, without needing to be chased, is described here as a luxury item. There are not many of him, and the people who have one know it.

Then v. 14 gives the opposite, and it is a picture anybody in a dry country would feel: like clouds and wind without rain is a man who boasts of a gift he does not give.

Everything that precedes rain is present. The sky darkens, the wind gets up, the smell changes, and every farmer in the valley looks up — and then nothing. That is the man who announces what he is going to do. The cruelty of it is not the failure to give; it is that hope was raised, and somebody made arrangements on the strength of it.

verseByVerse.quote: With patience a ruler may be persuaded, and a soft tongue will break a bone. If you have found honey, eat only enough for you, lest you have your fill of it and vomit it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
With patience a ruler may be persuaded, and a soft tongue will break a bone.

The second half is deliberately absurd, and the absurdity is the argument. A soft tongue — the least forceful instrument imaginable — is credited with breaking the hardest thing in the body.

And it is accurate. Hardness in a person is not usually overcome by pressure; pressure gives it something to brace against, and every man who has tried to argue a stubborn relative into a position knows what the attempt produces. What actually works is gentleness applied over time, and it works precisely because there is nothing to resist.

The word in the first half is patience — literally length of anger, a long fuse. So the two halves are one counsel: slowness, and softness, and neither of them looks like strength at any given moment. They simply keep being applied after the forceful approach has exhausted itself.

Then v. 16: if you have found honey, eat only enough for you, lest you have your fill of it and vomit it. The honey of 24:13, and now the other side. The thing is good — Proverbs said so — and it is possible to ruin a good thing purely by quantity, with no wrongdoing anywhere in the transaction except the not stopping.

verseByVerse.quote: Let your foot be seldom in your neighbor's house, lest he have his fill of you and hate you. A man who bears false witness against his neighbor is like a war club, or a sword, or a sharp arrow. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let your foot be seldom in your neighbour’s house, lest he have his fill of you and hate you.

Placed immediately after the honey, and the joke is deliberate: you are the honey. The same warning applies. A person can be genuinely welcome and become, purely by frequency, the thing somebody has had enough of.

And the verb is brutal — not tire of but hate. Which is an honest observation about how affection actually fails. Very few friendships end in a quarrel. A great many are worn through, by somebody who is always there, who does not notice the difference between an open door and an unlimited one.

Nobody wants to be told this and everybody has been on both sides of it. The person doing it is never aware; the welcome felt genuine, because it was.

Then v. 18: a man who bears false witness against his neighbour is like a war club, or a sword, or a sharp arrow. Three weapons at three ranges — the club in the hand, the sword at arm’s length, and the arrow, which reaches a man who never saw the archer. False testimony is being classed with armed assault, and the last of the three is the one it most resembles.

verseByVerse.quote: Trusting in a treacherous man in time of trouble is like a bad tooth or a foot that slips. Whoever sings songs to a heavy heart is like one who takes off a garment on a cold day, and like vinegar on soda. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Trusting in a treacherous man in time of trouble is like a bad tooth or a foot that slips.

Two small, precise, physical miseries, and both are chosen for the same feature: they fail under load. A bad tooth is fine until you bite. A foot that slips is a perfectly good foot until weight goes on it.

Which is exactly the character of an unreliable person, and it explains why he is so hard to identify in advance. He is entirely satisfactory in ordinary conditions. The failure only occurs where it matters, at the moment it matters, and by then a man has already put his weight on it.

Then v. 20, and it is the most pastorally useful verse in the chapter: whoever sings songs to a heavy heart is like one who takes off a garment on a cold day, and like vinegar on soda.

Two images and both are about a mismatch. Removing a coat in the cold is not merely unhelpful, it is the reverse of what the moment requires; and vinegar poured on soda fizzes violently, which is exactly what cheerfulness does when it hits grief.

And the singer means well. That is the whole difficulty. He is not mocking; he is trying to lift the atmosphere, and he has misread what is in front of him — and Scripture says elsewhere what to do instead, which is to weep with those who weep (Romans 12:15). Job’s friends were at their best in the seven days when they sat on the ground and said nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat, and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink, for you will heap burning coals on his head, and the LORD will reward you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat, and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink, for you will heap burning coals on his head, and the LORD will reward you.

Paul quotes this verse in full at the climax of his teaching on how Christians treat their enemies (Romans 12:20), which makes it one of the most load-bearing sentences in the Old Testament.

Begin with what it commands, because that is not in dispute. Not tolerance of an enemy, and not the avoidance of revenge — active provision. Bread and water, put into the hands of the man who wishes you harm, at your own expense.

Then the burning coals, which have been argued over for centuries. The likeliest reading is the shame that comes of being treated well by somebody you have wronged — a burning on the face rather than an injury, and the most effective thing that has ever been done to a hostile man. Some point to an Egyptian rite in which a penitent carried a dish of coals on his head as a sign of repentance, which would make the phrase a picture of an enemy brought to contrition rather than punished.

What the phrase cannot mean is a technique for hurting somebody by being nice to him, and Paul settles it by where he puts the quotation: it comes immediately before do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good. The aim is to overcome the enemy, which means to stop him being one.

And the reason a Christian can do this at all is that it was done for him first. While we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (Romans 5:10). Bread and water to a hostile man is a small imitation of a table set for people who were, at the time, in arms against the host.

verseByVerse.quote: The north wind brings forth rain, and a backbiting tongue, angry looks. It is better to live in a corner of the housetop than in a house shared with a quarrelsome wife. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The north wind brings forth rain, and a backbiting tongue, angry looks.

A weather observation used as a law of cause and effect. Something invisible arrives, and a predictable visible result follows — and the second half of the verse is about faces.

Which is the detail worth having. The result of backbiting is not stated as strife or as broken relationships, though it produces both. It is angry looks — the atmosphere in a room, the expressions people are wearing, before anybody has said anything.

Anybody who has walked into a church or an office and felt the temperature has met this verse. Nothing has been said in front of you and something has plainly happened, and the wind that brought it has already gone.

Then v. 24 repeats 21:9 word for word — the corner of the housetop again — and the repetition inside one book is Proverbs underlining. What was said there stands here: this is a measurement of how much misery a permanent low-grade conflict causes, the same fault is charged to men elsewhere in this book, and it is not counsel to leave.

verseByVerse.quote: Like cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country. Like a muddied spring or a polluted fountain is a righteous man who gives way before the wicked. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country.

The picture requires an ancient world to be felt. A man had a son or a brother somewhere beyond reach — trading, soldiering, settled at a distance — and there was no way whatever to find out whether he was alive. Months of not knowing, and then a traveller arrives with word.

Cold water to a man who is thirsty is not a pleasure; it is a relief that goes all the way down. And that is what news of the safety of somebody loved does to a person, which anybody who has waited for a phone call from a hospital knows exactly.

Which is also why the New Testament chose the word gospel, meaning good news, and why the Bible’s standing description of an evangelist is a man arriving with a report from far off (Isaiah 52:7). The message was not advice. It was word that somebody had won.

Then v. 26, and the image is spoilage: like a muddied spring or a polluted fountain is a righteous man who gives way before the wicked.

A spring is where a community gets its water, and a fouled one is worse than no spring at all, because people go on drinking from it. So the verse is not primarily about the righteous man’s own loss. It is about what happens to everybody downstream when a man known for standing firm quietly stops — and the ones who notice most are the people who had been navigating by him.

verseByVerse.quote: It is not good to eat much honey, nor is it glorious to seek one's own glory. A man without self-control is like a city broken into and left without walls. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is not good to eat much honey, nor is it glorious to seek one’s own glory.

The honey of v. 16 returns as the comparison, and the pairing is exact. Both are good things ruined by appetite. Honour is genuinely good — this book has promised it repeatedly — and the moment a man goes after it for himself the thing turns.

And the sentence is built so that its own logic performs the argument: it is not glorious to seek glory. The pursuit is self-defeating by definition. Whatever a man obtains by chasing it is not the thing he was chasing, because the honour Proverbs describes is always something conferred by other people, and it cannot be taken.

Then the chapter closes on one of the great images of the Old Testament: a man without self-control is like a city broken into and left without walls.

An ancient city was its wall. Everything else — the houses, the market, the temple, the families — existed because there was a line around it that decided what came in. Take the wall down and nothing inside has changed and everything is finished, because the city is now simply whatever happens to arrive.

That is a man without self-control, and the image is more sympathetic than it first appears. He is not described as wicked. He is described as broken into — something happened to him, and now every appetite, every impulse, every provocation walks straight in and there is nothing at the boundary to stop it. He is not choosing these things. He has no wall.

Which is why self-control is the last item in the fruit of the Spirit rather than a preliminary requirement (Galatians 5:23), and why it is fruit at all. Walls are built slowly, one course at a time, mostly on days when nothing is attacking — and no man ever built one by resolving to have one.

25.theology:
The Theology of Speech. Proverbs 25 presents speech as one of the central moral acts of human existence. The fitly spoken word (v.11), the faithful messenger (v.13), the soft tongue (v.15), the inappropriate song (v.20) — each is a form of power, either rightly or wrongly exercised. The New Testament elevates this: the Word became flesh (John 1:14), and the Spirit is given to fill our speech with wisdom. Speech is not merely communication; it is the primary medium of love and harm.

Cruciform Ethics. Verses 21–22 anticipate the Sermon on the Mount and Romans 12. Proverbs is not merely a book of prudential advice; it contains an ethics of enemy-love rooted in God's own character. The LORD rewards the one who feeds the enemy (v.22b), confirming that this is not merely clever strategy but a reflection of divine generosity — a God who causes his sun to rise on evil and good alike (Matt. 5:45).
25.examples:
Then: The Hezekiah scribal collection reflects a royal court that valued the art of persuasion and the discipline of speech. Ambassadors, advisors, and court officials lived or died by their words. The apples-of-gold image (v.11) suggests the aesthetic dimensions of wisdom that Israelite court culture cultivated. Verse 25's "good news from a far country" may have evoked the joy of a merchant's return or a military dispatch — news that changed everything.

Now: The pastoral word of verse 20 indicts the relentless positivity that refuses to make room for grief. Grief communities, cancer wards, and counseling rooms require the wisdom to be quiet when songs are wrong and to speak when silence has run its course. Verses 21–22 have a direct application in the age of social media retaliation and culture-war contempt: feeding the enemy is not weakness but the most subversive act available to the Christian. It reclaims the narrative from the logic of revenge.

26.title: Like a Dog Returns to Its Vomit

26.overview:
Chapter 26 is Proverbs' extended anatomy of foolishness, containing the book's most sustained portrait of three types: the fool (vv.1–12), the sluggard (vv.13–16), and the quarrelsome gossip (vv.17–28). It is the longest concentrated treatment of folly in the Bible, and it is written with a sharp, almost satirical wit.

The famous contradiction of verses 4–5 — "Answer not a fool... Answer a fool" — is deliberate. It is not an error but wisdom's acknowledgment that no single rule fits every case. Sometimes engaging a fool drags you down to his level; sometimes silence leaves him unchallenged in his self-delusion. The wise person reads the situation and responds accordingly. This is wisdom's practical epistemology: principles must be applied with judgment, not mechanical rule-following.

The chapter closes with the liar and flatterer (vv.23–28) — people whose words are weapons disguised as gifts. The hidden hatred will eventually be exposed (v.26). Proverbs consistently returns to this: truth is the ultimate victor because God, who is truth, governs history.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 26 — The Fool's Portrait Gallery and the Whisperer's Destruction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 26 is the most sustained satire in Proverbs: the first twelve verses are an extended portrait of the fool, using some of the most vivid comparisons in the book (snow in summer, a fluttering sparrow, a dog returning to its vomit). Then comes the sluggard (vv.13-16) and finally the quarrelsome, slanderous, deceptive person (vv.17-28). The chapter is a literary tour de force of negative wisdom—wisdom taught by negative example.
verseByVerse.theology: The apparent contradiction of vv.4-5 ('Do not answer a fool... Answer a fool...') is intentional: wisdom is not a formula but a judgment. Sometimes engaging a fool dignifies him; sometimes leaving him unanswered lets him appear wise. The wise person must read the situation and choose which danger is greater. No rule replaces discernment.
verseByVerse.examples: The dog returning to its vomit (v.11) is one of Scripture's most shocking images—Peter quotes it in 2 Peter 2:22 about those who return to false teaching after escaping it. The fool who repeats his folly is not just foolish but compulsively, self-destructively foolish. The image is meant to produce revulsion: do you really want to be that?

verseByVerse.quote: Like snow in summer or rain in harvest, so honor is not fitting for a fool. Like a sparrow in its flitting, like a swallow in its flying, a curse that is causeless does not alight. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like snow in summer or rain in harvest, so honour is not fitting for a fool.

Both images are weather in the wrong month, and in Israel the second was not merely odd but ruinous — rain at harvest flattens the standing grain and rots what has been cut. So the comparison is not that honour given to a fool is incongruous. It is that it does damage.

And it does, in every direction. It damages the fool, who now has standing he cannot carry and will use badly. It damages whoever gave it, whose judgment is now on display. And it damages everybody who was watching, because the currency has been devalued and honour will mean slightly less in that community from now on.

Then v. 2, and it is a verse that has quietly comforted a great many frightened people: like a sparrow in its flitting, like a swallow in its flying, a curse that is causeless does not alight.

The picture is a bird that will not settle. It comes toward the house, and it does not land, and it goes.

Which is aimed at a real and ancient fear, and one that has not gone away. People are afraid of words spoken against them — the parent’s prediction, the enemy’s wish, the thing said over somebody in anger years ago. Proverbs says a curse without cause has no power to come to rest. It is not that the words are harmless in the mouth of the speaker; it is that they have nowhere to land, because God, not the speaker, governs what happens to a man.

verseByVerse.quote: A whip for the horse, a bridle for the donkey, and a rod for the back of fools. Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest you be like him yourself. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
A whip for the horse, a bridle for the donkey, and a rod for the back of fools. Three creatures and three instruments, and the sting is in the classification. The fool is not being compared to an animal in general terms; he is listed alongside them, third in a series of things that respond to nothing but physical direction.

Then v. 4, and the two verses that follow are the most famous apparent contradiction in the Bible. Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest you be like him yourself.

The reason given is entirely about the answerer. Engage with foolishness on its own terms and you will adopt them. Anybody who has been drawn into an argument with somebody unreasonable has felt this happen: within ten minutes he is shouting, or being sarcastic, or making a point he does not believe in order to win, and afterwards he is not sure which of the two was the fool.

That is the danger of the second half of that sentence — not that you will lose, but that you will become like him. Folly is contagious at close range and it is caught by imitation, and the safest thing is to decline the exchange.

verseByVerse.quote: Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own eyes. Whoever sends a message by the hand of a fool cuts off his own feet and drinks violence. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own eyes.

And there it is: the exact opposite instruction, in the next verse, in the same words. Nobody should pretend this is not deliberate. The editor who set these two lines side by side knew what he was doing; they were placed together, and a book that had wanted to hide the tension would have put forty verses between them.

So the first thing to say is that this is not an embarrassment. It is a teaching method, and it is the clearest statement in Scripture that a proverb is not a law. A law applies always; a proverb is a tool, and using it requires judgment about which situation you are in. If v. 4 stood alone, somebody would make a rule of it. Set beside v. 5 it cannot be made into a rule by anybody, which is exactly the intention.

Then the two cases, because both are real and every reader will meet them.

Verse 4 governs the argument that cannot be won and can only degrade you — the online exchange, the relative who wants a row rather than an answer, the man whose position shifts every time it is addressed. There, engaging is the mistake, and silence is not cowardice.

Verse 5 governs the case where saying nothing will confirm him. Where a foolish claim is left standing in front of people who might believe it; where a bully in a meeting has learned that nobody ever replies; where the silence itself will be read as agreement. There, somebody has to answer — and according to his folly means on its own terms, taking the argument at the level it was made and showing where it goes.

Which is precisely what the Lord Jesus did, repeatedly, and both verses can be watched in one ministry. He answered Pilate’s question and was silent before Herod (Luke 23:9). He refused to say by what authority he acted, and he answered the question about tribute money by asking whose face was on the coin. The judgment about which verse applies is itself the wisdom, and no rule can be written for it — which is why God gave us two verses instead of one.

verseByVerse.quote: Like a lame man's legs, which hang useless, is a proverb in the mouth of fools. Like one who binds the stone in the sling is one who gives honor to a fool. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like a lame man’s legs, which hang useless, is a proverb in the mouth of fools.

The image is unsparing and it is precisely observed. The legs are there. They are the right shape, attached in the right place, and they do nothing — and the same is true of a genuine piece of wisdom quoted by somebody who has not understood it.

Everybody has heard this. The verse produced at the wrong moment; the true saying used to close a conversation that needed opening; the man who can quote the thing and cannot apply it and does not know the difference. What he is holding is not wrong. It is simply not connected to anything, and it will not carry weight when weight is put on it.

Then v. 8, and the image needs a moment: like one who binds the stone in the sling is one who gives honour to a fool.

A sling worked by releasing one end of the cord at exactly the right instant. Tie the stone in and the entire mechanism is not merely useless — it is dangerous, because the thing is now whirling round a man’s head at speed with no possibility of release.

That is honour given to the wrong person, and the picture is better than the abstraction. He now has momentum. He cannot be got rid of. And he is going round and round in the middle of the organisation, close to everybody’s head, with nobody able to let go of the cord.

verseByVerse.quote: Like a thorn that goes up into the hand of a drunkard is a proverb in the mouth of fools. Like an archer who wounds everyone is one who hires a passing fool or drunkard. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like a thorn that goes up into the hand of a drunkard is a proverb in the mouth of fools.

The second image for the same fault as v. 7, and it is worse. The lame legs were useless; the thorn does damage.

The picture is a drunk man with a bramble in his hand, waving it about. He cannot feel it and he has no control over where it goes, and everybody near him is at risk from something that is only dangerous because of who is holding it. Which is what happens when a hard truth from Scripture gets into the hands of somebody with no judgment: the verse is sharp, it was meant to be, and it is now being swung in a room.

Anybody who has watched a text about submission, or discipline, or God’s sovereignty used on a suffering person by somebody who meant well has seen this precisely.

Then v. 10, whose Hebrew is difficult and whose sense is not: like an archer who wounds everyone is one who hires a passing fool or drunkard. The wounding is indiscriminate, and the man responsible is not the archer. It is whoever put the bow in his hands — which puts the responsibility on the person doing the appointing, in a chapter otherwise entirely about the fool.

verseByVerse.quote: Like a dog that returns to his vomit is a fool who repeats his folly. Do you see a man who is wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like a dog that returns to his vomit is a fool who repeats his folly.

Proverbs is being deliberately disgusting, and Peter quotes it and adds a second proverb of the same kind about a washed pig going back to the mud (2 Peter 2:22). The revulsion is the argument: this is what repeated folly looks like from outside, and nobody inside it sees it that way.

And the accuracy is in the word returns. The dog is not encountering something new; it is going back to what it has already brought up, which is the exact shape of a besetting sin. The man has been here. He knows what it tastes like on the way back. And he goes.

Which raises the question the verse cannot answer, and it is the most important one in the chapter: what is to be done with a person who cannot stop returning? Proverbs has no remedy for a dog. It is describing a nature — and a nature is not corrected by information, which is why twenty-five chapters of excellent advice cannot reach this man.

The New Testament answers it in the only terms that could work, and it is not better resolve. If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17). The dog needs to stop being a dog.

Then v. 12, and it is the most alarming sentence in the chapter: do you see a man who is wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him.

After eleven verses of contempt for the fool, Proverbs finds somebody worse — and the reason is straightforward. The fool can be told. He may not listen, but there is a door. The man who is wise in his own eyes has no door, because the faculty that would open it is the one that has gone wrong, and every correction offered to him is assessed by the thing that needs correcting.

So the entrance requirement for wisdom is the same as the entrance requirement for the gospel, and it is the one nobody can supply for another person. The publican who could not lift his eyes went home justified, and the man who thanked God he was not like other men went home exactly as he came (Luke 18:14).

verseByVerse.quote: The sluggard says, "There is a lion in the road! There is a lion in the streets!" As a door turns on its hinges, so does a sluggard on his bed. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sluggard says, There is a lion in the road! There is a lion in the streets!

The lion of 22:13 again, and now there are two of them, and the sluggard has moved one into the street. Repetition is his method: the excuse improves each time it is told, and by now it is a settled account of the world rather than a reason for a particular morning.

Then v. 14, which is the funniest and most exact image in the book: as a door turns on its hinges, so does a sluggard on his bed.

Watch what the comparison is doing. There is movement — considerable movement, all night, back and forth. Energy is being expended. And the door is exactly where it was, because a hinge is precisely the mechanism that permits motion without travel.

That is the truest picture of a wasted life anybody has drawn. Not stillness. Activity, in volume, going nowhere — the man who is always busy and cannot name one thing that is further on than it was a year ago. And he is tired, honestly tired, which is the part that makes it so hard to see from inside.

verseByVerse.quote: The sluggard buries his hand in the dish; it wears him out to bring it back to his mouth. The sluggard is wiser in his own eyes than seven men who can answer sensibly. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sluggard buries his hand in the dish; it wears him out to bring it back to his mouth.

The joke of 19:24 retold with one addition, and the addition is everything: it wears him out. Now we are told how it feels to him.

He is not lying about the exhaustion. That is what makes the sluggard a tragedy rather than merely a comic figure. The smallest remaining task genuinely does feel insurmountable, and anybody who has been deeply stuck knows the sensation — the letter that needs one signature, the phone call that would take four minutes, sitting on the desk for a fortnight and getting heavier every day.

Then v. 16, and it is the hinge of the whole passage: the sluggard is wiser in his own eyes than seven men who can answer sensibly.

Which explains why none of this can be fixed by telling him. Seven competent people could give him the same counsel and he would still hold the private conviction that he sees the situation more clearly than all of them — because he has an account of his circumstances that nobody else has heard properly, and every piece of advice is measured against it and found not to fit.

And v. 12 has already given the verdict on that condition. The sluggard’s real problem in this chapter is not his bed. It is that he is wise in his own eyes, which is the one condition Proverbs says is worse than folly.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever meddles in a quarrel not his own is like one who takes a passing dog by the ears. Like a madman who throws firebrands, arrows, and death (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever meddles in a quarrel not his own is like one who takes a passing dog by the ears.

Half a line, and the picture is complete. A dog going past, minding its business, and a man who reaches down and grabs it by the ears — at which point he has a problem with no good exit, since holding on is dangerous and letting go is worse.

Which is the position of everybody who has waded into somebody else’s dispute. He is now committed. He cannot withdraw without both parties turning on him, and he cannot stay without being bitten, and the quarrel was never anything to do with him.

And the verse needs one guard, because Scripture elsewhere commands intervention. Proverbs 24:11 requires the rescue of people being taken to death, and Christ blesses peacemakers. The difference is between a man who is sent for, or who sees genuine harm being done, and a man who inserts himself because he has an opinion and enjoys the significance of being consulted. The dog in this verse was walking past. Nobody had asked him for anything.

Then vv. 18 and 19 begin one of the sharpest sayings in the book, and it takes both verses: like a madman who throws firebrands, arrows, and death…

verseByVerse.quote: is the man who deceives his neighbor and says, "I am only joking!" For lack of wood the fire goes out, and where there is no whisperer, quarreling ceases. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
…is the man who deceives his neighbour and says, I am only joking!

The comparison is deliberately excessive and it is exactly fair. A man throwing burning torches and arrows into a crowd, and then — this is the whole point — explaining that he did not mean anything by it.

The sin named here is not the joke. It is the second sentence: the retreat, made after the damage, which asks the injured party to accept that nothing happened. And it works, because the victim now has only two options, both bad. He can accept it, and carry the injury with no acknowledgement. Or he can object, and be told he has no sense of humour — which is a second wound delivered under cover of the first.

Everybody has met this and most people cannot name it. It is the remark with a barb in it followed by a laugh; the cruel accuracy about somebody’s weakness offered as banter; the thing said to a spouse in company that is genuinely funny and genuinely true and should not have been said. And I am only joking is the mechanism that makes it unanswerable.

Proverbs calls the man a madman throwing fire, which is a heavy verdict on somebody who is usually thought of as good company.

Then v. 20 changes the subject to fire of another kind: for lack of wood the fire goes out, and where there is no whisperer, quarrelling ceases. The mechanics of a fire are the mechanics of a feud, and the useful half is the first: a fire does not have to be extinguished. It has to stop being fed, and then it dies of itself.

verseByVerse.quote: As charcoal to hot embers and wood to fire, so is a quarrelsome man for kindling strife. The words of a whisperer are like delicious morsels; they go down into the inner parts of the body. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
As charcoal to hot embers and wood to fire, so is a quarrelsome man for kindling strife.

The image is exactly matched to the previous verse, and note what the quarrelsome man is: not the spark. Charcoal and wood are what a fire is fed with, and there is generally embers of some kind in any community — an old disagreement, a difficult history, a matter that was never quite resolved.

The man in this verse does not start anything. He arrives with fuel, and puts it where the heat already is, and then stands back and observes with interest that things seem to be flaring up again.

Then v. 22 reprints 18:8 word for word: the words of a whisperer are like delicious morsels; they go down into the inner parts of the body.

Proverbs almost never repeats a whole verse, and it has done so here — which is the book underlining. Gossip is a delicacy; nobody listens to it out of duty; and once swallowed it cannot be brought back up, so that a man will never again meet the person he heard about without carrying what he was told into the room.

verseByVerse.quote: Like the glaze covering an earthen vessel are fervent lips with an evil heart. Whoever hates disguises himself with his lips and harbors deceit in his heart; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like the glaze covering an earthen vessel are fervent lips with an evil heart.

Behind it is a cheap clay pot with a bright glaze fired onto it — the ancient equivalent of plating base metal, and it looked, at a distance and in the right light, like something valuable.

And the word for the speech is fervent, which is the striking choice. Not smooth, not plausible — warm. This man is not cold and calculating in his manner; he is enthusiastic, affectionate, unstinting in what he says about you, and it is a finish applied to a common vessel.

Then vv. 24-26 unfold the same man over three verses, and the first is the definition: whoever hates disguises himself with his lips and harbours deceit in his heart.

The verb is disguises — literally makes himself unrecognisable, the word for putting on another face. And the disguise is made of speech, which is the cheapest material available and requires no acting ability whatever, since almost nobody checks a warm sentence against the man saying it.

verseByVerse.quote: when he speaks graciously, believe him not, for there are seven abominations in his heart; though his hatred be covered with deception, his wickedness will be exposed in the assembly. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he speaks graciously, believe him not, for there are seven abominations in his heart.

An unusual command in a book that keeps warning against suspicion. Believe him not — and the instruction is given precisely at the moment the man is being pleasant, because that is when the evidence is least available.

And the counsel is narrower than it looks. Proverbs is not telling anybody to distrust warmth in general; the whole book is full of gracious speech commended. It is dealing with the specific case of vv. 23-24, where a man is already known to harbour hatred — and it says that his graciousness is not evidence against what is known. That is the mistake people make. The warm exchange in the corridor is taken as a sign that things must be all right, and it is simply the glaze.

Then v. 26, and it is the promise the passage has been moving toward: though his hatred be covered with deception, his wickedness will be exposed in the assembly.

Not necessarily soon. But the deception has a term on it, and the exposure is in the assembly — publicly, in the gathered community, in the one place he most needed the disguise to hold.

Hold that, if you are currently being harmed by somebody nobody else can see clearly. The situation in which a person is charming to everyone and cruel to one is among the loneliest in the world, and the loneliness is caused entirely by the glaze. Proverbs does not promise vindication next month. It promises that clay is clay, and that fired-on colour does not last as long as people think.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever digs a pit will fall into it, and a stone will come back on him who starts it rolling. A lying tongue hates its victims, and a flattering mouth works ruin. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever digs a pit will fall into it, and a stone will come back on him who starts it rolling.

Two pieces of physics used as one moral observation, and the second is the better image. A man levers a stone loose on a hillside to send it down onto somebody — and stones on hillsides do not travel in straight lines. It goes where the ground sends it, and the ground is not taking instructions.

That is the whole doctrine of this book about harm intended for others. Not that God intervenes to redirect the stone, though he governs it. It is that a man who sets a large thing in motion has released it, and released is exactly what it is: no longer his, no longer aimed, and coming back along a line he did not choose.

Then v. 28 closes the chapter, and both halves are surprising: a lying tongue hates its victims, and a flattering mouth works ruin.

The first says that lying is a form of hatred, which is not how a liar experiences it. He generally believes he is avoiding trouble, or being kind, or keeping the peace. Proverbs says that what he is actually doing to the person he lies to is contempt — because a lie treats a man as somebody who cannot be trusted with reality, and that is a judgment about him.

And the second half is the sharper, and it is where the chapter finally lands: a flattering mouth works ruin. After twenty-seven verses about fools, liars, whisperers and men with firebrands, the last thing named as ruinous is the person who says nice things.

He is doing more damage than any of them, because flattery is the only weapon in this chapter that the victim wants to be hit with. Nobody defends himself against being told he is right. And the man who has been surrounded by it for ten years has been steadily walled off from every correction that might have saved him — which is where v. 12 came from, and how a man becomes wise in his own eyes without ever deciding to.

Against all of which stands one who never flattered anybody, who told a rich young man the one thing he did not want to hear and watched him walk away, and who was killed for saying the truth in an assembly. The friend who wounds is faithful (27:6). The mouth that only ever soothes is the one this chapter ends by calling ruin.

26.theology:
The Anatomy of Folly. Chapter 26 shows that folly is not a single trait but a complex of related failures: the misallocation of honor (vv.1–3), the inability to learn (v.11), the closed-loop self-confidence (v.12), the laziness that rationalizes itself (vv.13–16), and the tongue used as weapon (vv.17–28). These are not unrelated vices but expressions of the one root: life lived as if God does not exist, with the self as the final reference point. Keller's insight is that the fool is the secularist — not necessarily the atheist, but the one who functionally excludes God from practical decisions.

Self-Deception and Grace. The man wise in his own eyes (v.12) is the hardest case because he is impervious to correction. The gospel's answer is not better argument but encounter with the living God — the experience that brought Isaiah to his knees ("Woe is me!") and Paul to the Damascus road. Conversion is the radical undoing of self-deception, and it is entirely a work of grace.
26.examples:
Then: Court politics made the sluggard (vv.13–16) a recognizable type — the official who invented elaborate reasons for inaction. The whisperer (v.20) operated in every ancient institution, and Proverbs knew that political conflict was usually sustained by informers and gossips, not by genuine grievances alone. The honor-for-fools warning (v.1) addressed a patronage culture where rulers could elevate incompetent favorites with destructive results.

Now: The social media age has made the man wise in his own eyes (v.12) ubiquitous — the confident amateur whose Dunning-Kruger blindness is now amplified to thousands. Verse 20 is a direct diagnosis of online conflict: Twitter feuds, church splits, and family estrangements are almost always sustained by whisperers adding wood. The vv.4–5 tension about answering the fool is the daily dilemma of anyone with a public platform: engaging every foolish take validates it; ignoring every challenge abandons truth. Wisdom, not a rule, is required.

27.title: Do Not Boast About Tomorrow
27.text: <sup>1</sup>Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring. <sup>2</sup>Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips. <sup>5</sup>Better is open rebuke than hidden love. <sup>6</sup>Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of a flatterer. <sup>9</sup>Oil and perfume make the heart glad, and the sweetness of a friend comes from his earnest counsel. <sup>12</sup>The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it. <sup>17</sup>Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another. <sup>19</sup>As in water face reflects face, so the heart of man reflects the man. <sup>20</sup>Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied, and never satisfied are the eyes of man. <sup>21</sup>The crucible is for silver, and the furnace is for gold, and a man is tested by his praise. <sup>23</sup>Know well the condition of your flocks, and give attention to your herds, <sup>27</sup>There will be enough goats' milk for your food, for the food of your household and maintenance for your girls.
27.overview:
Chapter 27 is one of Proverbs' warmest chapters, centering on the gifts of genuine friendship (vv.5–10, 17) while bookending with humility about the future (v.1) and the discipline of faithful work (vv.23–27). The famous verse — "Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another" (v.17) — is embedded in a larger account of what makes friendship transformative rather than merely pleasant.

The chapter distinguishes sharply between the flatterer and the faithful friend. Flattery gives kisses; friendship gives wounds. The wound of a friend is painful but constructive — it is love that refuses to leave you in your blind spots. The flatterer's kisses are pleasant but corrosive, feeding the self-deception that Proverbs constantly diagnoses as the root of folly.

The closing pastoral image (vv.23–27) is often overlooked: the wise man tends his flocks attentively, knowing that wealth is temporary and natural abundance cycles. This is wisdom applied to economics — attention, stewardship, patience. It is a far cry from the "riches sprout wings" speculation of the fool.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 27 — Friendship, Flattery, Faithful Wounds, and the Uncertain Future
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 27 is one of the most relationally rich chapters in Proverbs: the faithful wounds of a friend (v.6), the sweetness of earnest counsel (v.9), iron sharpening iron (v.17), and the heart satisfied by being known (v.19). The chapter also addresses boasting about the future (v.1), the contentious wife (v.15), and closes with a meditation on the diligent shepherd who knows his flocks.
verseByVerse.theology: The friend who wounds faithfully (v.6) versus the enemy who kisses abundantly is one of the most searching relational distinctions in the book. True friendship is willing to cause pain for the sake of the friend's good; false friendship maximizes pleasant feelings at the expense of honest engagement. The church needs more people who can give and receive faithful wounds.
verseByVerse.examples: Iron sharpening iron (v.17) has become one of Proverbs' most quoted metaphors for community: people form each other, the pressure of genuine relationship produces the friction that sharpens. But the metaphor is not only positive—friction implies contact, resistance, sometimes sparks. True community is not comfortable; it is formative.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring. Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; a stranger, and not your own lips. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring'—James 4:13-14 elaborates on this: the merchant who plans his itinerary without acknowledging divine sovereignty is foolish. The future belongs to God, not to the planner. 'Let another praise you, and not your own mouth'—self-praise is suspect because the praiser has an obvious motive for generosity. The praise that carries weight is unsolicited and comes from others. Kidner: self-recommendation is the least convincing form of recommendation; the person who constantly speaks well of himself reveals the anxiety underneath the boasting.

verseByVerse.quote: A stone is heavy, and sand is weighty, but a fool's provocation is heavier than both. Wrath is cruel, anger is overwhelming, but who can stand before jealousy? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A fool's provocation is heavier than both'—the weight comparison: physical burdens are manageable; the sustained irritation of a fool's provocation is the heaviest burden of all. 'Wrath is cruel, anger is overwhelming, but who can stand before jealousy?'—the escalating sequence: wrath and anger are fierce but can burn out; jealousy is relentless. Jealousy is anger combined with possessiveness and does not simply exhaust itself. Waltke: jealousy is the most sustained and consuming of the passions, which is why Proverbs and the prophets describe God's jealousy as an expression of his most intense covenant love.

verseByVerse.quote: Better is open rebuke than hidden love. Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Better is open rebuke than hidden love'—love that will not speak is not functioning as love. The rebuke that costs something to give is more genuinely loving than the affection that costs nothing. 'Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy'—one of Proverbs' most penetrating relational distinctions. The friend's wounds are 'faithful'—trustworthy, reliable as evidence of genuine care. 'Profuse are the kisses of an enemy'—not a few honest words but many empty ones. Keller: this is the friendship of Judas set against the friendship of Nathan to David. One kissed; one wounded. One destroyed; one restored.

verseByVerse.quote: One who is full loathes honey, but to one who is hungry everything bitter is sweet. Like a bird that strays from its nest is a man who strays from his home. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'One who is full loathes honey, but to one who is hungry everything bitter is sweet'—the relativity of desire to condition: the sated person cannot appreciate what is objectively good; the hungry person finds value in what is objectively poor. This is applied in spiritual direction: the spiritually satisfied person does not hunger for God; the spiritually desperate person finds him everywhere. 'Like a bird that strays from its nest is a man who strays from his home'—the bird away from the nest is exposed, unprotected, disordered. The wanderer from home loses the anchor that gives life its shape and safety.

verseByVerse.quote: Oil and perfume make the heart glad, and the sweetness of a friend comes from his earnest counsel. Do not forsake your friend and your father's friend, and do not go to your brother's house in the day of your calamity. Better is a neighbor who is near than a brother who is far away. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The sweetness of a friend comes from his earnest counsel'—not pleasant conversation or social enjoyment alone but the counsel that comes from genuine engagement with your situation. 'Do not forsake your friend and your father's friend'—long-term, inherited friendships are a social asset not to be discarded lightly. 'Better is a neighbor who is near than a brother who is far away'—the practical wisdom of proximity: the person who is actually present can help in ways that the geographically distant family member cannot, however deep the kinship. Kidner: this does not diminish family; it values the friend who shows up.

verseByVerse.quote: Be wise, my son, and make my heart glad, that I may answer him who reproaches me. The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Be wise, my son, and make my heart glad, that I may answer him who reproaches me'—the son's wisdom is the father's defense before critics; the child's life is the most powerful testimony to the parent's formation. 'The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it'—repeated from 22:3; the repetition underscores the strategic importance of foresight. The prudent person is not cowardly but is skilled at reading what is coming before it arrives. Avoidance of foreseeable disaster is wisdom, not weakness.

verseByVerse.quote: Take a man's garment when he has put up security for a stranger, and hold it in pledge when he puts up security for a foreign woman. Whoever blesses his neighbor with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, will be counted as cursing. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Take a man's garment when he has put up security for a stranger'—repeated from 20:16; the financial recklessness of co-signing for unknown parties warrants the security of collateral. 'Whoever blesses his neighbor with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, will be counted as cursing'—one of Proverbs' most socially astute observations: timing and volume matter as much as content. The exuberant early-morning blessing is an intrusion, not a gift. Good intentions expressed in ways that disregard the other person's actual situation are a form of relational incompetence.

verseByVerse.quote: A continual dripping on a rainy day and a quarrelsome wife are alike; to restrain her is to restrain the wind or to grasp oil in one's right hand. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A continual dripping on a rainy day and a quarrelsome wife are alike'—the relentlessness of the comparison: a dripping that never stops is maddening precisely because of its persistence, not its intensity. 'To restrain her is to restrain the wind or to grasp oil in one's right hand'—both are impossible; the attempt to control a quarrelsome person by force or manipulation always fails. Waltke: the proverb is not a misogynistic dismissal but a diagnostic: some patterns of conflict cannot be managed by external means. The solution lies elsewhere—in wisdom, prayer, and the long work of sanctification.

verseByVerse.quote: Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another. Whoever tends a fig tree will eat its fruit, and he who guards his master will be honored. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another'—one of Proverbs' most cited images for community formation: genuine relationship produces the friction that sharpens. The metaphor is physical: metal on metal, pressure and contact. True friendship is not frictionless. 'Whoever tends a fig tree will eat its fruit'—the faithful steward of another's resources benefits from his faithfulness. 'He who guards his master will be honored'—loyal service is rewarded with honor. Both proverbs make the same point: patient, faithful investment in something beyond yourself produces return.

verseByVerse.quote: As in water face reflects face, so the heart of man reflects the man. Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied, and never satisfied are the eyes of man. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'As in water face reflects face, so the heart of man reflects the man'—the heart is the truest mirror of who a person actually is; the face in water is the face that is really there, not the face one wishes were there. Self-knowledge requires looking at the heart. 'Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied, and never satisfied are the eyes of man'—the insatiability of death and of human desire placed side by side: the realm of the dead is always receiving and never full; the human eye is always wanting and never sated. Keller: only God himself can satisfy what the eye perpetually seeks, because only God is infinite.

verseByVerse.quote: The crucible is for silver, and the furnace is for gold, and a man is tested by his praise. Crush a fool in a mortar with a pestle along with crushed grain, yet his folly will not depart from him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A man is tested by his praise'—an unexpected testing ground: not adversity but success, not suffering but honor. How a person handles praise reveals more about him than how he handles difficulty. Pride swells under praise; the humble person is not inflated by it. 'Crush a fool in a mortar with a pestle along with crushed grain, yet his folly will not depart from him'—the most pessimistic statement about the fool in the chapter: even extreme punishment cannot remove folly from one who has chosen it as his identity. Folly has become structural, not behavioral. The remedy is not more correction but transformation (cf. Jer. 31:33).

verseByVerse.quote: Know well the condition of your flocks, and give attention to your herds, for riches do not last forever; and does a crown endure to all generations? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Know well the condition of your flocks, and give attention to your herds'—the chapter closes with the image of the faithful shepherd: attentive, present, personally engaged with the state of his resources. This is wisdom made agricultural. 'Riches do not last forever; and does a crown endure to all generations?'—the instability of inherited and accumulated wealth; even crowns pass. The person who attends carefully to his actual resources and knows their condition has what no financial abstraction can replace: genuine situational knowledge.

verseByVerse.quote: When the grass is gone and the new growth appears and the vegetation of the mountains is gathered, the lambs will provide your clothing, and the goats the price of a field. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'When the grass is gone and the new growth appears'—the faithful shepherd reads the seasons; he knows that after the grass fails, the new growth will come. This is long-term wisdom applied to agricultural cycles: the person who despairs at the end of the grass does not understand that the new growth is coming. 'The lambs will provide your clothing, and the goats the price of a field'—the compound return of faithful stewardship: the flock cared for provides clothing (wool), capital (price of a field), and sustenance (food). Faithful attention to what you have been given produces comprehensive provision.

verseByVerse.quote: There will be enough goats' milk for your food, for the food of your household and maintenance for your girls. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'There will be enough goats' milk for your food, for the food of your household and maintenance for your girls'—the conclusion of the shepherd's portrait: enough. Not excess, not abundance beyond measure, but enough. Proverbs ends this section with sufficiency as the goal of faithful stewardship. The wise person who attends carefully to his flocks and herds will have what he and his household need. Calvin: this is the practical shape of the covenant promise—not extravagant wealth but the reliable provision of a faithful God working through the faithful work of his people.

27.theology:
Friendship as Means of Grace. Chapter 27 treats friendship as one of God's primary instruments for human formation. The friend who wounds faithfully (v.6), the counsel that gladdens (v.9), the iron sharpening iron (v.17) — these are not merely social goods but spiritual mechanisms. The Reformers called preaching, sacraments, and prayer the "means of grace"; Proverbs adds to this the faithful friend whose love is too serious to be merely pleasant. The church at its best is a community of faithful wounders.

Creatureliness and Humility. Verse 1 ("you do not know what a day may bring") and the closing pastoral image (vv.23–27) together present a vision of creaturely wisdom: know your limits, tend what is given, plan humbly. The theological virtue behind this is not pessimism but trust — trust in a God who holds the future and who is worthy to hold it. Christian hope does not eliminate planning; it transforms its spirit from grasping to stewardship.
27.examples:
Then: Proverbs' audience would have known the pastoral life intimately — flocks, herds, seasonal rhythms. The closing section (vv.23–27) is not romantic but practical: attend to what you have, do not speculate beyond your means, sustainable abundance is preferable to volatile wealth. The friendship section spoke to a culture where patronage and flattery were the social currency of court life; genuine friendship of the kind Proverbs describes was rare and precious precisely because it was so counter-cultural.

Now: Verse 17 (iron sharpens iron) is widely quoted in men's ministries and leadership circles — rightly so, though its cutting edge is often dulled into something merely motivational. The real application is uncomfortable: who in your life is allowed to wound you faithfully? Who will tell you what your spouse, your employees, and your therapist might not? The Christian who cannot answer that question is almost certainly growing softer, not sharper. And verse 1 is a direct rebuke of the five-year planning culture that imagines the future as essentially controllable — wisdom builds plans lightly held.

28.title: The Wicked Flee When No One Pursues
28.text: <sup>1</sup>The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are bold as a lion. <sup>5</sup>Evil men do not understand justice, but those who seek the LORD understand it completely. <sup>6</sup>Better is a poor man who walks in his integrity than a rich man who is crooked in his ways. <sup>9</sup>If one turns away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer is an abomination. <sup>11</sup>A rich man is wise in his own eyes, but a poor man who has understanding will find him out. <sup>13</sup>Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy. <sup>14</sup>Blessed is the one who fears the LORD always, but whoever hardens his heart will fall into calamity. <sup>20</sup>A faithful man will abound with blessings, but whoever hastens to be rich will not go unpunished. <sup>25</sup>A greedy man stirs up strife, but the one who trusts in the LORD will be enriched. <sup>27</sup>Whoever gives to the poor will not want, but he who hides his eyes will get many a curse.
28.overview:
Chapter 28 is one of Proverbs' most theologically concentrated chapters, weaving together themes of conscience, confession, justice, and integrity. The opening verse sets the tone: the wicked flee even when unpursued — they are haunted by a conscience that cannot be quieted. The righteous are bold as a lion — not because they are braver by temperament, but because they have nothing to hide before God.

The chapter's pastoral center is verse 13: "Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy." This is Proverbs' most direct statement about confession and forgiveness, and it anticipates the New Testament's fuller development: 1 John 1:9, the prodigal son, the ministry of reconciliation. Concealment breeds shame and shame breeds the restless flight of verse 1; confession brings the boldness that only forgiveness can give.

Keller identifies this chapter as showing that integrity is not merely an ethical preference but a structural feature of a well-ordered soul. The person of integrity is not trying to avoid getting caught; they have nothing to manage, because they live openly before God.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 28 — The Righteous Are Bold, the Wicked Are Exposed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 28 is dominated by the contrast between the righteous and the wicked in the context of power and poverty.
