The wicked ruler who oppresses the poor (v.15-16), the poor person who walks in integrity (v.6), the one who confesses sins versus the one who conceals them (v.13), and the warning against rushing to be rich (v.20-22). The chapter is political, social, and deeply theological.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 13 is one of Proverbs' most pastorally significant: 'Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy.' The connection between honest confession and divine mercy is proto-evangelical; 1 John 1:9 makes the same claim with the blood of Christ as the basis. The person who covers sin is not protecting himself but preventing the mercy he desperately needs.
verseByVerse.examples: The poor who walk in integrity (v.6) are contrasted with the rich who are crooked (v.6) and those who oppress the poor (vv.3,8,15). Proverbs' consistent concern for justice to the poor runs through this chapter: God sides with the poor against the exploiter, and the person who honors God cannot oppress those God honors.

verseByVerse.quote: The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are bold as a lion. When a land transgresses, it has many rulers, but with a man of understanding and knowledge, its stability will long continue. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are bold as a lion'—the contrast of the guilty conscience versus the clear one: the wicked person is perpetually haunted by fear of exposure; the righteous person has nothing to hide and therefore nothing to fear. 'When a land transgresses, it has many rulers'—political instability is a symptom of moral disorder. 'With a man of understanding and knowledge, its stability will long continue'—wisdom in leadership produces civic durability. Waltke: good governance is not primarily a political but a moral achievement.

verseByVerse.quote: A poor man who oppresses the poor is like a driving rain that leaves no food. Those who forsake the law praise the wicked, but those who keep the law strive against them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A poor man who oppresses the poor is like a driving rain that leaves no food'—the most devastating irony: someone who has known poverty and still oppresses the poor. The driving rain that destroys rather than nourishes is the apt image: he who could empathize destroys. 'Those who forsake the law praise the wicked'—moral erosion produces a culture that celebrates what it should condemn. 'Those who keep the law strive against them'—the faithful remnant's contention with wicked culture is not optional; it is the necessary expression of their loyalty to God's standard.

verseByVerse.quote: Evil men do not understand justice, but those who seek the LORD understand it completely. Better is a poor man who walks in his integrity than a rich man who is crooked in his ways. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Evil men do not understand justice'—justice is not merely a legal concept but a moral one; those who have abandoned God have lost the framework within which justice makes sense. 'Those who seek the LORD understand it completely'—the fear of God is the epistemological foundation of justice; you cannot fully understand justice without understanding the God who is just. 'Better is a poor man who walks in his integrity than a rich man who is crooked in his ways'—the foundational better-than of chapters 28-29: integrity outranks wealth, character outranks status. The poor person of integrity is genuinely better off.

verseByVerse.quote: The one who keeps the law is a son with understanding, but a companion of gluttons shames his father. Whoever multiplies his wealth by interest and profit from the poor gathers it for him who is generous to the poor. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The one who keeps the law is a son with understanding, but a companion of gluttons shames his father'—law-keeping and understanding are linked; the lawbreaker is not only disobedient but unintelligent. 'Whoever multiplies his wealth by interest and profit from the poor gathers it for him who is generous to the poor'—a remarkable statement of divine economic redistribution: the wealth extracted from the poor by usurers will ultimately benefit those who are kind to the poor. Providence overturns unjust accumulation and reroutes it toward righteousness. Sproul: God has a long view of economic justice that looks nothing like human financial planning.

verseByVerse.quote: If one turns away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer is an abomination. Whoever misleads the upright into an evil way will fall into his own pit, but the blameless will have a goodly inheritance. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'If one turns away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer is an abomination'—the stunning claim: prayerlessness is not the only problem; prayer accompanied by willful disregard of God's word is rejected. The two-directional posture of receptivity (hearing the law) and address (prayer) must be held together. 'Whoever misleads the upright into an evil way will fall into his own pit'—the seducer shares the fate of the seduced; the person who leads another into sin does not escape the consequences of the sin he enabled. 'The blameless will have a goodly inheritance'—the positive outcome of integrity.

verseByVerse.quote: A rich man is wise in his own eyes, but a poor man who has understanding will find him out. When the righteous triumph, there is great glory, but when the wicked rise, people hide themselves. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A rich man is wise in his own eyes, but a poor man who has understanding will find him out'—money creates the illusion of wisdom; the rich person's opinions are taken seriously because of his wealth. But genuine understanding, found even in poverty, can see through the pretension. 'When the righteous triumph, there is great glory'—the flourishing of the righteous produces a social environment of honor and dignity. 'When the wicked rise, people hide themselves'—the rise of wicked power produces fear; people retreat and conceal themselves when evil governs. The difference in social atmosphere under righteous and wicked leadership is total.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy. Blessed is the one who fears the LORD always, but whoever hardens his heart will fall into calamity. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy'—one of Proverbs' most pastorally crucial verses (cf. 1 John 1:9; Ps. 32:3-5). The concealment of sin does not protect but prevents the mercy that God offers to those who confess. 'Blessed is the one who fears the LORD always'—the fear of God is not situational but constant; the person who maintains reverence for God at all times is characterized by the humility that confession requires. 'Whoever hardens his heart will fall into calamity'—hardening is the accumulation of small refusals to be moved by God's word.

verseByVerse.quote: Like a roaring lion or a charging bear is a wicked ruler over a poor people. A ruler who lacks understanding is a cruel oppressor, but he who hates unjust gain will prolong his days. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Like a roaring lion or a charging bear is a wicked ruler over a poor people'—the two most terrifying predators of the ancient Near East deployed to describe the wicked ruler's relationship to his people. He is not their shepherd but their predator. 'A ruler who lacks understanding is a cruel oppressor'—a lack of wisdom in leadership always expresses itself as some form of cruelty, because wisdom is what constrains power in the service of the people. 'He who hates unjust gain will prolong his days'—the ruler who refuses to exploit his position builds a sustainable reign. Calvin: the longevity of any government is directly proportional to its justice.

verseByVerse.quote: If one is burdened with the blood of another, he will be a fugitive until death; let no one help him. Whoever walks in integrity will be delivered, but he who is crooked in his ways will suddenly fall. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'If one is burdened with the blood of another, he will be a fugitive until death; let no one help him'—the murderer's life is defined by his crime; he cannot escape it and should not be helped to. 'Let no one help him'—the call to communal accountability; sheltering a murderer makes the community complicit. 'Whoever walks in integrity will be delivered, but he who is crooked in his ways will suddenly fall'—the suddenness of the fall is the key detail: the crooked person may walk a long time, but his fall when it comes is abrupt and unexpected. The crisis is not signaled; it simply arrives.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever works his land will have plenty of bread, but he who follows worthless pursuits will have plenty of poverty. A faithful man will abound with blessings, but whoever hastens to be rich will not go unpunished. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Whoever works his land will have plenty of bread, but he who follows worthless pursuits will have plenty of poverty'—the ironic parallel: work produces plenty of bread; the pursuit of emptiness produces plenty of poverty. Both people end up with plenty—the question is what kind. 'A faithful man will abound with blessings'—faithfulness (the daily, undramatic reliability of showing up and doing right) is rewarded with blessing. 'Whoever hastens to be rich will not go unpunished'—the haste is the problem: impatience with God's timeline produces shortcuts that carry their own consequences.

verseByVerse.quote: To show partiality is not good, but for a piece of bread a man will do wrong. A stingy man hastens after wealth and does not know that poverty will come upon him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'To show partiality is not good, but for a piece of bread a man will do wrong'—the cynical realism: judicial partiality is condemned but the proverb acknowledges that it takes very little to corrupt a man. The bribe does not need to be large. 'A stingy man hastens after wealth and does not know that poverty will come upon him'—the miser's obsessive wealth-pursuit produces the opposite of what he intends. His miserliness, cutting him off from the generosity that produces social return, ensures the poverty he most fears. Keller: the person who hoards out of fear of scarcity produces the scarcity he feared.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever rebukes a man will afterward find more favor than he who flatters with his tongue. Whoever robs his father or his mother and says, “That is no transgression,” is a companion of a man who destroys. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Whoever rebukes a man will afterward find more favor than he who flatters with his tongue'—the temporal dimension: the rebuke is hard to receive but produces gratitude over time; flattery feels pleasant but generates eventual contempt. 'Whoever robs his father or his mother and says, That is no transgression'—the self-justifying family thief: he has found a way to rationalize what the fifth commandment directly prohibits. 'Is a companion of a man who destroys'—the destroyer and the rationalizer are moral equivalents; the sophistication of the self-deception does not mitigate the wickedness.

verseByVerse.quote: A greedy man stirs up strife, but the one who trusts in the LORD will be enriched. Whoever trusts in his own mind is a fool, but he who walks in wisdom will be delivered. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A greedy man stirs up strife, but the one who trusts in the LORD will be enriched'—greed is the source of social conflict; the grasping person disturbs every community he enters. 'The one who trusts in the LORD will be enriched'—trust, not grasping, is the path to genuine enrichment. 'Whoever trusts in his own mind is a fool, but he who walks in wisdom will be delivered'—the contrast is between self-reference and the objective standard of wisdom. The self-trusting person has closed his epistemological circle; the wisdom-walker has opened himself to correction. Waltke: deliverance comes through wisdom received, not intelligence deployed.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever gives to the poor will not want, but he who hides his eyes will get many a curse. When the wicked rise, people hide themselves, but when they perish, the righteous increase. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Whoever gives to the poor will not want, but he who hides his eyes will get many a curse'—the positive and negative: generosity to the poor prevents the giver's own lack; willful blindness to poverty brings accumulated curses. 'Hiding your eyes' is the deliberate refusal to see what is there. 'When the wicked rise, people hide themselves, but when they perish, the righteous increase'—the closing symmetry with v.12: social environments are either liberating or terrifying depending on who has power. Righteous governance multiplies the righteous; wicked governance drives them underground.

28.theology:
Conscience, Confession, and the Mercy of God. Verse 13 is Proverbs' most direct engagement with the mechanics of mercy. The theological claim is that God's mercy is available — "will obtain mercy" is not conditional on sinlessness but on confession and forsaking. This is not a works-righteousness framework but a grace framework: mercy is given freely to those who stop hiding. The gospel deepens and perfects this: the confession that obtains mercy is made to a God who has already borne the penalty in Christ. Confession is not appeasement; it is homecoming.

The Boldness of Integrity. Verse 1 presents courage not as a gift of temperament but as a fruit of character. The righteous person is bold as a lion because integrity creates a kind of structural fearlessness — nothing to hide, nothing to protect, no secret that could be exposed. This is the "freedom of a Christian" Luther described: the person who lives before God without pretense is free from the anxiety that haunts those who manage appearances. Paul could say "I am not ashamed of the gospel" (Rom. 1:16) because the gospel had done precisely this work in him.
28.examples:
Then: Ancient Israelite legal culture required witnesses and public testimony; concealment was a constant temptation in legal disputes, land transactions, and communal life. Verse 13 spoke into that culture's pressure to manage reputation through concealment rather than facing consequences through confession. The poor man of verse 6 would have been a recognizable figure: the day laborer with an unblemished reputation in a world where bribery and corruption were available to those with means.

Now: Verse 13 is the most directly applicable verse in this chapter for pastoral ministry. The epidemic of unconfessed sin — hidden addiction, secret financial failure, private moral collapse — produces precisely the restlessness of verse 1. The church that creates a culture of safe confession (not therapeutic oversharing, but covenant honesty) creates the conditions for the boldness of verse 1. And verse 27 ("hides his eyes") describes the posture of studied indifference to need — the averted gaze that has learned, through habit, not to see the homeless person on the corner, not to read the email from the struggling church, not to answer the call from the difficult family member.

29.title: Where There Is No Vision
29.text: <sup>1</sup>He who is often reproved, yet stiffens his neck, will suddenly be broken beyond healing. <sup>2</sup>When the righteous increase, the people rejoice, but when the wicked rule, the people groan. <sup>7</sup>A righteous man knows the rights of the poor; a wicked man does not understand such knowledge. <sup>11</sup>A fool gives full vent to his spirit, but a wise man quietly holds it back. <sup>12</sup>If a ruler listens to falsehood, all his officials will be wicked. <sup>13</sup>The poor man and the oppressor meet together; the LORD gives light to the eyes of both. <sup>15</sup>The rod and reproof give wisdom, but a child left to himself brings shame to his mother. <sup>17</sup>Discipline your son, and he will give you rest; he will give delight to your heart. <sup>18</sup>Where there is no prophetic vision the people cast off restraint, but blessed is he who keeps the law. <sup>20</sup>Do you see a man who is hasty in his words? There is more hope for a fool than for him. <sup>23</sup>One's pride will bring him low, but he who is lowly in spirit will obtain honor. <sup>25</sup>The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe.
29.overview:
Chapter 29 gathers some of Proverbs' most quotable and weighty political and social wisdom, while returning constantly to the themes that have threaded through the whole book: the righteous vs. the wicked, the teachable vs. the stubborn, pride vs. humility. The famous verse 18 — "Where there is no prophetic vision the people cast off restraint" — is frequently misread as a vision-casting management principle, but its Hebrew context is far richer: without divine revelation, without the word of the LORD, human community loses its moral and social coherence.

The chapter also addresses the twin temptations of leadership: listening to falsehood (v.12) and the fear of man (v.25). The ruler who wants to be loved rather than just will tolerate flattery and generate corruption. The person who fears what others think becomes a snare to themselves — and a danger to those they lead. The antidote in both cases is the fear of the LORD, which is its own kind of freedom.

Keller reads verse 25 as one of Proverbs' most penetrating diagnoses of the human condition: the fear of man is not merely a social anxiety but a form of idolatry, a misplaced trust that enslaves precisely because it demands everything and delivers nothing lasting.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 29 — Correction, Justice for the Poor, and the Snare of People-Pleasing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 29 covers the son who accepts correction (v.1,15), the ruler who is just to the poor (v.14), the vision without which people perish (v.18), and one of Proverbs' most theologically searching statements: the fear of man is a snare, but the one who trusts in the LORD is safe (v.25). The chapter builds toward this climax, showing how justice, correction, and governance all depend on whether one fears God or fears men.
verseByVerse.theology: The fear of man (v.25) is the pastoral problem that underlies much of what Proverbs has diagnosed throughout. Every form of flattery, false witness, partiality, and sycophancy is an expression of the fear of man. The antidote is not courage in the conventional sense but the fear of God—a reverence so complete that it eclipses the terror of human disapproval.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 18—where there is no prophetic vision, the people cast off restraint—has been quoted in countless contexts. In its original meaning it concerns the absence of God's word through his prophets; where the word of God is not heard, social restraint dissolves. The connection between the word of God and civil order is theological and empirical.

verseByVerse.quote: He who is often reproved, yet stiffens his neck, will suddenly be broken beyond healing. When the righteous increase, the people rejoice, but when the wicked rule, the people groan. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'He who is often reproved, yet stiffens his neck, will suddenly be broken beyond healing'—the accumulated weight of refused correction: each rejection of reproof hardens the neck further, until the sudden catastrophic breaking. The suddenness is emphasized; the breaking is 'beyond healing.' There is a point past which correction becomes irreversible. 'When the righteous increase, the people rejoice, but when the wicked rule, the people groan'—the political thermometer: the spontaneous emotional response of the community reveals the moral temperature of its leadership. Joy and groaning are not policy judgments but visceral human responses to goodness and oppression.

verseByVerse.quote: He who loves wisdom makes his father glad, but a companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth. By justice a king builds up the land, but he who exacts gifts tears it down. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'He who loves wisdom makes his father glad, but a companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth'—the parental joy-grief contrast recurs; the father's gladness at the wise son is juxtaposed with the ruin that sexual immorality produces. 'By justice a king builds up the land, but he who exacts gifts tears it down'—the micro (family) and macro (kingdom) applications of the same principle: wisdom and justice build; folly and corruption destroy. The king who takes bribes is doing to the nation what the companion of prostitutes does to his inheritance.

verseByVerse.quote: A man who flatters his neighbor spreads a net for his feet. An evil man is ensnared in his transgression, but a righteous man sings and rejoices. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A man who flatters his neighbor spreads a net for his feet'—the flatterer does not merely deceive but entraps; the person who is flattered begins to believe what is not true and makes decisions on that basis, falling into the net the flatterer has spread. 'An evil man is ensnared in his transgression, but a righteous man sings and rejoices'—the contrasting outcomes: the evil person is trapped by his own sin (cf. 26:27), while the righteous person sings. Joy is the characteristic posture of the righteous person, not as a chosen attitude but as the natural overflow of a life in right relationship with God.

verseByVerse.quote: A righteous man knows the rights of the poor; a wicked man does not understand such knowledge. Scoffers set a city aflame, but the wise turn away wrath. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A righteous man knows the rights of the poor'—knowledge here is not merely intellectual but covenantal; the righteous person knows the rights of the poor because he knows the God who created and defends them. 'A wicked man does not understand such knowledge'—the wicked man's moral framework does not contain the poor as a category of concern. 'Scoffers set a city aflame, but the wise turn away wrath'—the scoffer's effect on communities is incendiary; wherever he operates, conflicts ignite. The wise person by contrast is a social fire-suppression system, turning away the anger that would otherwise consume.

verseByVerse.quote: If a wise man has an argument with a fool, the fool only rages and laughs, and there is no quiet. Bloodthirsty men hate one who is blameless and seek the life of the upright. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'If a wise man has an argument with a fool, the fool only rages and laughs, and there is no quiet'—the futility of rational engagement with those who have no commitment to reason or truth. The fool's response is either rage (when challenged) or laughter (when the point lands uncomfortably)—neither of which is genuine engagement. 'Bloodthirsty men hate one who is blameless and seek the life of the upright'—the mysterious reality that innocence provokes murderous hatred in the wicked. This is the pattern from Abel to Christ: the pure life is an implicit indictment of the impure, and the impure react with violence.

verseByVerse.quote: A fool gives full vent to his spirit, but a wise man quietly holds it back. If a ruler listens to falsehood, all his officials will be wicked. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A fool gives full vent to his spirit, but a wise man quietly holds it back'—the contrast of emotional management: the fool's interior life pours out unfiltered; the wise person's interior life is disciplined. 'Quietly holds it back'—the restraint is not suppression but governance; the wise person's emotions serve rather than command. 'If a ruler listens to falsehood, all his officials will be wicked'—the downstream corruption of leadership: when the leader accepts dishonest information, the whole system adjusts to provide more of it. A culture of sycophancy around a leader who rewards flattery is inevitable.

verseByVerse.quote: The poor man and the oppressor meet together; the LORD gives light to the eyes of both. If a king faithfully judges the poor, his throne will be established forever. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The poor man and the oppressor meet together; the LORD gives light to the eyes of both'—the leveling statement: both the poor and their oppressor stand before the same God who gave them both the capacity to see and understand. The oppressor cannot claim ignorance of his victim's humanity. 'If a king faithfully judges the poor, his throne will be established forever'—the highest political wisdom: justice for those who cannot advocate for themselves is the foundation of permanent authority. Waltke: the throne established by justice for the poor is the throne that approximates the divine throne, which is always on the side of the vulnerable.

verseByVerse.quote: The rod and reproof give wisdom, but a child left to himself brings shame to his mother. When the wicked increase, transgression increases, but the righteous will look on their downfall. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The rod and reproof give wisdom, but a child left to himself brings shame to his mother'—the two instruments of formation: the rod (physical correction) and reproof (verbal correction) work together. 'A child left to himself'—not abandoned but undirected, uncorrected, allowed to follow his own will. Such a child does not find wisdom; he finds his own folly. 'When the wicked increase, transgression increases, but the righteous will look on their downfall'—the demographic of wickedness affects the level of transgression in a society; but the righteous person who maintains his integrity lives to see the wicked fall.

verseByVerse.quote: Discipline your son, and he will give you rest; he will give delight to your heart. Where there is no prophetic vision, the people cast off restraint, but blessed is he who keeps the law. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Discipline your son, and he will give you rest'—the rest promised to the parent who endures the difficulty of discipline is real: a well-formed child brings peace. 'Where there is no prophetic vision, the people cast off restraint'—vision here is the word of God through his prophets; where divine revelation is absent or ignored, moral restraint dissolves. This is both sociological and theological. 'Blessed is he who keeps the law'—the individual response to the social crisis: even when the culture has lost its vision, the person who keeps the law is blessed. The righteous remnant is blessed amid the perishing crowd.

verseByVerse.quote: By mere words a servant is not disciplined, for though he understands, he will not respond. Do you see a man who is hasty in his words? There is more hope for a fool than for him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'By mere words a servant is not disciplined, for though he understands, he will not respond'—understanding and obedience are not the same thing; the servant who understands but does not respond requires more than verbal instruction. Discipline requires more than information; it requires consequences. 'Do you see a man who is hasty in his words? There is more hope for a fool than for him'—the hasty speaker is in a worse position than the acknowledged fool because the fool might be reformed; the person addicted to hasty speech has demonstrated a settled pattern of bypassing wisdom. Kidner: the mouth that outruns the mind is harder to stop than open foolishness.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever pampers his servant from childhood will in the end find him his heir. A man of wrath stirs up strife, and one given to anger causes much transgression. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Whoever pampers his servant from childhood will in the end find him his heir'—the servant who has been indulged without proper authority exercised over him will eventually claim what was never his. Formation requires the maintenance of appropriate authority relationships, not the softening of all correction. 'A man of wrath stirs up strife, and one given to anger causes much transgression'—the angry person is the originating point of much social sin; his anger provokes responses that escalate until transgression multiplies. The person given to anger is not just troubled himself but is a generator of trouble for everyone around him.

verseByVerse.quote: One's pride will bring him low, but he who is lowly in spirit will obtain honor. The partner of a thief hates his own life; he hears the curse but discloses nothing. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'One's pride will bring him low, but he who is lowly in spirit will obtain honor'—the kingdom inversion repeated: pride's destination is lowness; humility's destination is honor. This is not a social convention but a divine ordering. 'The partner of a thief hates his own life'—the accomplice is complicit; by association with wickedness he has put his own life at risk. 'He hears the curse but discloses nothing'—the accomplice maintains silence under oath (hearing the curse pronounced on those who withhold testimony) rather than disclose the truth. His loyalty to the thief is really hatred of himself.

verseByVerse.quote: The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe. Many seek the face of a ruler, but it is from the LORD that a man gets justice. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe'—the chapter's theological climax. The fear of man—the terror of disapproval, rejection, or punishment by other humans—is a trap; it distorts decisions, corrupts speech, and prevents faithfulness. 'Whoever trusts in the LORD is safe'—the only security that does not itself become a snare is trust in the LORD. Keller: the antidote to the fear of man is not courage but the fear of God—a reverence so complete that it makes human approval and disapproval comparatively irrelevant. 'Many seek the face of a ruler, but it is from the LORD that a man gets justice'—ultimate justice is not found in any human court.

verseByVerse.quote: An unjust man is an abomination to the righteous, but one whose way is straight is an abomination to the wicked. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'An unjust man is an abomination to the righteous, but one whose way is straight is an abomination to the wicked'—the mutual incompatibility of righteousness and wickedness: each finds the other repulsive. This is not mere social preference but moral necessity; righteousness and wickedness cannot coexist comfortably because they represent fundamentally different orderings of reality. The righteous person's very presence is an indictment of the wicked, and vice versa. Sproul: this explains the world's hostility to genuine holiness—it is not personality conflict but ontological conflict.

29.theology:
Revelation as Social Foundation. Verse 18 makes a claim that should trouble both secular and religious complacency: human society cannot sustain itself by human wisdom alone. It needs the word of God — not as a political imposition but as the moral grammar that makes community coherent. The history of every society that has tried to build order on human reason alone is the history of ideologies that eventually devour themselves. The church is, among other things, the community that keeps the word of God alive in the world — not for its own sake, but for the world's sake.

The Fear of the LORD vs. the Fear of Man. Verses 25 and 23 together present Proverbs' final pastoral diagnosis: pride (placing the self at the center) and fear of man (placing human opinion at the center) are two versions of the same disorder — life organized around anything other than the LORD. Both lead to a snare. Only trust in the LORD is safe, and only humility before the LORD leads to honor. This is the fear of the LORD in its final, practical form.
29.examples:
Then: The ruler who listens to falsehood (v.12) was an immediate practical concern in the ancient Near East — courtiers who told kings what they wanted to hear were a perennial danger, one that the prophets constantly opposed. The fear of man (v.25) was particularly acute for anyone in a patronage society: your livelihood, safety, and social standing all depended on powerful people's approval. Proverbs' call to trust the LORD rather than manage human opinion was countercultural in every ancient context.

Now: Verse 25 is the pastoral verse of the chapter — perhaps of the entire book — for contemporary application. The epidemic of anxiety, people-pleasing, cancel-culture terror, and social-media performance is Proverbs' "fear of man" writ large in digital ink. The pastor who preaches what the congregation wants to hear, the employee who never challenges injustice, the friend who flatters rather than wounds — all are in the snare. The antidote is not indifference but a stronger fear: the fear of the LORD that makes every other fear small.

30.title: The Words of Agur
30.text: <sup>1</sup>The words of Agur son of Jakeh. The oracle. The man declares, I am weary, O God; I am weary, O God, and worn out. <sup>2</sup>Surely I am too stupid to be a man. I have not the understanding of a man. <sup>3</sup>I have not learned wisdom, nor have I knowledge of the Holy One. <sup>4</sup>Who has ascended to heaven and come down? Who has gathered the wind in his fists? Who has wrapped up the waters in a garment? Who has established all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is his son's name? Surely you know! <sup>5</sup>Every word of God proves true; he is a shield to those who take refuge in him. <sup>6</sup>Do not add to his words, lest he rebuke you and you be found a liar. <sup>7</sup>Two things I ask of you; deny them not to me before I die: <sup>8</sup>Remove far from me falsehood and lying; give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the food that is needful for me, <sup>9</sup>lest I be full and deny you and say, "Who is the LORD?" or lest I be poor and steal and profane the name of my God. <sup>18</sup>Three things are too wonderful for me; four I do not understand: <sup>19</sup>the way of an eagle in the sky, the way of a serpent on a rock, the way of a ship on the high seas, and the way of a man with a virgin. <sup>24</sup>Four things on earth are small, but they are exceedingly wise: <sup>25</sup>the ants are a people not strong, yet they provide their food in the summer.
30.overview:
Chapter 30 is the most distinctive unit in the book of Proverbs — the words of Agur son of Jakeh, an otherwise unknown figure whose opening confession is one of the most startling passages in wisdom literature. He begins not with a proverb but with an admission of total inadequacy: "I am too stupid to be a man. I have not learned wisdom, nor have I knowledge of the Holy One" (vv.2–3). This is the fear of the LORD in its most radical form — a profound epistemic humility before the mystery of God.

The rhetorical questions of verse 4 — "Who has ascended to heaven and come down? Who has gathered the wind in his fists?" — echo God's speech from the whirlwind in Job 38–39 and anticipate the Prologue of John: the One who descended and ascended, who commands wind and wave, is the Son of God, the Word made flesh (John 3:13; Eph. 4:9–10). "What is his name, and what is his son's name? Surely you know!" is charged with irony — Agur does not know, but the reader of the whole canon does.

The prayer of verses 7–9 is one of the most theologically mature prayers in Scripture: give me neither poverty nor riches, only enough. It is the prayer of someone who understands the spiritual dangers of both extremes — the arrogance of abundance and the desperation of want. Keller calls it the perfect antidote to prosperity theology and poverty mysticism alike.

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 30 — Agur's Confession of Ignorance, Four-Things Sayings, and the Limits of the Creature
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 30 introduces Agur son of Jakeh, whose opening confession is one of the most startlingly humble passages in the Bible: 'I am too stupid to be a man. I have not the understanding of a man' (v.2). From this posture of radical epistemic humility, Agur moves to praise the reliability of God's word (v.5), requests for moderation in wealth and poverty (vv.7-9), and a series of numerical observations (the 'four things') that celebrate the wonder of creation.
verseByVerse.theology: Agur's theology begins with what he does not know (vv.2-4): a series of impossible questions about the cosmic creator, reminiscent of God's speech to Job (Job 38-41). The answer implicit in the questions is: only God knows, and only God has done these things. The creature who begins with this humility is properly positioned to receive wisdom from above.
verseByVerse.examples: The numerical sayings (threes and fours) are not mere curiosity but a poetic strategy for enlarging perception: the world is full of wonders that the person of limited vision misses. The leech that never says enough, the four never-satisfied things, the four things too wonderful, the four things too little but exceeding wise—all call the reader to attend more carefully to the creation that God made.

verseByVerse.quote: The words of Agur son of Jakeh. The oracle. The man declares, I am weary, O God; I am weary, O God, and worn out. Surely I am too stupid to be a man. I have not the understanding of a man. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The words of Agur son of Jakeh'—a new voice; Agur is otherwise unknown, which may itself be part of the point. He introduces himself with radical self-deprecation: 'I am too stupid to be a man.' This is not false modesty but genuine epistemic humility—he knows the limits of what he knows. 'I am weary, O God'—the Hebrew is difficult; it may be a prayer of exhaustion or a declaration of weariness with human speculation. Either way, Agur begins where wisdom must begin: with the recognition that he is a creature facing an infinite God, and that the gap between them is not bridgeable by his own effort.

verseByVerse.quote: I have not learned wisdom, nor have I knowledge of the Holy One. Who has ascended to heaven and come down? Who has gathered the wind in his fists? Who has wrapped up the waters in a garment? Who has established all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is his son's name? Surely you know! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'I have not learned wisdom, nor have I knowledge of the Holy One'—the creature's confession: wisdom is not self-generated; the Holy One is not accessible by unaided human reason. 'Who has ascended to heaven and come down? Who has gathered the wind in his fists?'—the rhetorical questions are not unanswerable but point to the One who has done all these things: God alone. 'What is his name, and what is his son's name? Surely you know!'—the sharp irony at the end: you who pretend to wisdom, do you know his name? Waltke: this anticipates the revelation of the Son; John 3:13 and Proverbs 8 resonate with this question.

verseByVerse.quote: Every word of God proves true; he is a shield to those who take refuge in him. Do not add to his words, lest he rebuke you and you be found a liar. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Every word of God proves true'—from the confession of human ignorance comes the affirmation of divine reliability: what God has said is thoroughly refined, tested, trustworthy. 'He is a shield to those who take refuge in him'—trust in God's word is protective; the person who relies on Scripture has a defense that no human philosophy can provide. 'Do not add to his words, lest he rebuke you and you be found a liar'—the canonical warning against supplementing divine revelation with human additions; to add to God's word is to imply that it is insufficient, which is a lie about its character. Sproul: Scripture's sufficiency is the necessary corollary of its truthfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: Two things I ask of you; deny them not to me before I die: Remove far from me falsehood and lying; give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the food that is needful for me, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Two things I ask of you'—Agur's prayer is one of the most balanced and self-aware in the entire Bible. 'Remove far from me falsehood and lying'—the first petition: integrity in speech. 'Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the food that is needful for me'—the second: economic moderation. The Hebrew for needful (hoq) means allotted portion—what is appointed for me. Agur is asking for his covenantal share, nothing more. Keller: this is the practical shape of give us this day our daily bread. Agur wants enough—no more, no less—because enough is what enables faithfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: lest I be full and deny you and say, “Who is the LORD?” or lest I be poor and steal and profane the name of my God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Lest I be full and deny you'—the danger of prosperity: satiation produces forgetfulness of God. Who is the LORD—the question of the comfortable, self-sufficient person who has edited God out of his account of life. 'Lest I be poor and steal and profane the name of my God'—the danger of poverty: desperate need produces temptation to sin, and sin among those who bear God's name dishonors him publicly. Agur understands that both extremes threaten his integrity. His prayer asks for the narrow path between them: sufficiency without satiation, provision without excess.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not slander a servant to his master, lest he curse you, and you be held guilty. There is a generation that curses its father and does not bless its mother. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Do not slander a servant to his master, lest he curse you, and you be held guilty'—the warning against meddling in hierarchical relationships by malicious speech; slandering a servant to his master is an act of social sabotage that rebounds on the slanderer. 'There is a generation that curses its father and does not bless its mother'—the first of the generational observations; the violation of the fifth commandment as a characteristic of a whole generation, not merely individual offenders. Waltke: the generation that dishonors parents has broken the intergenerational transmission of wisdom and is therefore in the process of moral self-destruction.

verseByVerse.quote: There is a generation that is pure in its own eyes but is not washed of its filth. There is a generation—how lofty are their eyes, how high their eyelids lift! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'There is a generation that is pure in its own eyes but is not washed of its filth'—the most dangerous form of moral failure: the utter absence of awareness of failure. The generation that has convinced itself of its own purity while covered in filth is beyond normal correction, because correction requires the recognition that something is wrong. 'How lofty are their eyes, how high their eyelids lift!'—pride expressed in the posture of the face; the haughty look is the outward expression of the inner conviction of superiority. Kidner: pride is universally condemned in Proverbs, but this generation has made pride its defining characteristic.

verseByVerse.quote: There is a generation whose teeth are swords, and whose fangs are knives, to devour the poor from off the earth, the needy from among mankind. The leech has two daughters: Give and Give. Three things are never satisfied; four never say, “Enough”: (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'There is a generation whose teeth are swords'—the predatory violence of exploitation made visceral: those who consume the poor are described as if they are devouring them with razor teeth. 'The leech has two daughters: Give and Give'—the transition to the numerical sayings; the leech is the image of insatiable greed. Its daughters are both named the same: all they know how to say is give me more. Waltke: the leech is the emblem of disordered desire—it exists only to take and can never be satisfied.

verseByVerse.quote: Sheol, the barren womb, the land never satisfied with water, and the fire that never says, “Enough.” The eye that mocks a father and scorns to obey a mother will be picked out by the ravens of the valley and eaten by the vultures. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Sheol, the barren womb, the land never satisfied with water, and the fire that never says, Enough'—the four never-satisfied things: death, childless desire, drought, and fire. All are real and profound human experiences of insufficiency. They form a meditation on creaturely limitation and the restlessness that only God can ultimately satisfy. 'The eye that mocks a father and scorns to obey a mother will be picked out by the ravens'—the horror of the image matches the severity of the offense: to mock one's parents is to dishonor the source of life, and the punishment is graphic and total abandonment.

verseByVerse.quote: Three things are too wonderful for me; four I do not understand: the way of an eagle in the sky, the way of a serpent on a rock, the way of a ship on the high seas, and the way of a man with a virgin. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Three things are too wonderful for me; four I do not understand'—the shift from horror to wonder: Agur's vision is wide enough to include both judgment and beauty. 'The way of an eagle in the sky'—flight without visible means of support. 'The way of a serpent on a rock'—motion without limbs. 'The way of a ship on the high seas'—navigation across an apparently featureless expanse. 'The way of a man with a virgin'—the mysterious arising of love between two people. All four share the quality of traceless, inexplicable movement toward something beautiful. Kidner: Agur is the wisdom teacher who finds God's world endlessly astonishing.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the way of an adulteress: she eats and wipes her mouth and says, “I have done no wrong.” Three things make the earth tremble; under four it cannot bear up: (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'She eats and wipes her mouth and says, I have done no wrong'—the adulteress appears in the midst of the wonder-sayings as a dark contrast: the same traceless quality that makes the eagle wonderful makes her dangerous. She leaves no evidence, acknowledges no wrong, and continues. The moral blindness is total. 'Three things make the earth tremble; under four it cannot bear up'—the next numerical saying moves to social disorder: inversions of the proper order of authority and relationship that strain the fabric of human society to breaking point. What follows are four social disorders that the earth cannot bear.

verseByVerse.quote: a slave when he becomes king, and a fool when he is filled with food; an unloved woman when she gets a husband, and a maidservant when she displaces her mistress. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'A slave when he becomes king'—authority without the formation that prepares a person for it is socially explosive. 'A fool when he is filled with food'—prosperity given to the fool only multiplies his folly. 'An unloved woman when she gets a husband'—not that unloved women should not marry, but that unresolved bitterness finding an outlet in marriage creates destructive dynamics. 'A maidservant when she displaces her mistress'—legitimate social order inverted by manipulation rather than genuine merit. Waltke: all four cases involve people gaining position without the character to sustain it; the gap between status and formation is the source of social breakdown.

verseByVerse.quote: Four things on earth are small, but they are exceedingly wise: the ants are a people not strong, yet they provide their food in the summer; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Four things on earth are small, but they are exceedingly wise'—a third class of numerical sayings, celebrating creatures that embody wisdom without strength. 'The ants are a people not strong, yet they provide their food in the summer'—the ant's wisdom is preparation: storing during abundance against the season of scarcity. This is applied human wisdom. The ant does not need to be strong if it is provident; planning compensates for the absence of power. The entire Proverbs work-ethic tradition (6:6-11; 10:5) is compressed into the ant's summer labor.

verseByVerse.quote: the rock badgers are a people not mighty, yet they make their homes in the cliffs; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The rock badgers are a people not mighty, yet they make their homes in the cliffs'—wisdom compensates for weakness by choosing a location that turns weakness into strength. The cliff-dwelling badger is safe precisely because of what it cannot do on open ground: it does not need to be strong if its home is impregnable. Kidner: the badger teaches that knowing where to live is as important as knowing how to fight. The wise person does not try to win fights he cannot win but chooses terrain that makes his weakness irrelevant.

verseByVerse.quote: the locusts have no king, yet all of them march in rank; the lizard you can take in your hands, yet it is in kings' palaces. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The locusts have no king, yet all of them march in rank'—the spontaneous order of a locust swarm: no central authority, yet perfectly coordinated. This is social wisdom without hierarchy—the coordination emerges from shared instinct. 'The lizard you can take in your hands, yet it is in kings' palaces'—the lizard's genius is access: small enough to go anywhere, bold enough to go where few dare. The lizard's presence in the palace is a parable of the resourceful person who compensates for smallness with audacity. Kidner: all four creatures teach the lesson that wisdom and wit can achieve what strength and size cannot.

verseByVerse.quote: Three things are stately in their tread; four are stately in their stride: the lion, which is mightiest among beasts and does not turn back before any; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Three things are stately in their tread; four are stately in their stride'—the final numerical saying celebrates confident, dignified motion: creatures that move with the authority of what they are. 'The lion, which is mightiest among beasts and does not turn back before any'—the lion's courage is not calculated but constitutional; he does not weigh the odds. This is the image used in 28:1 of the righteous who are bold as a lion. Proverbs consistently borrows the lion's confidence as the paradigm of righteous boldness.

verseByVerse.quote: the strutting rooster, the he-goat, and a king whose army is with him. If you have been foolish, exalting yourself, or if you have been devising evil, put your hand on your mouth. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The strutting rooster, the he-goat, and a king whose army is with him'—three more stately creatures: each moves with confidence because of what stands behind or with it. 'If you have been foolish, exalting yourself, or if you have been devising evil, put your hand on your mouth'—the practical application of the chapter's humility theme: recognizing folly or evil, stop talking. The hand on the mouth is the physical gesture of self-restraint after recognizing that what was about to be said—or has already been said—should not be. Waltke: wisdom does not require that you never fail; it requires that you recognize failure and stop.

verseByVerse.quote: For pressing milk produces curds, pressing the nose produces blood, and pressing anger produces strife. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Pressing milk produces curds, pressing the nose produces blood, and pressing anger produces strife'—the triple analogy for the inevitable consequence of sustained provocation: every kind of pressing produces a result. Press milk long enough and it changes form; press the nose and blood flows; press an angry person and strife erupts. The point is not that these results are surprising but that they are predictable. Kidner: the person who keeps poking at an angry situation is not merely unwise but culpable for the strife that results. Stop pressing before the blood flows.

30.theology:
Agur's Confession and the Knowledge of God. Verses 2–4 present what theologians call the via negativa — the approach to God through what cannot be said rather than what can. Agur knows that the gap between human knowledge and divine reality is infinite. The only bridge is revelation — "every word of God proves true" (v.5). This epistemological structure is precisely what Paul describes in 1 Corinthians 1–2: human wisdom cannot know God; God reveals himself through the "foolishness" of the cross. The wise person is the one who, like Agur, knows what they do not know and receives what God has given.

Contentment as Theology. The prayer of verses 8–9 embodies what Paul calls "learned contentment" (Phil. 4:11). Contentment is not a natural temperament but a theological achievement — the fruit of trusting that God's provision, whatever its form, is sufficient. It requires a prior conviction about God's goodness and sovereignty that prosperity theology undermines and asceticism misunderstands. Agur's prayer is the wisest financial philosophy in Scripture: enough, by the hand of a good God.
30.examples:
Then: Agur's confession (vv.2–4) would have been startling in a culture of competing wisdom schools, each claiming to have the key to the good life. A sage who begins by confessing ignorance is subverting the genre from within. The numerical sayings (three things / four things) were a recognized teaching form — the pattern held attention and the final item delivered the punch. The prayer of vv.8–9 addressed a society in which both the prosperity of the few and the poverty of the many were daily realities.

Now: Agur's prayer (vv.8–9) is the most direct rebuke of the prosperity gospel available in the Old Testament — and it also rebukes the romanticization of poverty. "Give me neither" is the prayer of someone who has seen clearly what both do to the soul. In an age of financial anxiety and comparison culture, "feed me with the food that is needful for me" is a radical act of trust. And verse 4's cascading questions ("What is his name, and what is his son's name?") invite the reader who knows the New Testament to feel the full weight of the answer: the name that is above every name (Phil. 2:9).

31.title: The Excellent Wife
31.text: <sup>1</sup>The words of King Lemuel. An oracle that his mother taught him: <sup>2</sup>What are you doing, my son? What are you doing, son of my womb? What are you doing, son of my vows? <sup>3</sup>Do not give your strength to women, your ways to those who destroy kings. <sup>4</sup>It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine, or for rulers to take strong drink, <sup>8</sup>Open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute. <sup>9</sup>Open your mouth, judge righteously, defend the rights of the poor and needy. <sup>10</sup>An excellent wife who can find? She is far more precious than jewels. <sup>11</sup>The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he will have no lack of gain. <sup>20</sup>She opens her hand to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy. <sup>25</sup>Strength and dignity are her clothing, and she laughs at the time to come. <sup>26</sup>She opens her mouth with wisdom, and the teaching of kindness is on her tongue. <sup>28</sup>Her children rise up and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praises her: <sup>29</sup>"Many women have done excellently, but you surpass them all." <sup>30</sup>Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised. <sup>31</sup>Give her of the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates.
31.overview:
Chapter 31 is the crown of the book of Proverbs — and it is breathtaking in its literary architecture. The final poem (vv.10–31) is an acrostic: each verse begins with a successive letter of the Hebrew alphabet, from aleph to taw. The entire alphabet is enlisted to praise this woman. Nothing has been left out; she is the complete embodiment of wisdom.

The poem must be read in light of the whole book. Proverbs 1–9 introduced Lady Wisdom and Lady Folly as two great feminine figures calling to humanity. Lady Folly was seductive, loud, and ultimately fatal (ch.7). Lady Wisdom called from the heights, offered life, and pointed to the fear of the LORD (ch.8–9). Now, in the book's final movement, Lady Wisdom is embodied in a particular woman whose life is the concrete shape of wisdom incarnate: she fears the LORD (v.30), she opens her hand to the poor (v.20), she speaks with wisdom (v.26), she is clothed with strength and dignity (v.25).

This woman is not a job description for wives but a portrait of wisdom as it appears in an actual human life. She is also, for the Christian reader, a type of the church — the bride who fears the Lord, who does good rather than harm, who is praised at the gates. And she points ultimately to Christ himself, the Wisdom of God in whom all the treasures of wisdom are hidden, who "surpasses them all" (v.29).

verseByVerse.ref: Prov. 31 — The Queen Mother's Instruction and the Poem of the Excellent Wife
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 31 closes Proverbs with two remarkable pieces: the words of King Lemuel taught to him by his mother (vv.1-9) and the acrostic poem of the excellent wife (vv.10-31). The queen mother's instruction (vv.1-9) focuses on two dangers for the king: women and wine. The excellent wife poem is an alphabetic acrostic (each verse beginning with successive letters of the Hebrew alphabet), a form that signals comprehensiveness: this is the A to Z of wisdom embodied in a woman.
verseByVerse.theology: The excellent wife (eshet chayil—woman of valor or strength) is the culmination of Proverbs' vision of wisdom. She is the embodiment of everything chapters 1-9 commended as the goal of wisdom's formation. She is also Lady Wisdom made flesh—the personification of wisdom encountered in 1:20-33 and 8:1-36 now taking human form in a household. Waltke: the poem is not a job description for wives but a vision of human flourishing.
verseByVerse.examples: The poem's closing verses (vv.28-31) give the excellent wife what she has not sought: public praise from her husband and children, and honor at the gates. She who worked faithfully without seeking recognition receives it. The woman who fears the LORD (v.30) is contrasted with the woman of beauty who is vain—fear of God outlasts physical beauty and produces lasting honor.

verseByVerse.quote: The words of King Lemuel. An oracle that his mother taught him: What are you doing, my son? What are you doing, son of my womb? What are you doing, son of my vows? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The words of King Lemuel. An oracle that his mother taught him'—the queen mother's instruction is elevated to the status of an oracle; the woman's wisdom is treated with prophetic seriousness. Lemuel is otherwise unknown; some identify him with Solomon. 'What are you doing, my son? What are you doing, son of my womb? What are you doing, son of my vows?'—the triple address escalates: son, son of my body, son of my prayers. The mother's claim is biological, physical, and spiritual. She has the right to speak because she has invested everything in this child.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not give your strength to women, your ways to those who destroy kings. It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine, or for rulers to take strong drink, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Do not give your strength to women, your ways to those who destroy kings'—the queen mother knows the vulnerabilities of kings: sexual appetite and alcohol are the two pathways of royal destruction. History confirms this: powerful men have been undone by both more reliably than by military defeat. 'It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine'—the repetition underlines urgency. What may be acceptable for a private person is not acceptable for the king whose judgment affects thousands. Power demands sobriety of a higher order than ordinary life.

verseByVerse.quote: lest they drink and forget what has been decreed and pervert the justice due to any of the afflicted. Give strong drink to the one who is perishing, and wine to those in bitter distress; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Lest they drink and forget what has been decreed and pervert the justice due to any of the afflicted'—the connection is precise: intoxication produces forgetfulness of what is owed to the afflicted, which produces injustice. The king's first duty is to the poor and afflicted; anything that compromises his capacity to discharge this duty is a royal sin. 'Give strong drink to the one who is perishing, and wine to those in bitter distress'—the counterpoint: what is poison to the powerful may be mercy to the suffering. The person whose life is ending or whose grief is unbearable may need the numbing that the king must avoid.

verseByVerse.quote: let them drink and forget their poverty and remember their misery no more. Open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute. Open your mouth, judge righteously, defend the rights of the poor and needy. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
'Let them drink and forget their poverty and remember their misery no more'—not a prescription for medicating the poor but an acknowledgment that some human suffering is so extreme that temporary relief is merciful. 'Open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute'—the positive royal obligation: speak for those who cannot speak for themselves. The king's voice is the amplification of the voiceless. This is the political theology of Proverbs in miniature: power exists to serve the powerless.

'Open your mouth, judge righteously, defend the rights of the poor and needy'—the queen mother's instruction ends where Proverbs' social ethics consistently end: justice for those who have no other recourse.

verseByVerse.quote: An excellent wife who can find? She is far more precious than jewels. The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he will have no lack of gain. She does him good, and not harm, all the days of her life. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary:
'An excellent wife who can find?'—the rhetorical question signals extreme rarity and value, like wisdom in 8:11. The 'excellent wife' is eshet chayil—woman of valor, strength, capacity. The word chayil is used of warriors and armies; she is a person of formidable strength. 'She is far more precious than jewels'—the same comparison made of wisdom in 3:15 and 8:11. The excellent wife IS the embodiment of wisdom.

'The heart of her husband trusts in her'—the deepest form of human reliance: not merely practical dependence but heart-trust. The husband can commit his full confidence to her. 'He will have no lack of gain'—her competence produces economic sufficiency; trust in her is financially rational. 'She does him good, and not harm, all the days of her life'—the temporal comprehensiveness: not occasionally, not usually, but all the days. This is the covenant faithfulness of hesed applied to the marriage relationship. Waltke: she is the living expression of steadfast love—the attribute of God himself—enacted in a human household.

verseByVerse.quote: She seeks wool and flax, and works with willing hands. She is like the ships of the merchant; she brings her food from afar. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'She seeks wool and flax, and works with willing hands'—the active posture: she seeks, not waits; she works willingly, not grudgingly. The delight of her hands is the delight of wisdom applied to material. 'She is like the ships of the merchant; she brings her food from afar'—she is not limited to what is locally available; her range of provision extends to what requires initiative and enterprise to obtain. The merchant-ship comparison is powerful: she operates with the energy, ingenuity, and reach of commercial enterprise in service of her household.

verseByVerse.quote: She rises while it is yet night and provides food for her household and portions for her maidens. She considers a field and buys it; with the fruit of her hands she plants a vineyard. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'She rises while it is yet night'—not the sluggard's bed but the predawn rising of one whose vision of the day's work energizes her before the sun. 'Provides food for her household and portions for her maidens'—she thinks of others before herself; the household and the servants are provided for before she turns to her own needs. 'She considers a field and buys it'—she is an investor: she evaluates, decides, and acts in the economic sphere with authority and competence. 'With the fruit of her hands she plants a vineyard'—her labor produces capital that she reinvests in a long-term productive enterprise.

verseByVerse.quote: She dresses herself with strength and makes her arms strong. She perceives that her merchandise is profitable. Her lamp does not go out at night. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'She dresses herself with strength and makes her arms strong'—not merely metaphorical: she is physically capable, working with her body as well as her mind. The physical strength is the outward expression of the inner strength (chayil) that defines her. 'She perceives that her merchandise is profitable'—she evaluates outcomes; she is not naively generous but discerning about what is working. 'Her lamp does not go out at night'—the lamp burning through the night signals industry, vigilance, and the refusal of the sluggard's early retirement. She works as long as the work requires.

verseByVerse.quote: She puts her hands to the distaff, and her hands hold the spindle. She opens her hand to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'She puts her hands to the distaff, and her hands hold the spindle'—the specific craft of spinning: her hands are literally productive, creating textile from raw material. 'She opens her hand to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy'—the same hands that work the spindle open in generosity. Her industry is not self-consuming; it produces surplus that she gives away. Kidner: the excellent wife is not a workaholic who hoards the fruits of her labor but a woman whose productivity flows into both her household and the community's most vulnerable members.

verseByVerse.quote: She is not afraid of snow for her household, for all her household are clothed in scarlet. She makes bed coverings for herself; her clothing is fine linen and purple. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'She is not afraid of snow for her household, for all her household are clothed in scarlet'—her planning eliminates anxiety: she has prepared for the worst weather, so snow holds no fear. 'All her household are clothed in scarlet'—double clothing of the finest quality; scarlet was expensive. Her household's clothing reflects her own competence and generosity. 'She makes bed coverings for herself; her clothing is fine linen and purple'—she also cares for herself: fine linen (the fabric of the priestly garments, Ex. 28) and purple (the color of royalty). She adorns herself with dignity, not neglect.

verseByVerse.quote: Her husband is known in the gates when he sits among the elders of the land. She makes linen garments and sells them; she delivers sashes to the merchant. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Her husband is known in the gates when he sits among the elders of the land'—she has made his public life possible by managing the private sphere so completely. His prominence in civic affairs is partly her creation. Waltke: the excellent wife is not hidden but publicly impactful through her husband's freedom to engage in civic life. 'She makes linen garments and sells them; she delivers sashes to the merchant'—she is an entrepreneur: producing goods for the commercial market, negotiating with merchants. Her economic activity extends beyond the household into the marketplace.

verseByVerse.quote: Strength and dignity are her clothing, and she laughs at the time to come. She opens her mouth with wisdom, and the teaching of kindness is on her tongue. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Strength and dignity are her clothing'—the ultimate garment is not linen or purple but character itself. 'She laughs at the time to come'—not frivolity but the deep confidence of the person who has prepared well and trusts the God who governs the future. The laughter is the opposite of anxiety; it is faith expressing itself as joy in the face of uncertainty. 'She opens her mouth with wisdom, and the teaching of kindness is on her tongue'—she is the embodiment of Lady Wisdom from chapter 9; her speech is characterized by wisdom and hesed. Keller: she is the wisdom of chapters 1-9 made human.

verseByVerse.quote: She looks well to the ways of her household and does not eat the bread of idleness. Her children rise up and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praises her: (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'She looks well to the ways of her household and does not eat the bread of idleness'—the comprehensive oversight: she attends to the whole household, not just one part of it. 'Does not eat the bread of idleness'—the bread of idleness is the sluggard's diet; she will not touch it. 'Her children rise up and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praises her'—the recognition comes from those who know her best. The ultimate commendation is not public acclaim but the praise of those who have lived with her and experienced what she is. This is more reliable than any outside evaluation.

verseByVerse.quote: “Many women have done excellently, but you surpass them all.” Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Many women have done excellently, but you surpass them all'—the husband's tribute places her in the context of other excellent women and affirms her supremacy. He has known others and he has known her, and his verdict is clear. 'Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised'—the contrast that reorders all aesthetic and social values: charm lies about character; beauty dissolves with time. But the fear of God is the foundation that remains and that deserves permanent praise. Sproul: this verse is not anti-beauty but rightly ordered: beauty is a gift but not an identity; the fear of God is an identity that beauty cannot provide.

verseByVerse.quote: Give her of the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Give her of the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates'—the closing command: give her what she has earned, and let her works be her testimony in the most public place in the city. The gates—where legal proceedings happen, where elders gather, where commerce is transacted—are the place of her ultimate praise. She who worked faithfully without seeking recognition receives it in the most public forum. And so Proverbs ends: wisdom, embodied in a woman who fears the LORD, praised at the city gates. The book that began with 'fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom' ends with the woman whose fear of the LORD is the source of a life that all must honor.

31.theology:
Lady Wisdom Embodied. The structural genius of Proverbs is now fully visible: the book opens with a father urging his son to seek wisdom and avoid folly (chs.1–9), personified as two women. The book closes with wisdom embodied in a particular woman whose final credential is the fear of the LORD (v.30). The frame is complete. Lady Wisdom is not an abstraction; she is what a human life looks like when it is ordered toward God. For the Christian reader, Christ is the fullness of this embodiment: "Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption" (1 Cor. 1:30).

The Fear of the LORD as Crown. Proverbs 1:7 begins: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom." Proverbs 31:30 ends: "a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised." The book is a vast unfolding of what lies between these two statements — the practical wisdom of a life lived in the fear of God. That fear is not dread but the relational posture of the creature before the Creator, the redeemed before the Redeemer. It issues in generosity, diligence, faithful speech, care for the poor, and the peculiar joy of the woman who laughs at the time to come. This is Proverbs' final word, and it is the beginning of the gospel.
31.examples:
Then: The acrostic form (aleph to taw) was a literary statement: this is everything, the complete alphabet of a wise life. Israelite readers would have recognized the woman of chapter 31 as the antithesis of Lady Folly (ch.7) and the embodiment of Lady Wisdom (ch.8). Her economic activity — buying fields, trading, making linen garments — was entirely realistic for a woman of means in the ancient Near East, where women managed households that were also small enterprises. Her praise "at the gates" was public honor in the place where civic life happened.

Now: Chapter 31 has sometimes been weaponized as a productivity checklist for Christian women. The poem resists this. It is not a job description but a portrait — and its crown is not efficiency but the fear of the LORD. Any reading that focuses on the woman's activities while ignoring verse 30 has misread the poem. More broadly, the chapter invites readers to ask: what does wisdom look like in a full, concrete human life? The answer is not a set of rules but a person — generously open-handed, dignified under pressure, laughing at the future, speaking with wisdom and kindness. The church is called to embody this portrait collectively: the community that fears the LORD, opens its hand to the poor, and lets its works praise it in the gates of the city it inhabits.
